Round 2001.decision_summary:
Item 473 -- the aggregation planes cannot reach a table tool -- is closed for
the keyexpr throughput plane, and the round opened by re-establishing the item
rather than trusting it.

Its evidence was "grep found no CSV emitter", which is the class that produced
three false filings in Round 1996. The authoritative population is the SHIPPING
ENUM: `Format` has exactly `Text` and `Json`, with 84 consumption sites. So the
item was true -- and the same measurement said something the item did not: 84
match arms is what makes `Format::Csv` the WRONG shape. A CSV stream holds one
table, and the report is a nested document; rendering it as one would be a
third opinion about what a row is before a single row was written.

So the rendering is not of the report. It is of a PLANE, and it derives from
the same typed tables `census_json` derives from -- which is what the item's own
prohibition asked for. `census_csv::keyexprs_csv` reads `ThroughputTable` and
`KeyexprRow` through the same accessors, so a row here is a row there by
construction rather than by agreement, and the leg that pins it compares the two
renderings of ONE table instead of comparing either to a transcript.

Three decisions worth naming. `--csv` REPLACES the report, because a second
table appended after the first is a file no reader of this format can open --
which is also why it is refused beside `--json`. `--csv <plane>` turns that
plane's census ON, because a rendering of a table the run never folded emits a
header and no rows, and that is what an empty capture looks like. And
`share_bp` is an EMPTY field, never `0`: `census_json` emits null there because
a zero would read as "this topic carried nothing", and CSV has no null.

The scope is one plane and the entry says so. `CsvPlane::NAMES` is the set's
single source, the refusal lists it rather than saying "unknown", and the other
four planes are one enum line and one emit each.

recur, because a previous round had built the thing that refuses it.

C1bz. The budget-lowering note R1998 wrote went INSIDE the `budget="..."`
string. Everything between those quotes is data -- the reader splits on

not a workspace member`. ⚠ THE LOCAL PRE-PUSH SUBSET COULD NOT HAVE SEEN IT,
and says so in its own output: "the stale-budget-line check needs the full
lane". The subset checks counts against budgets; the membership check is the
full lane's. So this is a shape that is structurally invisible before a push.

Round 2003.decision_summary:
Round 2000 measured that three of the six items filed in Round 1996 were false
and asked whether the rest of the roster was suspect. This round answers with
the only thing that can: it PROBED the five oldest open entries, and all five
are still true.

That inverts the worry. The failure was not the register's age; it was the act
of filing without probing, which is exactly what the rule those rounds produced
already says. An entry written from a run stays true; one written from a
reading was never true. The old entries were written by rounds that had just
done the work.

Two of the five gave up something the register did not know it had.

239 -- the misleading error a consumer gets when `dissect` is off -- reads as
cheap and is not, and the reason is a language fact: `compile_error!` is not
lazy. Putting one on the off arm fails EVERY default build, and declaring the
module unconditionally so the error can be nicer means compiling a body that
must not compile. There is no obvious prescription, which is why the item has
outlived several rounds that would happily have taken a cheap one. That is now
in the item rather than in a reader's head.

243 -- `SkipCensus::held` is a class nobody judges -- has a POPULATION OF ONE
today: `held()` returns `ip_fragment_pending` and nothing else. So a gate built
by "add a second member and check it is judged" would be building its own
subject, and the honest shape is this workspace's standing one: PIN THE SET, so
a second member reds until somebody judges it.

242's proposed mechanisation has the same hazard from the other side. Its own
text says the rows whose reason names a JSON key could assert that key's absence
on the far surface -- but no row's reason names a key today, so that gate would
be green over nothing.

None of the five moved the count, and the round says so: what it added is an
EVIDENCE LINE on each, naming the command that establishes it and marked RUN or

nothing in the register recorded it.

Round 2004.decision_summary:
Round 2003 read three reds on main and reported them as ONE debt already paid.
That was right about two of them and this round found it was wrong about the
third, by doing what the rule says and reading each run's own jobs rather than
the first one's: `9b612207` fails on FOUR lanes, not two. C1bn and C1bz are
R1998's, fixed. `Layer C1 — cargo test --workspace` and `Layer C0mut` are
Round 2001's, and nobody had looked.

The C1 failure is one line: `missing field 'csv' in initializer of
wz_analyze::Request`, in `wz-replay`. Round 2001 widened a PUBLIC struct,
changed `wz-analyze` and `wz-capture`, and the pre-push hook tests the crates a
push CHANGES -- so `wz-replay`, which merely depends on one of them, was never
built locally and has not compiled since that push.

C0mut is not a second defect and this entry will not count it as one. Its suite
includes `wz-replay`, so it refused: "the UNMUTATED tree is not green
(uncompilable). Over a red tree every mutant is red and this sweep would report
every leg load-bearing while measuring nothing." A gate that declines to measure
over a broken tree is a gate working.

THE PART WORTH FREEZING IS WHERE THE WARNING WAS. Inside that very initializer,
above the field that broke, R311y857 had left a paragraph describing this exact
sequence: the field arrived, this initializer was not updated, wz-replay had not
compiled since, and nothing local caught it because the hook tests what a push
changes. A session read that file, added a field below the paragraph, and
reproduced it. A COMMENT IS NOT A GATE -- the same finding Round 1994 made about
a discovery floor whose instruction to bump it sat beside the constant and was
not followed.

The fix is one field. The RECURRENCE is filed as item 475 rather than fixed,
and deliberately: pre-push is what R311y386 ratified as a FAST gate and
explicitly not a CI mirror, `doclink_dependents.py` records that a core crate's
reverse dependencies are nearly the whole workspace, and widening the hook to
build dependents would overturn that policy. Three candidate shapes are in the
item and choosing between them is closer to an owner decision than to debt work,
so it is filed in the owner-decision class.

Round 2006.decision_summary:
Item 243 is closed. R311y860 gave `SkipCensus::total()` the property that a
field belonging to NO class drops out of the sum and reds; the hole it left is
one step inside, and 243 is that step: a field ADDED to the `held` class is

`held` is the class whose fate is not the census's to know. Its members are
counted at the door, at the one moment nothing can yet say whether the rest of
the datagram arrives, and the verdict is reached elsewhere -- for the one member
there is today, by the reassembly table, because only it knows how a chain
ENDED. A member with no elsewhere is therefore a skip that quietly means
nothing: it inflates a total and answers no question.

TWO MECHANISMS, AND NEITHER WORKS ALONE. A destructure makes a new field on
`SkipCensus` a compile error in the test, so the table cannot silently stop
covering the struct -- that is the half R311y860 already taught this file. The
new half is a table naming, for each field the class ACTUALLY SUMS, the thing
that judges it.

The set is DERIVED, not transcribed, and that is the whole design. Each field is
set to one in isolation and `held()` is asked whether it moved; the members fall
out of the accessor rather than out of a list someone typed. A transcript would
agree with itself and go on agreeing after the accessor changed. Because it is
derived, a round that moves a field into `held` reds HERE without touching this
test, and the red is the demand to name a judge.

The population is one, which is exactly why the gate had to be about the SET.
Round 2003 measured that and said so; building a second member to test against
would have meant the gate constructing its own subject.

The probe is asserted alive rather than assumed. `held()` returning zero for
everything would make the comparison pass over two empty lists -- this
workspace's most expensive recurring shape -- so the same derivation is run over
`bytes_absent()` and the two sets are required to be non-empty and disjoint. A
derivation reading nothing cannot satisfy that.

Item 244 is closed. The completeness verdict counted abandoned fragment chains
and never measured them, so `3 unfinished` reached an operator who could not
tell three ARP-sized datagrams from three 64 KiB ones -- a rounding error and a
real hole in the capture, reported identically.

The item said where the number was free and where it stops being possible: the
pieces sit in the reassembly table WITH their lengths right up to the moment
they are dropped. Both drop sites now take the measurement inside themselves --
the deadline's `retain` predicate, and the entry the concurrency cap's `remove`
hands back. One line later the entry is gone and the question cannot be asked.

WHAT IS COUNTED IS WHAT WAS WRITTEN, not what was allocated, and that
distinction is the difference between a number and a lie. A chain whose only
piece landed at offset 60 000 has a buffer grown to 60 002 and holds two bytes.
Reporting the buffer would tell an operator a 60 KiB hole exists where two bytes
were received, which is worse than reporting nothing at all -- so the sum is
over the written runs, which are the evidence.

The new figure is summed from the same three sources as the chain count, in the
same order -- expired, evicted, still open -- so the two numbers are about one
set rather than about two that happen to move together. It reaches both health
renderings beside the count, on the same line in the text, because a reader who
saw only the count has been told the wrong half.

reader to discover. It counts bytes this reader RECEIVED and could not use. The
pieces that never arrived are not in it and cannot be: their length was never on

half of that is now written down rather than left implicit: THIS TREE CANNOT
CHECK THE KERNEL'S CLAIM, because no kernel is here. What it can check is the

named -- and the op space is swept the same way, returning exactly
`AF_VSOCK_OP_PAYLOAD`. Saying which half was measured is the closure; claiming

hand-written encapsulation list. This round answered "what is furniture" by
enumeration; 250 is the same question asked of "what is a tunnel", and the

Round 2010.decision_summary:
Item 250 is NOT closed and this round does not claim it. What it did is find
three encapsulations the list had been missing, and pin the set so it cannot
shrink without saying so.

The item is that `is_encapsulation` is ten numbers somebody typed, so an
encapsulation it omits is furniture BY OMISSION -- filed as "could not have
carried a session" for no reason but absence, which is precisely the defect
R311y862 measured on protocol 4 and this item says survives one number away.

Asking the item's own question of IANA's assignments turned up three:
protocol 55 (MOBILE, RFC 2004 minimal encapsulation -- the body is an IP
datagram behind a short forwarding header), 98 (ENCAP, RFC 1241, an
encapsulation by its own name), and 108 (IPComp, RFC 3173 -- the body is a
COMPRESSED IP datagram, which this build cannot open, making it a tunnel not
opened rather than a protocol that terminates). Each was reaching the furniture
arm. Each carries bytes that could be a session.

The classification is now pinned rather than asserted: the set is DERIVED by
sweeping the predicate, so a number removed from it reds without anyone editing
the test, and a one-digit typo was used to prove that. The partition is also
shown TOTAL -- 2 transports, 13 encapsulations, 241 furniture, no number in two
classes, all 256 accounted for.

⚠ AND THE 241 IS THE ITEM, restated with a number attached. Each of those
carries the claim "could not have carried a session", and for ICMP and IGMP that
claim is argued while for the rest it is inherited from absence. Nothing here
distinguishes the two, because the honest gate is a comparison against IANA's
table and this tree has none.

Round 2011.decision_summary:
Item 252 CLOSED. A tunnel's CARRIER addresses were known at walk time and
discarded, so three different topologies rendered as one page: a session
tunnelled from site A, the same session tunnelled from site B, and the same
session on the wire it was addressed on.

The discard was one line. `walk_ip_chain` stepped through each carrier with
`cursor = d.payload; continue;`, and the header's addresses exist only at that
instant -- everything downstream is keyed by the INNER header, correctly, or a
tunnel's every session would collapse into one flow. So the carrier reached no
row, no counter and no line, and the report could not say a capture came off a
concentrator at all.

The fix records the chain rather than the outermost hop. `TunnelHop` is one
carrier (its two addresses and the protocol number that made it a carrier) and
`Tunnel` is the chain, outermost first, bounded by the walk's own depth limit.
The outermost pair alone would have answered "which site" for a one-hop tunnel
and lied about a two-hop one: an overlay inside a VPN has two sites, and
reporting only the outer names the concentrator every tenant shares.

BOTH DOORS STAMP IT, and that is the half a naive fix leaves behind. A whole
packet reaches `decapsulate`; a fragmented carrier never does -- the outer
header is consumed by the reassembler before `transport_from_ip` is called, so
a chain rebuilt inside that function starts one hop short. That is also the
COMMONEST shape, since a carrier adds bytes to a packet already at the path
MTU, so the door left out would have been the one that mattered. `start_tunnel`
folds the caller's chain in, exactly as `start_depth` and `start_checksum`
already did, and the fragment table carries the first piece's chain across
reassembly.

Per flow rather than per packet, because that is the question a reader has, and
with two facts a bare list would have dropped: whether the flow was ALSO seen
arriving direct (what a capture at a tunnel egress looks like), and whether
more distinct chains arrived than the reader keeps.

⚠ AN EXISTING GREEN TEST WAS ASSERTING THE DEFECT.
`a_pico_raweth_frame_reads_the_same_inside_a_gretap_tunnel_as_outside` compared
the tunnelled and bare readings as whole values with `assert_eq!`. That was the
right claim about the PARSE and the wrong one about the packet: the tunnelled

layer decided is equal and the carrier is the ONE thing that differs, from both

different carrier folded into the same entry unseen. That was reasoning. A
fragmented carrier is fragmented at the CARRIER's own header, so the carrier's
addresses are what the fragment key holds: two carriers are two keys and
neither datagram completes. The correction is a test, not a comment.

Round 2014.decision_summary:
Item 261 CLOSED. `strip_gre` read the `C` bit only to SIZE the header and
stepped over the two bytes it announced, so the carrier's own integrity was the
one judgement this reader never made -- and, because it was never made, never
reported as absent either. Every other verdict here is reported; that is what
`Checksums` is for.

MEASURED first. A throwaway probe fed two captures that differ in one field:
one GRE header carrying checksum `0xDEAD`, one carrying `0x0000`. The answer
was `identical page: true`, with identical health. Corruption present, page
silent -- the item, verbatim, before anything was touched.

The verdict is RFC 2784 §2.5's: the field holds the one's-complement checksum
of the GRE header and the payload packet, so the sum over the whole span with
the field in place must be zero. The same property `ipv4_header_ok` already
uses, over a different span, with the primitive this file already had.

It is FOLDED across the chain rather than read off the outermost carrier, for
the reason the walk folds `ip`: reporting only the outer would let a tunnel
whose inner header is corrupt read as verified. Three states and each is a real
answer -- `Some(false)` if any carrier that had a checksum failed, `Some(true)`
if at least one had one and all passed, `None` if none did, which is the

Item 262 CLOSED. `MAX_ENCAPSULATION_DEPTH` counts CARRIERS, and R311y864 made

bound was written when every carrier was an IP header; a GRE carrier's header
is not the same size, and a GRETAP carrier is not even the same SHAPE, since it
adds a whole Ethernet header the count never sees.

CLOSING IT MEANT RECORDING THE CHOICE, NOT CHANGING IT, and the distinction is
the round's whole argument.

A carrier is the right unit for what this bound protects: the walk's own
RECURSION, which advances once per carrier whatever the header weighs. Bounding
header BYTES would bound a different quantity — and worse, it would make the
limit depend on GRE's optional fields, Key and Sequence and Checksum, which the
SENDER chooses. A bound a sender can move is not a bound. So the unit stands.

What was missing was the record, and a record nobody can check is the same
class of nothing this workspace keeps finding. So the asymmetry is measured
rather than asserted: the same four carriers cost 80 header bytes as IPIP, 96
as GRE and 152 as GRETAP. Equal counts, unequal cost, all three admitted, one
more of any of them refused. A round that changes the unit now fails a test and
has to say what it did.

Round 2046.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 419: the auth foreign witness held exactly ONE value against
anything -- the username -- and the item said what that left open. This round
closes both halves of it, and the reason it was worth taking first is that its
prerequisite was not a test at all but a hole in what the analyser surfaced.

The item's two claims, both confirmed by RUNNING the witness before touching
anything rather than by reading it:

  A Init/usrpwd enc=Some(1) read=[]        <- the acceptor's Z64 CHALLENGE
  B Open/usrpwd ... hmac=<32 byte(s)>      <- the initiator's ANSWER

The challenge showed no reading AT ALL. Not because the dissector dropped it --
`SCALAR_Z64_BODIES` declares `(Auth, usrpwd)` scalar for a good reason, and
`walk_ext_entry`'s Z64 arm pushes the value unconditionally -- but because the
witness harness folded `value` away as ENVELOPE for every row alike. The one
number in this handshake that keys everything else was invisible to every
assertion in the file. And the `hmac` was checked only for being a non-empty
ZBuf of its own, which is a claim about LENGTHS: any other 32-byte span
satisfied it, and `user` being the FIRST of the two records meant nothing
constrained where the second one started.

⚠ WHAT IS BOUND HERE IS NOT PRODUCER PARITY, and the distinction is the whole
point. `usrpwd_zenohd_interop.rs` already proves wz COMPUTES this digest
correctly -- a wrong one fails the handshake, so authentication succeeding IS
that proof. What no amount of successful authentication can show is that the
DISSECTOR names the right bytes. That is what a mis-framed walker gets away
with, and it is what this round pins.

Round 2050.decision_summary:
ITEM 390 CLOSES. R2049 took the `shm` half and measured why the JOIN half could
not follow through the same door; this round built the door.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY MISSING WAS A HARNESS, NOT A CONFIG. Upstream carries
`ext_qos` on a Join only when `next_sns.len() == Priority::NUM`
(`multicast/link.rs:476-490`), which needs a MULTICAST transport with
`transport/multicast/qos/enabled`. Multicast is UDP datagrams and
`wire_tap::tap_proxy` is a TCP relay, so the three witnesses sharing
`ext_bodies` could not reach the body at all — and this tree had no multicast
datagram capture of any kind. `synthesise_multicast_pcap` is the datagram
sibling of the TCP synthesiser, written beside it in the module whose whole
justification is that the envelope rules are ONE fact.

AND THE TOPOLOGY IS THE SIMPLEST IN THE FAMILY, once the harness exists: a
group needs no relay, so the test joins it. It is also the only ONE-directional
capture here, correctly so, because a Join is an announcement rather than an
exchange.

THE WHOLE DATAGRAM PLANE IS GRADED, NOT ONLY THE WALKER. The recorded
datagrams are wrapped as a pcap and handed to `wz_capture::Dissection`, so the
L2 multicast MAC mapping, IPv4, UDP, the datagram framing decision and the
zenoh observer are all on the path. Feeding `dissect_transport_message` the
bytes directly would have been shorter and would have graded one function
instead of the route a reader opens a capture through.

⛔⛔ AND THE SHARED HARNESS HAD A HOLE THAT ONLY A MULTICAST CAPTURE COULD
SHOW. `ext_bodies::MESSAGE_NAMES` had no `Join`, so the Join's `qos` — walked
correctly, every field right — was attributed to `?`. Not a WRONG carrier: a

⛔⛔⛔ THE PUSH NOTIFICATION SAID `exit code 0` WHILE THE PUSH HAD FAILED. The
status file said 1, and `git ls-remote origin main` still pointed at the red
commit. A background job's completion status is the COMPOUND command's, and the
compound ended with a successful `echo`. This is the exact trap the operating
rule was written for, and here it caught a real failure rather than a
hypothetical one. ▶ Judge a push from its own status file and from `ls-remote`.
The notification is a wake signal, not a verdict.

⛔⛔ AND THE PUSH FAILED FOR A REASON THE SEPARATION ITSELF CREATED. The pin bump
was deliberately left OUT of the commit -- unstaged, so it would land as its own
change. But a submodule's revision is WORKING-TREE state, not index state, so
"kept out of the commit" did not keep it out of the commands that commit ran.
The build wrapper compared the two trees, found this one at the new rev and the
build machine at the old, and refused. That refusal then failed the push of an
UNRELATED commit.

And the refusal was not bad luck: it is STRUCTURAL for an unstaged submodule
bump. The wrapper reconciles a far side by running `git submodule update
--recursive --force` there, which can only check out the revision the
SUPERPROJECT RECORDS. While the bump is unstaged, the recorded revision is still
the old one, so the far side is pinned to the state this tree has just left and
no amount of syncing can close the gap. Committing the bump is what makes the
two reconcilable -- which is why this round pushes them together rather than
keeping the separation it started with. ▶ A change held back from a commit is
still present in every lane that commit runs, and a submodule held back is
additionally UNREACHABLE to anything that reconciles by the recorded rev. Do NOT
paper over that refusal by forcing the build local: the hook's own comment says
a refusal is a verdict, and re-running the gate locally is how a hook reports
green about a tree nobody checked.

manifests is what says so. ▶ "Does this upstream change reach us" is a question
about OUR manifests. The shape of the upstream diff cannot answer it, and an
upstream diff that looks irrelevant is the most persuasive way to get it wrong.

any host-processor symbol across `crates/` and `out/`. The rest of that crate's
diff is doc-citation renames, `W3C SCXML B.2.8.1` becoming `§scxml-B-2-8-1`.

THE DEBT SAID ONE LINE. IT WAS 48. Open debt 490 read: the client role has no
name in `--help` -- `--connect` is it, and the fix is a line. The instance was
real. The class it belongs to is that 48 of the 106 flags this binary accepts
are never printed by `--help` at all, and among them, until this round, was the
ONLY run mode that announces the zenoh router role on the wire.

⚠ AND THE FIRST MEASUREMENT OF THAT CLASS WAS WRONG, in a way worth naming
because the signal was visible before the answer was. Sweeping `args.rs` gave
106 -> no, gave 37 parser flags and 19 absences. But the same diff run backwards
-- flags PRINTED that no parser names -- returned 42, which is not a plausible
residue for a help text. A large residue in BOTH directions is what a wrong
population looks like. The parser surface is `main.rs` (98) plus `args.rs` (37),
union 106, and only then do the two directions settle: 48 absent one way, 3 the
other, and those 3 are prose prefixes (`--declare-`, `--on-remote-`) plus
`--features`. ▶ Check a set difference in BOTH directions. The direction you did
not ask about is the one that tells you the population is wrong.

▶ THE INSTANCE IS PAID, AND THREE SIBLINGS WITH IT. `--connect` now says it is
the zenoh client role and that there is no `--client` flag to look for.
`--listen` and `--peer` name their peer role. `--router` now says outright that
DESPITE ITS NAME it announces peer, not router -- which is the sharper defect,
because a wrong name is worse than a missing one and `NodeKind::Router` maps to
`WhatAmI::Peer`. And `--router-hat` gets an entry at all: it is the one mode
that puts the router role on the wire, and it was not in the help text.

⛔⛔ THE FILE ALREADY ARGUED WHY THIS IS A DEFECT -- ABOUT A DIFFERENT LIST.
`usage.rs` says of its feature-key list: "an omission does not read as silence;
it reads as 'that flag is off'". The same sentence reaches the flag list, which
is the bigger of the two, and nothing enforced it. Whole families are missing:
every `--tls-*`, every `--quic-*`, every `--storage-*`. Those are precisely the
answers to "zenoh does this -- does wz?", and the help text says no by omission.

▶ A RATCHET, NOT A FIX, AND THE SET IS PINNED RATHER THAN THE COUNT. Deciding
all 48 is its own work and some may deserve to stay hidden; what must not happen
is a 49th joining unnoticed. So the gate fails on a new absence AND on a
documented one, telling the author to shrink the list in the same commit -- a
backlog that cannot shrink is a count, not a ratchet. Filed as open debt 494.

⛔ ONE TRAP THE LIST ITSELF CREATED, AVOIDED BY CONSTRUCTION. The pinned set
lives inside `args.rs`, which the sweep reads. Written as `"--acl-deny"`
literals it would have entered its OWN population, so a flag deleted from the
parser would still look present and the gate would go quietly blind. The entries

⚠ AND THE ROLE RULE HAD TO BE A PHRASE, NOT A WORD. Asserting that `--router`'s
entry "contains peer" passed BEFORE the fix -- "multi-peer router mode" already

the old text said. A rule that its own defect satisfies is not a rule.

true of no tree that ever existed. It cost only a re-run here, but the shape is

⚠ THE RE-RUNS THEN DIED TWICE, AND "KILLED" WAS NOT A VERDICT EITHER. Layer 0

Round 2069.decision_summary:
TWO HOSTED REDS ON 18c6c441, IN TWO DIFFERENT JOBS, AND THEY WERE ONE CAUSE
WEARING TWO NAMES. `validate + codegen` failed at "Layer C0 (armed) — gate
provenance citations resolve"; `validate + verify + test` failed at "Layer C0 —
binary-dep test" and again at "Budget margin". Reading ci.yml settles the first
pair: the step called "binary-dep test" runs `run-ci.sh --layer C0`, the whole
layer, and its name is historical. So both C0 steps died on the same lint.

⛔⛔ THE LINT WAS RIGHT AND R2064 WAS WRONG. `home-path-scan.sh` shipped with no
provenance citation, so nothing could say mechanically which register item it
answers for -- which is the entire point of that lint, and the reason it exists
is that a gate written in a hurry lands there or nowhere. This one landed there.
The citation is `(no register item)`, and that needed a sentence rather than a
token: the class was raised by the owner directly, the residue it could NOT
close (137 home-path lines already inside the append-only ledger) is item 492 in
the operator's register, and that register lives OUTSIDE the store -- which is
what this citation resolves against. Naming a store id would have meant
inventing one, and that collision has been paid for here before.

⛔⛔⛔ AND THE THIRD RED WAS A LIE THE GATE TOLD ABOUT ITSELF. `Budget margin`
runs `job-budget-margin.sh` with a FLOOR: fail if the job used too LITTLE of its
budget, on the argument that a timeout nothing can approach cannot fire. It
fired here at 13% -- and the job had used 234 seconds of 1800 because it DIED at
Layer C0. The floor's own error message opens with the words "Nothing failed."
The script had no way to know that; it never saw the job's status. Worse, the
step is `if: always()`, so this is not an accident of one run: EVERY fast
failure in this workflow manufactures a second red underneath the first. ▶ When
a message asserts a premise, ask what checks it. This one asserted the premise
that the gate is structurally unable to see.

▶ FIXED WHERE THE PREMISE LIVES. The script now takes the job status as an
optional fifth argument and applies the FLOOR only when it is `success`. The
ALARM stays unconditional on purpose -- a job that ran long and then failed did
still approach its timeout, and suppressing that would trade one blind spot for
another. The four call sites in ci.yml pass `${{ job.status }}`; the default is
`success`, so a caller passing no status keeps the old behaviour rather than
going quietly silent.

⛔ THE SELFTEST'S NEW ARM IS A PAIR AT THE SAME PERCENTAGE, and that is what
makes it an arm. 50% under a floor of 60 must FAIL with a success status and
PASS with a failure status; only the status differs between the two calls, so
neither a floor that stopped firing nor a status check that ignores its argument
can satisfy both. Proven by mutation on the SHIPPED script rather than a copy:
making the floor status-blind again -- exactly the pre-fix code -- reds Layer

ONE VERDICT WAS ANSWERING TWO QUESTIONS, AND THE SECOND ONE HAD NO READER.
`ZenohNodeConfig::validate` refuses an endpoint whose scheme stock zenoh does
not carry, and for the EMIT direction that is exactly right -- a config
generated for a real zenohd is coherent whatever this binary was built with.
But wz's own links are every one of them a cargo feature, and the default build
carries `tcp` + `udp` only. So a config naming `vsock/...` or `serial/...`
passed clean and the node then failed at bind, which is precisely the post-start
log line that verdict exists to precede.

⛔⛔ THE HARM WAS PROVEN BEFORE ANYTHING WAS WRITTEN, by a probe that FAILED:
`vsock/2:7447` on a tcp+udp build, `running 22 tests`, that one red. Reading the
code would have said the same thing and would have been worth less.

▶ THE SHAPE IS A SECOND VERDICT, NOT A NARROWED CONSTANT.
`session_open::COMPILED_IN_LINK_SCHEMES` derives this build's schemes from the
very `#[cfg]` predicates that gate the `dial_locator` / `bind_locator` arms, and
sits directly above them. `validate_for_build(Option<&[&str]>)` takes that set
OPTIONALLY and emits `ProtocolNotCompiledIn`; the option is what keeps the emit
path from narrowing, and the first half of its test asserts exactly that the
emit verdict did not move. `crate::compiled_in_link_schemes()` is the
always-compiled accessor, answering EMPTY for a build without the session-open
module -- honest, because such a build can open no scheme at all, tcp included.

⛔⛔⛔ THE CENSUS IS BOUND TO BEHAVIOUR, NOT TO A LIST. Its oracle is
`bind_endpoint`, asked once per scheme in `ZENOH_LINK_PROTOCOLS`: a scheme the
census calls compiled-in must not refuse for want of a backend, and one it omits
must refuse for exactly that. The population is the UPSTREAM surface, so a
scheme zenoh gains arrives as a missing probe rather than as silence. The
catalogue's SECOND column -- which cargo feature turns a scheme on -- is checked
against the refusing arm's own words rather than against a second copy of the
pairing, which is what a swapped row would otherwise slip past.

⛔⛔⛔ AN EXISTING GATE REFUSED HALF THIS CHANGE, AND THAT WAS THE FINDING. The
honoured-key coverage fixture states the TLS root-CA case over a `tls/...`
endpoint, because `--tls-ca` has an endpoint-scheme precondition -- so on a
default build the new refusal fired before any key was read. The cause was that
ONE function was answering two questions that only look alike: "does this key
reach a flag" is about the READER and is true whatever links are compiled in,
while "can this node open that endpoint" is about the BUILD. Splitting it into
`expand_stock_zenoh_config_for_build(.., compiled_in_schemes)` makes each test
name the reader it is judging; the coverage test says "a build with every link"
and every other test keeps the shipped path, census and all.

read this tree and reported `ws` as an ABSENT transport. It is implemented,

feature, and nothing said so where a reader would look. `LINK_SCHEME_FEATURES`
is that place, and it is why the defect message now ends with the flag to flip
instead of leaving an operator to guess it.

Round 2071.decision_summary:
A DOC PROMISED A SCOPE THE CODE DID NOT HAVE, AND THAT IS WORSE THAN A MISSING
CHECK. `ZenohNodeConfig::validate` answered "can this topology work" -- in the
module doc and in its own -- while its receiver is ONE config and its body reads
`self`. There was no channel through which a second node could be seen, so three
defects were structurally invisible: a node dialing an endpoint nobody listens
on, two nodes claiming one address, and a set of nothing but clients. Each ends
the same way, with the nodes starting cleanly and nothing attaching, which is
the failure `Unreachable`'s own doc calls the most expensive to diagnose. A
reader who believed the word "topology" stopped looking for it.

▶ THE FIX IS A SIBLING, NOT AN EXTENSION. `validate_topology(&[ZenohNodeConfig])`
is a free function with its own defect type, because every question it asks is
unanswerable from one config: folding them into the per-node verdict would hand
a single-node caller a false positive on all three. The wording of both docs was
corrected in the same round, which is the half of this item that is about the
promise rather than about the check.

⛔⛔⛔ EVERY DEFECT IS STATED AS A PAIR, AND THE CONTROL IS THE HARDER HALF. Each
of the three has a LEGITIMATE shape one character away from it, and a false
positive here tells an operator their working deployment is broken:

  - two nodes on `tcp/0.0.0.0:7447` are two machines doing the ordinary thing,
    not a collision, so a listen only counts as a claim when its address pins
    ONE machine -- a routable literal or a name, never a wildcard, never
    loopback, never a path-shaped scheme whose `/tmp` each host owns;
  - a wildcard listen must be credited with answering a dial addressed to a
    NAME it could never be compared against, since that pair -- a router on
    `0.0.0.0`, its clients on a hostname -- is the commonest deployment there
    is. The port and the scheme still decide, which is what keeps that
    generosity from becoming "anything matches anything";
  - a name against a literal is left ALLOWED on purpose. Only the network knows
    whether they are the same host, and this verdict resolves nothing.

⛔⛔ THE COLLISION COUNT IS BY SLICE POSITION, AND A CONTROL FOUND THAT. The
first cut grouped every (node, endpoint) pair, so a node listing one endpoint
twice collided WITH ITSELF -- already `DuplicateListenEndpoint` from the per-node
pass. Deduplicating by NAME would have fixed the symptom and swallowed the real
collision between two nodes that share an `id`; position does neither.

▶ THE CLIENT CLAIM IS SOURCED, NOT ASSUMED. Upstream `start_client`
(`zenoh/src/net/runtime/orchestrator.rs`) reads `connect` and the scouting block
and binds no listener at all, so a closed set of clients has nothing to attach
to. Read directly at the pinned checkout rather than recalled.

⚠ AND THE LIMIT OF THIS ROUND'S EVIDENCE, STATED: there is NO foreign witness.
The same file says a client with default retry calls `peer_connector_retry` and
returns `Ok`, so it retries forever instead of exiting -- which makes every one
of these three defects observable only as a TIMEOUT, a negative. The per-node
pass could use a real zenohd because zenohd refuses those configs itself and the
observable is an exit. That asymmetry is the reason this round stops at
deterministic unit witnesses, and it is filed rather than left implied.

`wz_reads_a_stock_zenohd_config`'s first leg does that on purpose, so the two

meets, which is a file that omits most keys. Two readers can agree on every
stated byte and still describe two different nodes. `ZenohNodeConfig::default`'s

struct covers" -- and nothing measured it. LEG 6 does, against the same real

Round 2074.decision_summary:
A COUNT GUARD THAT PIPES CARGO INTO `grep -q` IS SAFE ONLY WHILE ITS CARGO RUN
SELECTS ONE TARGET, AND NOBODY WAS MEASURING THAT. `grep -q` exits at its first
match; if cargo writes anything after it, the write lands on a closed pipe,
cargo dies, and `set -o pipefail` reports rc=101 with no attribution at all.
R2072 gave `wz-ap-demo` a second test target and eight such guards went red at
once -- six in Layer C1bl (hosted run 32679319923, read from its log) and two
more in Layers E6u/E7u -- while every command inside them passes when run alone.
That gap between "the lane is red" and "every part of it is green" is what cost
this round.

▶ THE OTHER TWENTY WERE NEVER CAREFUL, ONLY LUCKY. Measured: every remaining
bare guard in the file names `--lib` or `--test NAME`, so its cargo run writes
exactly one summary and the match is the last line. Nothing chose that; it is an
accident of how those lanes happened to be written, and an accident is not a
property.

⛔ SO THE FIX IS A GATE, NOT EIGHT EDITS. `count_guard_lint.py` already walks
every bare guard in `run-ci.sh`; it now FAILS one that selects no target, and
says why in the message rather than leaving the next reader to re-derive rc=101.
The eight are converted to `_runci_guarded_test`, whose own doc named this exact
hazard -- "a `... | grep -q` stage races its upstream's SIGPIPE against grep's
early exit under this script's `set -o pipefail`" -- years before it fired. The
helper captures the output instead of racing it.

⛔⛔ THE GATE FOUND TWO THE HAND SWEEP MISSED, WHICH IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT. A
`grep` for `cargo test .* grep -q` on single lines found six. The lint joins
line continuations the way the shell does and found eight -- E6u and E7u were
already broken and nobody had looked. A filter must read the string its subject
actually presents, and that is this workspace's own recurring lesson, met again
from the wrong side.

(`commons/zenoh-config/src/mode_dependent.rs:78`) is either the value or a

of the keys wz honours are declared with it. Two of them are `listen/endpoints`
and `connect/endpoints`. So the refusal reached the most ordinary config a
deployment has, and the item's scope was an underestimate rather than a
description.

▶ THE READER RESOLVES IT THE WAY UPSTREAM DOES, AND THE STRUCT DOES NOT MOVE.
`for_this_mode` is `.get(whatami)`: a table yields THIS node's row, and a table
with no row for this node is NO INSTRUCTION -- the same fallback a real zenohd
takes, not an error. `ZenohNodeConfig` stays flat because it describes ONE node;
what was missing was the resolution, not a richer field.

keystroke from `router:`, and reading such an object as a plain value would let
an operator believe a setting took effect. The mode table's own leaves are also
kept out of the ignored partition: reporting `listen/endpoints/router` as a key
wz does not honour would contradict the resolution that had just consumed it.

check from `all` to `any` reddened nothing, because the fixture carried only an

agreed. The MIXED table (`{ router: [..], rooter: [..] }`) is where they differ,
and it is also the realistic operator mistake: the half that works is silent
about the half that does not. With it in, the mutation reds and prints the harm.

zenohds of different modes over the SAME bytes and requires each to bind its own
row and NOT the other's, which is what makes the table a per-mode selection

Round 2077.decision_summary:
R2076 SHIPPED A ROW THAT PASSED FOR A REASON THAT HAD NOTHING TO DO WITH ITS
LABEL, AND THIS ROUND FOUND IT THE SAME WAY IT FOUND EVERYTHING ELSE: by reading
what zenohd actually said. LEG 8's base document states `mode`, `listen` and
`scouting`; the row labelled "mode table, typo'd mode name" put its table on
`listen.endpoints`, so the file carried `listen` TWICE and zenohd refused it for
`duplicate field "listen"`. The row asserted only that zenohd refused, so it was
green while measuring a JSON5 collision instead of a mode-name typo.

⛔ THE SAME TRAP KILLED FOUR PROBES IN THE SAME SESSION. A sweep meant to measure
whether upstream accepts mode tables on unhonoured keys came back "refused" four
times; the messages said `duplicate field "listen"` / `duplicate field
"scouting"` and the fixtures, not upstream, were the reason. A negative result
and a dead probe are indistinguishable from the outside — reading the MESSAGE is
what separated them, and it is the only thing that could have.

▶ TWO CHECKS, BECAUSE THE DEFECT HAS TWO HALVES. The first is a COLLISION GUARD:
each row's document is parsed with wz's own reader and its top-level names must
be unique, so a fragment can never re-state a key the base already has, whatever
it spells. The second is a REASON COLUMN: every refusing row now names the text
zenohd's refusal must carry, and the leg waits for THAT rather than for any
death. "zenohd said no" was never the measurement; "zenohd said no BECAUSE of the
thing this row is about" is.

⚠ WHAT R2076'S MUTATIONS COULD NOT HAVE CAUGHT, STATED PLAINLY. They proved the
leg really asks both implementations — flip a claim about reality and the right
half reds. They could not prove a row measures its own LABEL, because a
well-formed row and a mislabelled one both answer the question the code asks.
That is a different property and it needed a different check.

on every key whose subtree is opaque, when zenohd prints its resolved config in
about sixty milliseconds; reading incrementally and killing on the marker took it
from ~7 minutes to 198-219 seconds. What remains is 111 refusals paying zenohd's

has a 120-minute budget, so this is about 3% of it — and pre-push never runs

slow a push.

runs is this project's own recurring complaint, and the log line is the answer to

⛔⛔ A HOLE FOUND IN THIS ROUND'S OWN TOOL, AND CLOSED IN IT. The script reads the
Rust constants by regex, so a reformat that split one differently would be read

Round 2084.decision_summary:
THIS ROUND DOES NOT MOVE THE ANALYZER PLANE AND SAYS SO FIRST. It repairs a
defect the previous round shipped and gates the class that defect belongs to.
The census stands where R2083 left it.

R2082 added a Layer Z leg that opens its own TCP listener, spawns wz-ap-demo at
it, and reads the demo's first frame. `TcpListener::accept` has no deadline and
`#[tokio::test]` imposes none, so the leg's liveness rested entirely on the
demo dialling. A separate defect -- the missing Layer E skip token R2083 fixed
-- sent that leg into a lane whose demo is built WITHOUT `zenoh-config`, and
such a build exits on `--config` and never connects.

WHAT THE HOSTED RUN THEN REPORTED WAS NOTHING. The `demo-spawning e2e` job was
CANCELLED on its timeout, not failed: no test named, no verdict, every lane
after it lost. The run's two real reds were found only because two OTHER jobs
happened to fail on the skip-token gate. A test that waits forever does not
fail -- it spends the job's budget and takes the rest of the job with it.

THE DEADLINE PROVED ITSELF WITHIN THE HOUR. Re-running the ten Layer Z legs
after the fix, the demo binary in this tree had been rebuilt without
`zenoh-config` by an earlier lane. Under R2082's code that is the infinite
block; under this round's it is a 20-second failure that names the cause. Two
sibling legs already carried that guard and only mine did not.

SO THE FIX IS ONE DEADLINE AND THE ROUND IS A GATE. The rule was already this
tree's convention: of the 29 accept sites in test files that spawn an external
process, 21 were deadlined before any gate existed. It had nothing holding it,
so eight had drifted off -- five pico interop legs and three in wz-replay's
live.rs. `accept_deadline_lint.py` (Layer C0) now holds it.

THE BOUNDARY IS DRAWN AT WHO OWNS THE PARTNER, AND IS PRINTED RATHER THAN
ASSUMED. In scope: the partner is a process the test spawned, which can die,
mis-read its argv, or lack the feature under test, and nothing in-process will
ever wake that accept. Out of scope: an in-process partner -- a different
failure mode with a different fix. Sweeping all 58 of those in would open the
gate with 58 violations, which makes it a ceiling to ratchet rather than a rule
to keep. The gate counts both halves out loud so the boundary stays visible.

Round 2085.decision_summary:
THE ITEM LISTED THREE ROUTES AND THE ANSWER WAS A FOURTH, WHICH WAS ALREADY
PUBLIC. Open debt 505 said `lease` cannot be proven on the wire because it is
announced in the OPEN, and a listener that never answers the InitSyn gives the
node no reason to send one. That much was right. Its candidate list was not: it
read "the test drives the accept side" as re-implementing wz's accept FSM -- a
second opinion about the protocol -- and concluded the only clean route was a
NEW production observation surface, the very thing item 211 had refused.

`handshake_encode::encode_init` is `pub` (handshake_encode.rs:65). The leg does
not reproduce anything: it answers the demo's InitSyn with an honest InitAck
built by THIS TREE'S OWN encoder, then reads the OPEN that follows and hands it
to THIS TREE'S OWN dissector. Instrument made of wz's codec at both ends, zero
new public surface, and what is judged is still only the bytes the demo wrote.
That is the same shape R2082 chose for the dissect half.

SO `transport/link/tx/lease` JOINS `id` AND `batch_size`. Both values item 211
named are now read back off the wire, and the honoured surface's effect
partition moved with it, measured rather than asserted: wire 3 / no sink 6 /
argv only 21 of 30, where R2083 measured 2 / 6 / 22. Open debt 220 shrank by
exactly the mechanism it says is the only one that shrinks it.

THE UNIT OF A LEASE IS ON THE WIRE, SO THE LEG READS IT. The OPEN's `t` flag
means seconds. Comparing the raw number would have tied a leg about wire
fidelity to whichever unit the encoder happened to pick, so the flag is read and
the value normalised through `lease_from_wire` -- the same function the
receiving side uses -- and both fixture values are deliberately NOT whole
seconds so a unit bug cannot hide behind an equal number.

depth is right, and it has a cost nobody bills: the outer check makes the inner

round installs the same rule in two places.

branch that has no route from argv. Pick the instrument by what can REACH the

and a unit test is the only thing that touches it.

convention breaks -- a `<summary>` swallowing a roster line, a fence left open

Round 2088.decision_summary:
THE ROUND THAT CLOSED 506 LEFT ITS OWN GUARD UNWITNESSED, AND A SWEEP MEASURED
IT RATHER THAN SUSPECTING IT. R2087 put the qos x lowlatency rule in two places
on purpose: `main`'s argv parse, so nothing is dialled, and `initiator_offer`,
so the library-facing seam cannot be bypassed. Its binary witness proves the
first. Replacing `exclusive_modes(..)?` inside `initiator_offer` with a
discarded call left `exclusive_transport_modes_binary` GREEN and the whole
wz-ap-demo suite green -- because `main` refuses before that function is ever
reached with the pair. The guard was unreachable from argv by design, and
therefore indistinguishable from dead code to anyone who came to delete it.

⛔ THAT IS OPEN-DEBT ITEM 479's CLASS, ONE LAYER BELOW WHERE R2087 CLOSED IT.
R2072 learned the lesson in the other direction -- a shipping seam witnessed
only by units -- and its fix was to add a binary. The inverse holds here: the
shipping seam already HAS its binary, and what has no route from argv is this
branch, so a unit test is the only instrument that can reach it at all. Choosing
by shape rather than by the slogan is the point; "unit tests are weaker" is a
statement about what a test can REACH, not a ranking.

▶ WHAT THE MUTATION PRINTED IS THE ARGUMENT FOR KEEPING THE GUARD. With the `?`
discarded, `initiator_offer(true, true, ..)` returns
`SessionOffer { mode: LowLatency, .. }` -- it silently picks a winner by
statement order, which is the exact order-dependence `SessionOffer` was built to
make unrepresentable. The guard is not redundant with `main`; it is what stops a
future caller assembling a `Role` by hand from getting a wire form it did not
ask for.

the one that was right, which is the worst arrangement of those two facts. The

directions against a fixture, because a check that only ever fails is not a
check.

Round 2090.decision_summary:
R2090 is a repair round: R2089's witness was written, run, mutated and layered,
and then REFUSED at push time by a gate its author never invoked.

The rejection is the finding. pre-push gate C1cf (reduced feature combination)
compiles every CHANGED crate with `cargo clippy -p <pkg> --no-default-features
--all-targets -- -D warnings`, and the new leg tripped two lints there:
`clippy::type_complexity` on the collection vector and `clippy::map_identity` on
a `map` that rebuilt the tuple it was given. Neither is reachable from anything
R2089 ran. That is the general shape and it is worth stating plainly: a new test
FILE is a new compilation target, so it enters lanes chosen by the CRATE's
feature axis, not by the features the test itself needs. The round built the
demo with three features and ran the leg; the lane that broke compiles the test
crate with NO features and lints it.

The fix is not an `allow`. The tuple was doing the work a name should do, so it
got one: an `Answer` record of the Hello bytes and the two strings the node said
about itself, with a `Verdict` alias over it. The three fields are cross-checked
against each other by the assertions below them -- the Hello must carry the
locator this node's own advertise seam chose, and the banner is what the
run-mode INTENDED, quoted back when the wire disagrees -- so a record with named
fields is what that reading site wanted all along, and the identity `map`
disappears once the constructor names its own fields.

One instrument lesson, its third recurrence in this tree: the background job's
completion notice said "exit code 0" for a push that FAILED. The status it
reports is the compound's last command, which was the echo writing the rc file.
The judges are that rc file -- which read 1 -- and `git ls-remote origin main`,
which had not moved off the previous round's commit. Neither the notification
nor a wrapper's own exit code is admissible for a push.

Round 2091.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 508 CLOSED: one stock zenoh router config file, dropped in
with no other argument, now brings up a wz node that announces the ROUTER
role on the wire and answers Scouts -- and the binary's own report stops
calling a key applied when its flag reached nothing.

THE TOPOLOGY DECISION, which is what item 508 said this round had to make:
`mode: "router"` selects `--router-hat`, and it is NOT `cfg!`-guarded.

zenoh's `mode: "router"` names a node that puts WhatAmI::Router on the wire
and hosts the discovery a stock client's `autoconnect: ["router"]` default
asks for. `--router` is neither: `demo_session_init_params` maps
NodeKind::Router to WhatAmI::Peer (a stand-in kept so the R121c/e accept
tests are unchanged) and `run_router` spawns no responder. `--router-hat` is
wz's router -- WhatAmI::Router on the wire, and since R2089 the responder
host. So the file that deploys a zenoh router used to produce a wz node in a
different role that nothing on the network could find.

NO GUARD, and that is the decision rather than an omission. A `cfg!` guard
would make the SAME file come up in a different run-mode depending on which
features the binary carries, which is worse than a refusal: the operator
gets a node that starts and is the wrong thing. R311y844's rule -- a key
whose SINK is compiled out must not turn a valid stock config into a node
that refuses to start -- governs OPTIONAL keys, whose honest fallback is to
drop them. `mode` has no such fallback, because dropping it IS the
different-node-per-build disease.

And the refusal class is not new, measured rather than argued: on a build
carrying `router-hat-router` and not `routing-router`, this same file
already exited 2 with "--router requires the `routing-router` feature".
After this round that build runs it. The set of files that refuse to start
got SMALLER, not larger.

The third half of the item -- the report -- was a wider lie than the item
recorded. `applied()` was derived from a per-BUILD list of keys with no
sink, so every key whose flag carries an INVOCATION precondition was counted
as applied while the expansion silently withheld it. Six of the honoured
keys have such a precondition. The verdicts are now decided at the site that
decides the flag, and the not-applied half names WHY for each key.

Round 2092.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 511 CLOSED. The run-mode a stock config selects is now the
ROLE the document names; the endpoint lists only supply its address.

THE DECISION, stated because the item is one: `mode` picks the run-mode.
When the document names no `listen/endpoints`, upstream's own mode-dependent
default supplies the address; when it NAMES the key -- an explicitly empty
list included -- that default is suppressed, because upstream suppresses it
too.

The item was registered with two shapes and the oracle made it three. Each
row was put to a REAL zenohd before it was written down, on the ground that a
DIVERGENCE cannot be adjudicated by one of the two implementations:

- `{ mode: "peer", listen: [..] }`. zenohd binds it and is findable. wz chose
  `--listen`, the one-shot acceptor: it answers no Scouts and leaves after a
  round-trip, which is not a peer deployment at all.
- `{ mode: "router", connect: [..] }`, no listen. zenohd binds port 7447 on
  every interface and is a ROUTER. wz chose `--connect` and came up a CLIENT.
- `{ mode: "client", listen: [..] }`. zenohd starts and binds NOTHING, naming
  no locator. wz bound the endpoint. THIS ROW WAS NOT IN THE ITEM. It runs the
  other way -- wz doing something upstream does not -- and only asking the
  oracle could have produced it.

and nowhere else.

THE SEAM MOVED, and where it moved to is the decision. `FaceSources.qos_link`
-- a field that could carry a declared QoS band and nothing else -- becomes
`FaceSources.offer`, a whole `SessionOffer`. `FaceQosLink`, `qos_link_offer`
and the four cfg twins around the open entrypoints go with it: the
`_with_offer` pair is unconditional now, so there is no second shape left to
keep in step with the first.

simplification made for convenience. zenoh builds `StateOpen`
(io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/establishment/open.rs:605-636) and
`StateAccept` (io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/establishment/accept.rs:725-755)
from the SAME `manager.config.unicast.{is_qos,is_lowlatency,is_compression}`,
so a capability is a property of the NODE and not of which end dialled. It was
read this round, not remembered. The alternative -- a dial offer and an accept
offer as separate fields -- would have made "a wz node configured for
lowlatency accepts an inbound link and does not negotiate lean" representable,
which is not a state a drop-in for zenohd may reach.

argued: the only one of the four flags any mesh lane passes is `--qos`
(wz_peer_multilink_qos_reach, wz_qos_link_zenohd_interop), and `--qos` already
produced `TransportMode::Qos` through the band's implication.

let `--qos-band --lowlatency` reach `with_qos_link`, whose `with_mode(Qos)`
would overwrite the lean mode the operator asked for -- the exact silent drop

Open-debt item 516 is CLOSED: the AGGREGATING (`--max-links > 1`) open path
carries the whole capability offer, so a mesh node's `--qos` / `--lowlatency`
/ `--compression` / `--shm` reach the wire on both of `peer_loop`'s dial
paths. R2095 wired the single-link dial and could not reach this one: the
aggregating entrypoints took `(pref, qos: bool, band)` and staged no
`SessionOffer` at all, so the same flag reached the InitSyn at `--max-links 1`
and nothing at `--max-links 2`, from the same configuration file. R2095 met
that with a REFUSAL and named the residual rather than dropping it silently.

THE SSOT DECISION, which the item asked to be made and recorded: the
`SessionOffer` is the SSOT and `qos: bool` is GONE -- from the two
`*_with_multilink` signatures, from `FaceSources`, and from every caller.
Three reasons, in the order they decide it. First, `SessionOffer` exists to
make the qos x lowlatency pair UNREPRESENTABLE rather than merely rejected
(its own module doc), and an independent boolean beside it re-opens exactly
the contradiction the type removes -- `qos: true` with
`offer.mode == LowLatency` would type-check. Second, `apply_offer` is the one
validated staging seam: it returns `UnsupportedCapability` for a capability
this build cannot honour, where `set_qos_offer` silently elides. Third,
upstream reads all four capabilities off ONE place --
`manager.config.unicast.{is_qos,is_lowlatency,is_compression}` builds both
`StateOpen` (io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/establishment/open.rs:605-636)
and `StateAccept` (.../accept.rs:725-755) -- so one value is the faithful
shape and two are the divergence. "Does this session offer QoS" is now read in
exactly one way: `offer.mode == TransportMode::Qos`.

THE SHAPE IS A SHARED BODY, NOT A WIDER SIBLING. `initiator_open_offering` and
`accept_open_offering` now carry the offer half of every capability-aware
open, and the `*_with_offer` pair and the `*_with_multilink` pair are both
CALLERS of them. That is the fix for what item 516 actually was: the
aggregating entrypoint had been written as a sibling of the composing one, so
it re-derived a fraction of `apply_offer` and three capabilities had no route
through it. A capability added to `SessionOffer` later now reaches both paths
by construction. The `stage` hook takes what is deliberately NOT in the offer
-- the 0x4 dispatch, the link reliability preference, the QoS-priority band --
which is the line `SessionOffer`'s own doc already drew.

THE BAND STAYS A SEPARATE PARAMETER, and that is the same line: it is not
negotiated at the handshake, it is a LOCAL `select_link` routing decision, and
it is per PHYSICAL LINK where the offer is per session. It is applied only
under a QoS offer, which is now read off the offer instead of being told
twice.

Round 2098.decision_summary:
The free tier moves from LGPL-3.0-or-later to AGPL-3.0-or-later, keeping
the commercial alternative unchanged. This is an owner decision, not a debt
anyone had filed, and it is recorded here because it changes the terms under
which every file in this tree is offered.

What the change actually buys, stated rather than assumed. Under LGPL-3 a
proprietary product could link watching-zenoh and satisfy the free tier by
shipping relink information; under AGPL-3 the combined work is covered, and
dynamic linking is not a way around it. The clause with no LGPL-era analogue
is section 13: a MODIFIED watching-zenoh reached by users over a network
obliges its operator to offer them the Corresponding Source. That closes the
"we only operate it, we never ship it" route through the free tier, which is
the route a router or an analyzer would most plausibly take.

What it costs, equally plainly. AGPL is refused outright by many corporate
intake policies, more often than plain GPL is, so the free tier becomes
harder to adopt rather than easier. That is the intended direction for a
dual-licensed project -- the free option is deliberately the demanding one --
but it is a cost, not a free win.

Earlier revisions are unaffected and cannot be made so. A licence already
granted is not withdrawable: copies obtained under the LGPL expression keep
it. Every licence document in this tree now says that in its own words rather
than leaving a reader to infer it.

Open-debt item 509 is CLOSED: every document this library hands a consumer
now carries its OWN revision, and a key rename or removal cannot ship without
moving it.

What was missing, stated as the contradiction it was. `wz_dissect.h` tells a
consumer to read the returned JSON BY NAME and tolerate unknown keys, and
states that `wz_dissect_abi_version` moves "when a SYMBOL or the memory rule
changes, never when the JSON gains fields". Both halves are right. Together
they left a key RENAMED or REMOVED -- a real break for a name-reading consumer
-- with no number anywhere that could express it. Item 288's landing pinned
the census document's key set for the AUTHOR; the CONSUMER had no signal at
all, and item 509 filed exactly that residue.

PER DOCUMENT, NOT PER LIBRARY, and the item left this round to decide it on a
measurable basis: does the consumer read the documents as SEPARATE symbols?
Read off the header, it does -- `wz_dissect_pcap_census`,
`wz_dissect_pcap_fields`, `wz_dissect_pcap_summary`,
`wz_dissect_readable_surfaces`, `wz_dissect_selector_diagnose` and
`wz_dissect_declarations_diagnose` are six doors and a consumer calls the one
it wants. A single library-wide number would tell a reader of the census that
the shape moved when what moved was the field document it never calls, and the
only safe response to a number that moved is to re-check -- so a coupled
number costs exactly the audits it cannot justify.

THE DANCE IS THE POINT. With a per-document revision a rename stops being a
break and becomes a two-step edit: append a revision emitting BOTH names with
the old one in `retiring`, then append the next revision that drops it.
`audit` makes that the ONLY expressible path -- a key that vanishes between
consecutive revisions without having been announced in the older one is an
error -- so a silent removal cannot be written down at all. That is what
unblocks 455 (`first_packet` is a byte offset over a stream link and the name
says packet) and 460 (two structurally-zero counters that cannot be removed):
both were waiting for a way to TELL a consumer, and both are now ordinary.

`wz_dissect_transport_message` is deliberately out of scope, and that is a
decision rather than an omission: its document is a FIELD TREE whose keys are
the walkers' own names, generated per protocol element, so there is no fixed
key set for a revision to be about. The walkers' naming contract is a
different one and belongs with them. The header says so in its own words.

revision 1's key set IN PLACE: a round that renamed a key in the emitter and
in the table in one commit would pass. The announce-before-remove rule bites
only once a document has a second revision to look back from. That is a
smaller hole than the one item 509 named -- a break is now EXPRESSIBLE and the
edit lands on a table where the author must state it, which is what the item
asked for -- but it is not zero, and the frozen-prefix checksum that would
close it is not in this round.

Round 2102.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 524 is CLOSED: the dissection C ABI has a LIVE door -- a
handle that outlives its call, packets fed one at a time, and decoded
messages drained as fixed-layout binary records into a buffer the caller
owns. ABI 10 -> 11, and this is the first bump that moves for the MEMORY
RULE as well as for symbols.

What was missing, and it was not an engine gap. All fifteen doors this
header exported took a whole capture and returned a JSON document. That is
right for a FILE, which ends, and wrong for a LINK, which does not: a
consumer watching a running system could re-hand the same growing buffer and
pay a full re-dissection per call, or cut the stream into windows and lose
every message straddling a cut. The engine had been feedable a packet at a
time since R311y594 and `DissectionLimits::for_live_tap` existed for exactly
this. What was missing was the door.

THE FIRST MEASUREMENT THE ITEM ASKED FOR was the memory rule, and the answer
is a REVISION rather than a quiet widening. `wz_dissect.h` promised three
things: every char* is the library's, no callbacks run, and no handle
outlives the call that made it. The first is untouched. The second is
untouched and the design is built to keep it -- a drain writes into a buffer
the caller sized, so no function pointer of the consumer's runs inside this
library, which is the ground open-debt item 237 was refused on. The third
cannot survive a live tap and is now stated as having exactly one named
exception. The header's opening paragraph carries the revision itself, not a
note beside it, and the ABI version moves for the rule as it moves for a
symbol.

THE DESIGN PROBLEM IS THE BOOKMARK. Draining incrementally means remembering
what was already taken, and an index into a flow's message list is a wrong
bookmark in a way that is silent: a bounded dissection trims from the FRONT
and evicts whole flows, so an index means something different after every
trim. Two facts were added to make a sound one. `MessageList::produced`
counts what was ever appended and no trim moves it, so `produced - len` is
the produced-index of the oldest message still held and a watermark below it
is EXACTLY what was discarded unseen. `MessageListOrigin` names WHICH list
in the wire's own terms -- flows are evicted from the middle of their table
and QUIC streams appended to theirs, so an ordinal points elsewhere after
either, and a TCP and a UDP flow can carry the same 5-tuple.

Those two are what make `wz_dissect_live_lost` a measurement rather than a
field that is always zero, which is this workspace's standing rule reaching
the live surface: a bound that discards and does not say so reports a floor
as a total.

Round 2103.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 521 is CLOSED: every cdylib this workspace emits now carries a
SONAME, and a gate DERIVES the population it checks from cargo metadata rather
than from a list.

The defect, and it is a consumer's rather than this tree's. Cargo emits a
cdylib with no DT_SONAME, and the ELF rule is then that the linker records, in
the CONSUMER's DT_NEEDED, whatever string it used to find the library. Link by
PATH -- which is what CMake's `target_link_libraries(app /abs/path/lib.so)`
generates, the ordinary way to consume a prebuilt shared object -- and that
string is an absolute build-tree path. Measured before the fix, a one-line C
consumer linked against this tree's dissection library recorded
`NEEDED [/home/.../crates/target/release/libwz_capi_dissect.so]`. That binary
cannot be shipped: an absolute DT_NEEDED is not a search key, the dynamic
linker OPENS it, and RPATH, $ORIGIN and LD_LIBRARY_PATH are never consulted.
The downstream consumer that reported this was carrying
`patchelf --set-soname` over every copy it took, which is a cost paid again by
every consumer there will ever be.

IT IS WIDER THAN THE REPORT, and that is the finding worth keeping. The report
named four libraries. This workspace emits FIVE cdylibs: `wz-volume-example`
was in nobody's list. A gate written from the report would have been wrong on
the day it was written, so the population comes from `cargo metadata` -- which
targets cargo itself calls cdylibs -- and an EMPTY population is a FAILURE
rather than a quiet pass. One of the four is `wz-capi-c`, whose entire claim is
that it is a binary drop-in for zenoh-c; a library a consumer cannot
redistribute is not a drop-in for one it can.

WHY A CRATE AND NOT FIVE COPIES. `wz-cdylib-build` is a build-script helper on
the `wz-codegen-build` precedent, which exists in this workspace for the same
stated reason: the sce-codegen lookup had been duplicated across three build
scripts. The only judgement in this helper is which target platforms take
`-Wl,-soname` (the ELF ones), and a judgement duplicated five times is one that
gets corrected in fewer than five places. The emit is
`cargo:rustc-cdylib-link-arg` and not `rustc-link-arg`, because three of the
five callers also build an rlib that is compiled into Rust test binaries and
into the `wz` facade -- a link argument reaching those would be putting a
shared-object name on an executable.

WHY THE GATE READS THE ARTIFACT. Neither half is parsed out of source text: the
library list is cargo's answer, and the SONAME is `readelf -d` over the linked
`.so`. A gate that grepped build.rs for `-Wl,-soname` would be checking the
line its author had just written against itself, and would be structurally
blind to the one mistake the build script cannot catch on its own. A build
script has no environment variable for a lib TARGET name, so `emit_soname` has
to be TOLD the name; being told the wrong one produces a SONAME that names no
file on disk, and only the artifact can say so.

The residue this states rather than hides: the SONAME is `libwz_capi_c.so`, the
file cargo produces, not `libzenohc.so`. A true drop-in might want upstream's
name and a symlink beside it. That is a separate decision, and if it is ever
taken this gate is what will refuse the mismatch until both halves move.

Round 2104.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 522 is CLOSED: the apt census now measures SHORTFALL as well as
excess, and the two packages it found missing are installed by name in every
workflow that needs them.

The asymmetry this ends. `apt_package_census.py` has asked one question since
it was written -- is every installed package justified -- and that question
cannot find a package nobody installed. Both failures are real and only one was
gated, so the tree carried the other for its whole life. Measured from a
downstream report: `libxml2-dev` appears ZERO times in any workflow and the
build requires it; on a clean ubuntu:24.04 the build dies with "The system
library `libxml-2.0` required by crate `libxml` was not found". Every hosted
run has passed because the GitHub runner image happens to carry libxml2 -- an
inheritance nothing declares and nothing would notice the removal of.

KNOWING WAS NOT ENOUGH, and that is the part worth recording. The requirement
was written down in THREE places already: ci.yml's own comment says the
resolved tree "pulls bindgen (libclang), libxml, and the vendor/sce crates"
while the install line directly beneath it names only `libclang-dev clang
perl`; run-ci.sh states "CI Linux has libxml2 (it builds ...)" as a fact about
someone else's image; and the `portability` job installs libxml2 through vcpkg
on Windows under a paragraph explaining exactly why the build needs it. Three
statements of the requirement, no installation of it. A prose statement is not
a gate, and this is the third time this workspace has paid to learn it.

WHAT THE NEW ARM DERIVES. Not a list anyone typed. `cargo metadata
--all-features` resolves the real graph; every package in it that has a build
script has that script READ; and the pkg-config module names those scripts
probe for are the system libraries the build will demand. That yields exactly
one today -- `libxml-2.0`, wanted by the `libxml` crate, which is the crate the
downstream error names. An empty population is a FAILURE, because "found
nothing" and "nothing is wrong" must not print the same line.

Which jobs need it is derived too, by walking cargo's resolve graph backwards
to the workspace members that reach the probing crate and asking which jobs run
them -- the same machinery the `cmake` arm uses. The answer came back EQUAL to
the `libclang-dev` job set, which is the cross-check worth having: two lists
that agree by derivation rather than by habit, and that now red when they stop
agreeing.

The module-to-package map is the one hand-written thing, and it is not
believed: where pkg-config and dpkg both exist the gate resolves each row
(`--variable=pcfiledir`, then `dpkg -S` on the .pc) and reds on a row naming
the wrong package.

THE SCOPE WAS WIDER THAN THE REPORT, twice. The `pkg-config` TOOL was riding on
the image for ten of the thirteen jobs -- a probe shells out to it -- which
refutes the reason the old ADJUDICATED row gave for carrying it on only three.
And `release.yml` had the same hole: it runs `cargo test --workspace` with
neither package. So the shortfall arm reads every workflow under
.github/workflows and understands both install spellings, `apt-install.sh` and
a bare `apt-get install`. The excess arm keeps its narrower, documented subject.

STATED LIMIT: this arm sees pkg-config consumers and nothing else. `libclang`
is dlopen'd by clang-sys rather than probed, `perl` is a program, and
`libpcap-dev` is here for a header a gate reads. Those stay adjudicated as
prose. The class this closes is the one that actually bit.

The defect. The mode was decided by `check_only = "--check" in sys.argv`, so
every other input fell through to the REWRITE path. Measured before the fix:
`relicense_spdx.py --help` printed `relicense-spdx: rewrote 0 file(s)` and
exited 0. A person who typed `--help` to learn what the program does had it
walk 1000+ tracked files with write intent; a CI step reaching for the gate
with `--chek` would have edited the tree instead of grading it. It was harmless
only because the tree carries ZERO occurrences of the old expression today —
a property of today, not of the program, and one that stops holding at exactly
the moment this file is next used.

THE DECISION WAS NOT "DEFAULT TO --check", and that is the part worth
recording. Defaulting to the safe mode removes the damage and leaves an
ambiguity pointing the other way: someone with the old habit types the bare
command expecting a rewrite, gets a check, reads `OK`, and believes the rewrite
happened. A silent no-op wearing a success message is the shape this workspace
names most often. The two modes here are READ and WRITE — opposites, not a
default and a variant — so the program refuses to guess. The write mode is
named `--apply`.

Nothing had to follow it: `run-ci.sh`'s gate already passed `--check` and no
caller in the tree invoked it bare. CLAUDE.md's licence section now states the
contract, because that section is where a person looks before running it.

WHY argparse's OWN `required=True` COULD NOT BE USED. A required mutually
exclusive group is checked BEFORE argparse complains about unrecognized
arguments, so `--chek` came back as "one of the arguments --check --apply
--selftest is required" — true, and silent about the typo that is the entire
reason the reader is looking at the message. The group is declared without
`required`, and the two refusals are ordered by hand after
`parse_known_args()`: unknown arguments first, named; then the missing mode.
Naming the typo is the thing item 523 asked for.

Round 2107.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 527 is CLOSED: this workspace can now measure what a decoded
byte costs, separately from what a decoded packet costs. And the instrument
earned its keep on its first run by REFUTING the hypothesis that prompted it.

The debt was never "it is slow". A downstream consumer measured
`Dissection::push_packet` at ~963 ns/packet, described the shape as a fixed
cost plus a few ns per byte, and inferred from the byte-proportional part
standing an order of magnitude above memcpy that the reassembly path holds
several copies. Measured on this tree: ZERO `[[bench]]` targets and zero
`benches/` directories anywhere. So the figure could be neither reproduced nor
contradicted here, and the actual defect was the absence of any instrument that
could settle a claim about a cost.

A FIT RATHER THAN A NUMBER. "963 ns/packet" is not a fact about the decoder; it
is a fact about the decoder AND the packet size used. The gradable claim is the
SHAPE, so the sweep measures six payload sizes and least-squares fits
`ns = fixed + slope * bytes`. The memcpy floor is measured in the same process,
on the same sizes, through the same clock — a ratio against a number from
another machine would be arithmetic rather than evidence.

WHAT IT FOUND, WITH A CONTROL. The sweep runs twice, once under
`DissectionLimits::for_live_tap()` and once unbounded, and the only difference
between the two runs is the ceiling:

    bounded (live tap)   21 100 ns/byte
    unbounded                48 ns/byte
    memcpy floor            0.004 ns/byte

The bounded/unbounded ratio is 437x. Almost the whole per-byte cost of a live
tap is the ceiling's TRIM, not the decode — so the downstream inference, that
copies on the reassembly path explain the slope, is refuted by this tree's own
measurement. A round that had gone hunting copies would have dug in the wrong
place. The trim itself is filed as open-debt item 528, with the hypothesis
about `remove(0)` marked as a hypothesis rather than a finding, because reading
a line is not measuring it.

NO THRESHOLD IS ASSERTED. A wall-clock ceiling on a shared runner is a flake
generator, and an arbitrary one is this workspace's "population of zero wearing
a unit". What Layer C1bn asserts is that the instrument RAN: `--selftest`
recovers known coefficients from synthetic data and refuses a degenerate fit,
and the sweep's population floor is derived from the payload. The numbers go in
the log for a person to read, which is precisely the capability that did not
exist before.
verification_bullets: THE POPULATION GUARD CAUGHT THIS ROUND TWICE, and both times the timings it
was hiding behind looked entirely reasonable. That is the whole reason it
exists and it is worth recording in the order it happened.
1. The first payload was `0x5a` filler. Junk does not decode, so the message
layer never ran and the sweep timed link + IP + TCP reassembly while
reporting decode cost. It printed a confident 57 ns fixed and 0.05 ns/byte
at a 7.2x memcpy ratio — numbers a reader would have believed.
`produced()` said 0.
2. Corrected to real KeepAlives, every frame still carried `seq = 1000`, so
TCP reassembly correctly treated 19 999 of 20 000 packets as
retransmissions of bytes it already held. Only the FIRST packet's 466
messages were ever decoded. That printed 68 ns fixed, 0.04 ns/byte — even
more plausible than the first — and `produced()` returned 466 where a
population scaling with the sweep was due.
THE FLOOR HAD TO BE DERIVED, and its first two forms were too weak: `produced >
0` passed case 2 outright, and `produced >= iters` passed it at the three
larger sizes (466 clears 100). A floor that does not scale with the sweep is a
floor the sweep walks under. It is now `iters * size / UNIT_LEN`, computed from
the payload the fixture builds.
TWO MUTATIONS, both red, run through the lane:
1. payload restored to `0x5a` -> red, naming all five sizes with (size, 0,
expected).
2. `seq` advance removed -> red, naming the real counts (21 and 85 at the
small sizes under `--quick`). This is the exact bug the round shipped
twice, reproduced on demand.

an exact line's coefficients are recovered; a FLAT line returns slope zero
rather than being refused, because "no per-byte cost" is an answer; an
all-identical-x sweep is REFUSED rather than yielding a division by zero
wearing a unit; a single point is refused; and the frame builder is asserted to
grow with the payload, without which the fit's input would be the degenerate
case wearing real timings.
THE MEASUREMENT, with its control (2 000 packets x 6 sizes): bounded
