The defect. `wz_dissect_record_v1` gave a consumer `flow_id`, `anchor` and
`anchor_space`. One flow carries several message LISTS at once, and the
QUIC-stream ones are byte offsets that each start at zero — so a consumer
grouping by `(flow_id, origin)` puts two streams' byte 0 in one space and reads
two distinct messages as one. `origin` cannot express the difference, because a
stream's identity is a number the wire chose. The same happens when a flow is
evicted and reopened under one 5-tuple: the successor's offsets restart.
`list_id` is a per-list number on the same counter as `flow_id`, so the two can
never collide and two anchors are comparable exactly when it matches.

downstream consumer's report predates that push and says its integration

attaching a permanent `_v2` to a struct hours old is the cost this refused.

Also carried: `DeclarationText` is the TEXT spelling and a
`FormatMap` holds the operator's spelling. Anything added to this
dialect later must decide which side it is on and convert at

changes_bullets: `ESCAPE`, `escape_field`, `unescape_field` and
`rsplit_once_unescaped` are the whole mechanism.
The splitter scans LEFT TO RIGHT even though it wants the last match,
and that is load-bearing rather than stylistic: whether a character is
quoted is a fact about what PRECEDES it, so a right-to-left scan
cannot tell `\:` from a colon that follows a quoted backslash
(`\\:`), and would split the second one in the wrong place.
`DeclarationText` keeps borrowing the line and keeps carrying the
TEXT spelling -- the quoted one. `FormatMap::declare` is the single
boundary that unquotes into the map's own spelling, and
`FormatMap::declarations` quotes on the way back out. Putting the
conversion at that one seam is what let the type stay borrowed
instead of becoming `Cow`, and it means the round-trip contract
`parse_declaration(&declaration_text(d)) == d` still holds in the
spelling it was written for -- including for the patterns this round
makes expressible, which is where it would otherwise have broken.
Malformed quoting is REFUSED, not passed through: a trailing lone
backslash, or a quote of anything but the three reserved characters.
Passing them through would make `a\b` and `ab` the same declaration,
so an operator's pattern would silently match a different topic.
Both `pattern.contains(':')` refusals are GONE -- from `insert` and
from `name_field`. Removing them is the item. R311y923 added them so
a colon-bearing pattern could not install and read back as the other
spelling, which was right while the grammar had no way to write one:
it made the loss loud instead of silent, and left the capability
missing. Upstream permits `:` in a key expression, so a wz that
cannot map a format onto `demo/temp:c` is a replacement with a hole.
Round 2111.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 462 is CLOSED by putting a QUOTING escape into the
declaration grammar, which the owner had already decided (2026-08-24)
because it breaks nothing: every declaration written without a
backslash means exactly what it meant.

What this round had to decide was the escape character, and the
register told the starting round how: choose it against upstream's
key-expression canon, because "a legal character as the introducer
re-creates the same ambiguity". MEASURED, and that instruction is
wrong. `zenoh-keyexpr`'s own per-chunk character loop
(`key_expr/borrowed.rs`, the `TryFrom<&str>` impl) refuses exactly
four things: `#`, `?`, an unbound `$`, and a bare `*`. Every other
byte is legal inside a chunk, backslash included.

So there is NO character a key expression cannot carry, and the
escape introducer cannot be chosen the way the register says -- the
method has no candidates. What works instead is DOUBLING: `\\` is a
literal backslash, `\:` a literal colon, `\=` a literal equals. That
is immune to which characters upstream permits, which is precisely
the property the register wanted when it refused to move the
discriminator to `#` or `?`: wz is zenoh's replacement, and a canon
that widens tomorrow must not force the same break again.

A second correction, and it runs the other way. The register's own
2026-08-24 note says the Name spelling could ALREADY declare a
colon-bearing pattern, so the item's first sentence was "too wide".
That is true only of the text parser: `FormatMap::name_field` refused
`pattern.contains(':')` outright, exactly as `insert` did. Both doors
were shut, and the correction overshot in the opposite direction from
the sentence it was correcting.

Open-debt item 237 CLOSED: a deployment can DESCRIBE its own payload format,
in text, and both consumption surfaces decode with it. No new symbol, no new
flag, and no code crosses the boundary.

The item, and why the obvious remedy was refused. `PayloadFormat` is an
extension point whose own doc says a consumer implements it "without patching
this crate" - true for a Rust consumer, and a deployment that LINKS the C ABI
had no way in at all: to see its own payloads it had to build this workspace.
The obvious shape is a decoder callback, and `wz_dissect.h`'s memory rule is
the ABI's whole contract: "no callbacks run". A callback is the caller's
control flow executing inside this library on a stack this library owns, so
closing the item that way would have voided the header's contract to gain a
feature. What crosses instead is TEXT, through the door that already takes
declaration text and the door that already validates it without a capture.
Data can be versioned, diagnosed and refused by line; it has no lifetime and
no stack.

The grammar gained a THIRD spelling, `#<name>=<layout>`, and a rule names it
like any other format. A layout is a fixed record - `<name>:<type>` items in
order, with an optional `rest` last for a variable tail - because that is what
a profile table is. Conditionals, lengths read from the payload and repetition
are deliberately absent: each is a small interpreter, and an interpreter
reached from a C string is a far larger promise than "your record has these
fields at these offsets".

The marker is QUOTABLE, and that is the part with a history. Item 462 paid for
the lesson that this grammar must not bet on a character upstream's keyexpr
canon rejects, so `\#topic=cbor` is a rule about a topic named `#topic`. That
`#` happens to be illegal in a chunk today - so no declaration already written
changes meaning - is a convenience, not the argument.

Ownership. The map now OWNS described formats, because they did not exist
until a line of text was read, and a rule points at one by index rather than
by a reference into the map's own vector. `for_keyexpr`'s return lifetime moved
from the map's parameter to `&self`; every caller holds a `&'a FormatMap<'a>`,
so not one call site changed.

described: its PREMISE was refuted by measurement, and the work became holding
down the property that had quietly become true.

What the item said. A new consumer of `wz-capture` gets `could not find
'fields_json' in 'wz_capture'` -- the module is not missing, the feature is off
-- and "nothing at that point tells them which feature". It also recorded why
the obvious fix is wrong: `compile_error!` is not lazy, so an arm carrying one
breaks every default build.

What is actually true, measured before anything was written. A real consumer
crate outside this workspace, naming the gated path against a default build,
gets:

    error[E0433]: cannot find `fields_json` in `wz_capture`
    note: found an item that was configured out
       |   ------------------- the item is gated behind the `dissect` feature

on rustc 1.97, and a `use` import (E0432) gets the same note. The toolchain
grew the diagnostic and the register entry outlived the thing it described --
open-debt item 47's class, arriving in a register entry rather than in a code
comment.

Why that is not the close. "The compiler handles it" is precisely the sentence
that rots next, and this workspace has a rule about prose that is not a gate.
The note appears only while the `#[cfg(feature = ...)]` sits ON the item it
configures out. Move the gate into a `cfg_if`, behind a re-export, or one
module further in, and it goes -- silently, because the consumer who would have
noticed is not in this repository. MEASURED, not feared: the empty-stub shape
the item itself names as a tempting non-fix (`#[cfg(not(feature))] pub mod
fields_json {}`) degrades the error to `cannot find function 'fields_json' in
module 'wz_capture::fields_json'`, with the feature named nowhere at all.

So the compiler became an ORACLE rather than a claim. `feature_gate_diagnostic.py`
builds a throwaway consumer against a feature-off `wz-capture` and reads what
rustc says. It fails three ways, and the middle one is the reason it exists:
the probe COMPILES (the path is reachable without the feature, so the probe has
been measuring nothing -- a dead probe and a negative result share an exit
code); the build fails and the note does not name the feature (the item); or a
declared feature has neither a probe nor a stated reason (silence).

The population is cargo's, not a grep's: the feature map and the transitive
closure of `default` come from `cargo metadata`, and the feature set each probe
builds against is DERIVED as `default-features = false` plus that closure minus
the feature under test -- one recipe that works the same for a default-on
feature as for a default-off one.

The bound is stated as a number rather than left as an impression. The axis
covers ONE package, and the banner says how many workspace packages it does
not. That residue is filed as item 532 with its own measurement, because it is
a different question from this one: not "is the consumer told", which now has
an instrument, but "how many of the other 521 non-default features gate a
public path at all", which needs an API-diff instrument before it can be
answered honestly.

Round 2116.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 466 CLOSED: `wz_dissect.h` now records which doors were
subsumed, and the SHIPPED LIBRARY is what decides whether it is telling the
truth.

The gap, re-measured before anything was written. R311y932 gave
`wz_dissect_readable_surfaces` a `doors` axis, so a program can ASK which door
is the current shape for each job. A person reading the header still saw nine
entry points in a row with nothing separating a current one from an older one.
Sweeping the header for `subsume`, `supersede`, `prefer` and `instead` returns
six hits and not one is about a door: they are ordinary prose ("a document
instead of a struct tree"). A header is what a linking consumer reads first and
often only, so "ask at runtime" is an answer for a program and none at all for
the person choosing a symbol.

Why not just write the comments. The item names that trap itself: comments are
prose, and prose is what item 450 already cost a round for. A line nobody
measures goes stale on the day a tenth door lands, and it goes stale in the
worst direction -- a consumer told a door is current when it is not.

So the comment got a checkable FORM and the artifact became the oracle.
`SUBSUMED BY <successor>` must sit inside the comment block that precedes that
door's own declaration, and the gate cuts that span mechanically: from the end
of the previous `int wz_dissect_*(` to the end of this one. What the header
claims is held against what the release cdylib answers when
`wz_dissect_readable_surfaces` is called through ctypes -- deliberately NOT
against the Rust `Door` walk, which would be comparing two files in the same
commit with each other.

Four ways to fail, and each was driven: no marker where the library says
subsumed (which is how the header actually stood -- the gate's first run named
all five); a marker naming a different successor than the library does; a
marker beside a door the library calls current; and a marker sitting beside no
declaration at all, which states a fact a reader can only find by searching.
The gate also refuses to run over nothing: an absent cdylib and a zero-door
document each fail rather than pass quietly.

The mutation found a hole in the GATE, which is the part worth keeping. A span
carrying two markers -- the true successor and a contradicting second line --
passed a membership test, while a reader in front of it has two answers and no
way to pick. The check is now exact-one. A gate that under-reports is the one
failure a gate must not have, and it was three characters of leniency.

The candidate the round did not take: generating the header from the `Door`
walk so the comments have a single source. That would replace a hand-written
header that `capi_abi_pin.py` already pins, which is a larger decision than
this item; the trade taken here is the tree's usual one -- the prose stays
hand-written and a gate holds the fact inside it, the shape item 526 used for
build prerequisites.

Open-debt item 498 CLOSED: a deployment that is a FRAGMENT can say so, and

The gap. `--check-topology` reads its files as a closed deployment, which is
the contract that makes a dangling dial findable at all. The shape this project
is measured against is not closed: wz nodes attached to a stock zenohd somebody
else runs. Against that set every outward dial came back a defect and the whole
surface was unusable -- the verdict correct, the tool useless for the ordinary
case.

The trade the item flagged, and why this round did not have to make it. The
item's own note said the obvious fix inverts the false-positive direction:
widening a listener set can only ever SILENCE a defect, so a careless
declaration turns the next real typo quiet, and "that trade is not for one
round to decide alone". It is not decided here either -- it is removed. The
widening is BIDIRECTIONAL. A declaration that answers no dial is reported. One
the set already listens on is reported, against the node that answers it, so
the reader is sent to the config that makes the declaration wrong rather than
to a machine that has nothing to do with it. One that does not parse is
reported rather than dropped, because dropping it widens nothing while the
operator believes it did. A declaration has to earn its place.

And a green verdict says what it assumed. Every dial an external declaration
answered comes back in the report as its own line, on the failure path too: a
set with one real dangling dial and three externally answered ones is a
different thing to go and look at. Without that, a fragment that checks out
reads exactly like a closed deployment answering for itself, which is the
quietest way to be wrong here.

of clients attached to an external router is the single most ordinary fragment
there is; reporting "every node is a client" at it would fail the exact

THE RENAME WAS ALWAYS FREE, AND THE BELIEF THAT IT WAS NOT COST A ROUND.

Item 467 is the priority queue's head. It says `max_messages_per_flow`

C has no named arguments. A prototype's parameter name is documentation,
not ABI. The artifact says so this round rather than the prose: after the
rename `capi_abi_pin.py` reads ABI 12 and 21 exported symbols out of the
release cdylib, set unchanged. Nothing moved, which is what the item's own

WHAT THE ITEM'S SCOPE MISSED. It named ONE parameter. Deriving the
population from the header instead of from the item found EIGHT
bound-shaped parameters over SEVEN doors, in THREE disciplines a reader
cannot tell apart by looking: `trims-output` (the document is shortened
after the walk is paid for), `work-ceiling` (the walk itself is bounded),

THE GATE'S CERTIFIER IS A COMPILER, NOT ITS OWN REGEX. `gcc -aux-info`
re-emits every prototype it parsed, with full parameter types and no
names. Names are the one thing it discards -- which is exactly the half
wanted here -- so the gate refuses to run unless its own extraction agrees
with GCC function for function and type for type, and then reads names out
of a declaration a compiler has already bounded. A population of zero is a
FAIL: an absent compiler, an unreadable header and a header that bounds
nothing are otherwise one exit code.

declared discipline is TRUE OF THE CODE. That is a claim about behaviour
and behaviour holds it -- R311y933's test, which item 450 bought. This gate
holds the NAME to the declared discipline; that test holds the discipline
to the library. A gate implying it had checked both would be the same false
comfort the name itself was.

it, and the run is green. So presence is asserted against a declared list
of shared groups and agreement against the intersection -- two questions
that fail differently, because one population can shrink and the other
cannot.

because it answers half of "how much" and none of "where".

R311y918 stopped the census reporting `[419, 0]`. A row is keyed on the
keyexpr alone, so it folds every flow and both directions, and an anchor is
a byte offset inside ONE direction of a stream or a packet index -- two
coordinate systems with nothing on a frame saying which. It gave the pair
to the space that opened it and refused foreign anchors, which made the
interval true. It also DISCARDED those foreign anchors after using them to
set a flag, so the reader was told the interval covers part of the row and
could not tell whether the rest was one record or a thousand.

WHERE THE DISCARDED ANCHORS WENT IS THIS ROUND. Each row now carries one
extent per contributing space -- first, last, the space's name, and the
number of records in it.

KEYED ON THE TOKEN AND NOT ON THE KIND, which is the part that would have
been easy to get wrong. Two directions of one stream are two spaces wearing
one name, so merging by `AnchorSpace` would rebuild the impossible interval
this whole axis exists to prevent. Measured rather than argued: the
mutation that merges by kind prints `first: 0, last: 448` for a row whose
two directions never shared a coordinate system.

THE RECORD COUNTS ARE THE LOAD-BEARING PART, NOT THE EXTENTS. Extents alone
are the crate asserting its own arithmetic. The counts are summed against
`totals().messages()`, which is accumulated on a DIFFERENT path -- the five
per-kind counters -- so a record that lands in no extent, which is exactly
what the old walk did, fails here instead of being invisible. That is the
one assertion a build cannot satisfy by being self-consistently wrong.

classification from being a label nobody honours -- each reporting field's

printed the same key one line down. A witness any line may satisfy is a
witness for the report as a whole and for no axis in it. The check now
takes the LABEL as an argument and looks only at that line. This is the
second consecutive round where designing the mutation, rather than running
it, is what found the hole -- and the first where the mutation had already
been run and passed before the hole was understood.

THE ITEM ASKED FOR A LINT AND SAID IN THE SAME BREATH THAT THE LINT WOULD

Round 2126.decision_summary:
THE CHECK COMPARED KEYS BY WHERE THEY SAT, AND FOR HALF THE KEYS THAT IS
THE ONE THING THAT CAN NEVER MATCH.

Item 447 is the priority queue's head. Item 441 built RFC 8949 §5.6
duplicate detection on path-segment equality, which is exactly right for a
NAMED key -- the segment is derived from the value, so the immediate `1`
and the one-byte `1` land on one string where byte comparison would have
called them two. It is exactly wrong for the rest: a container, tag or
indefinite-length key gets a `\x<offset>` locator, an offset is unique by
construction, and so two identical container keys were two different
segments that could never be counted. R311y916 pinned that gap in a test
rather than leave it to be found, and item 447 named inverting that test as
the landing signal.

THE OWNER'S RULING, AND WHAT IT SAID NOT TO DO. Fix it by normalised
comparison; and the reason is NOT frequency -- if §2's data model calls two
things one key and the checker counts two, that is the checker being wrong,
whatever publishers happen to do. The item's own "measure the frequency
first" prescription was retired in the same breath, so no round burns
itself measuring something that cannot change the answer. None was.

THE ITEM'S OWN PROPOSAL WAS THE WORSE ANSWER AND IS THE INTERESTING PART.
It proposed comparing the key item's BYTE SPAN. Bytes make `[1]` and
`(_ 1)` different keys, which §2 says they are not -- so the fix would have
traded item 441's missed duplicates for invented ones, and item 434's whole
subject is that a false "invalid" on a well-formed publisher's traffic
costs more than a missed one. Canonicalising the bytes instead means
writing a second CBOR encoder beside this decoder, which is the "second
opinion about what CBOR is" this module refuses on the same grounds
`json_keys` refuses a second parser.

SO THE IDENTITY IS WALKED, NOT SLICED. An unnamed key is walked into a
SCRATCH emitter and the rows it produces -- paths and renderings, both
already value-derived -- are the description compared. Encoding variance
folds away for free, because it had already been folded away for every
named key. `, indefinite` is stripped: it is a wire fact the document
carries on purpose, and §2 equality is not about the wire, so keeping it
would have made `[]` and `(_ )` two keys and half-closed the item with a
new wrong answer in the other half.

THE COST ITEM 441 NAMED IS STILL PAID WHERE IT WAS. The scratch emitter is
installed only when rows are being emitted, so `scan_cbor` -- the path
every payload in a capture runs through -- still allocates nothing here.

Round 2127.decision_summary:
THE ITEM READ THE RIGHT BRANCH AND MISSED WHO TAKES IT.

Item 497 is the priority queue's head. R2071 read upstream's
`connect_peers_single_link` and found that on the retry path it calls
`peer_connector_retry` and returns `Ok(())`, so a node with nowhere to
attach retries for ever and never exits. From that it concluded that all
three topology verdicts -- `DanglingConnectTarget`,
`ListenEndpointCollision`, `NoNodeAccepts` -- have only a timeout NEGATIVE
for an observable, and that a foreign witness would need a non-default
`connect/retry/timeout_ms = 0` fixture to force an exit.

The branch is real. Which nodes take it is MODE-DEPENDENT, and that is what
the item did not carry. Read this round at the pinned rev, in
`commons/zenoh-config/src/defaults.rs` rather than in the JSON5 comments:

  * `connect::timeout_ms` is `{ router: -1, peer: -1, client: 0 }` and
    `ms_to_duration` maps a negative to `Duration::MAX` and `0` to zero. So
    `get_global_connect_timeout()` is ZERO for a client, a client takes the
    `is_zero()` branch, and its failed dial falls through the loop to
    `Err`. It is the router and the peer that retry for ever.
  * `connect::exit_on_failure` is `{ router: false, peer: false, client: true }`.
  * `listen::timeout_ms` is `Unique(0)` and `listen::exit_on_failure` is
    `Unique(true)`, for every mode.

So two of the three verdicts had a foreign witness at STOCK CONFIG all
along, and the third needs only a client. The fixture the item proposed is
not needed and is not used -- which matters beyond tidiness: a witness that
has to bend the config is evidence about the bent config, not about a
deployment anybody runs. That is the second round running where the item's
own prescription was the thing that most needed probing.

WHICH NODE EXITS IS THE CONTENT OF THE TEST, because it differs per defect
and naming it is what makes each arm a witness rather than a coincidence.
The collision is observable only once the FIRST binder holds the address,
so that arm holds it up for the whole arm and watches the second. The
dangling target is the dialling client, in a set that has a listener
elsewhere so the verdict under test is that one and not `NoNodeAccepts`.
`NoNodeAccepts` is the only node there is, and upstream refuses it with
`No peer specified and multicast scouting deactivated!` before any dial is
attempted at all.

THE CONTROL HAD TO BE A PAIR. A single node that starts is no control here:
every arm below ends in a client exiting, and "a client exited" is as well
explained by "a client always exits". So the control is a peer that listens
and a client that dials it, and the client staying UP is what makes the
three exits mean something.
verification_bullets: THE PREMISE WAS RE-DERIVED FROM UPSTREAM, not from the item: `zenoh/src/net/runtime/orchestrator.rs` at the pinned rev `49c8a53` for the branch, and `commons/zenoh-config/src/defaults.rs` for the values that decide which node takes it. The JSON5 comments agree, but the constants are what was read.

`connect::timeout_ms = { router: -1, peer: -1, client: 0 }` with `ms_to_duration` mapping a negative to `Duration::MAX`; `connect::exit_on_failure = { router: false, peer: false, client: true }`; `listen::timeout_ms = Unique(0)` and `listen::exit_on_failure = Unique(true)`. `get_retry_config` resolves both by `whatami`, so the mode-dependence is real and not a reading of the defaults file alone.

`zenohd_refuses_every_topology_the_validator_rejects` runs in Layer Z against a real zenohd: each arm asserts the validator reports the expected `TopologyDefect` FIRST, then watches the node upstream refuses exit, then reads the captured output so an unrelated crash cannot pass for the predicted refusal.
The positive control is a listener/client pair and requires the CLIENT to stay up. It is the arm that makes the other three mean anything, because every one of them ends in a client exiting.

Round 2128.decision_summary:
THE ITEM'S OWN PROBE WAS WRONG IN THE ONE DIRECTION A GATE MUST NOT BE.

Item 479 is the priority queue's head. It recorded that among the `&self`
accessors of `Dissection` and `DissectionHealth`, two had callers only inside
`mod tests`, and it offered its own sweep as the draft for the instrument: for
each accessor, grep for `.name(` outside test regions.

Both halves were re-measured this round and both moved.

The COUNT: rustdoc reports 32 public `&self` accessors on those two types, not
31. The item's number was a round old.

The PRESCRIPTION is the one that matters. A name sweep UNDER-REPORTS, which is
the single defect a gate may not have, and `Dissection::flow` is the witness.
Its only `.flow(` call site in 836 tracked files is `wz-analyze/src/lib.rs:2798`
-- a call to `FieldNote::flow`, a PRIVATE method on a different type in a
different crate. The sweep credits that call and reports the accessor reached.
It is not reached: it has no caller of any kind anywhere in the tree. The sweep
finds 3 members; the gate finds 21; the one it swallowed is the one its own
draft could not have seen. That is the second round running in which the item's
prescription was the part most needing a probe.

WHAT ANSWERS INSTEAD IS THE LINKER. Rust mangling -- legacy `_ZN` and v0 `_R`
alike -- writes a path as a run of `<len><ident>` pairs, so `10Dissection5flows`
names the method AND the impl type it hangs off, and `FieldNote::flow` mangles
under `9FieldNote`. No namesake can be confused for another. This is the same
move as `capi_abi_pin.py` making `gcc -aux-info` the authenticator rather than
a reader of prototypes.

The boundary guard belongs on the LEFT only, and the right-hand one was written
and then removed: the length prefix already pins the identifier's extent, while
v0 appends a disambiguator digit directly after it
(`22evict_flows_beyond_cap0NC`), so a non-alphanumeric check on the right
rejects real matches.

THE POPULATION IS A CLOSURE, NOT A LIST. Start at `Dissection`, follow the
struct types in each inherent method's return position, repeat: 33 types. The
item named two, and 17 of the 21 members reported sit on types it never
mentioned. A hand-listed population would have reproduced the blindness the
item is about.

ONE AXIS, DELIBERATELY. "Test-only" and "called by nothing at all" are
different states -- `chain_bytes_lost` has two tests, `flow` and
`serial_messages` have no caller at all -- and this does not split them.
Deriving that split soundly needs the test binary of every member that could
hold a caller, and reading whichever ones happen to be built is the defect the
cdylib SONAME probe was caught by on 2026-08-25: a population taken from what
was lying in the target directory. A half-derived second axis is
under-reporting wearing a hat, which is the call item 531 made about the second
delivery degree.

Round 2129.decision_summary:
ITEM 302'S FINDING REPEATS IN ITS DENOMINATOR AND NOT IN ITS RATIO.

Item 480 is the priority queue's head. It asked what the `FieldNote` sentence
costs -- the third note row kind, sibling to the two item 302 measured and
stopped at -- and recorded two things to check rather than trust: that the
answer would look like 302's, and that the plane is "per flow".

Both were re-derived and both moved.

THE RATIO DOES NOT REPEAT. Measured through the real renderers, one realistic
instance per kind, JSON bytes against the sentence inside them:

    not_decrypted                257 / 171  (66%)
    nothing_walkable             158 /  69  (43%)
    capture_not_reread           108 /  69  (63%)
    payload_rule_refused         173 / 132  (76%)
    payload_declaration_unbound  161 / 120  (74%)
    omitted                      109 /  18  (16%)
    disagreement                 227 /  95  (41%)

1193 bytes carrying 674 of prose, 56% over the plane. Item 302 found BOTH its
row kinds at a steady 63%; these run from 16% to 76%. The cheap ones are cheap
because the sentence is a count -- `omitted` is 18 bytes of prose -- and the
dear ones are dear because the sentence is the only place the remedy is
written. A single ratio describes none of them, so the ratio is not the finding
here. The rows are also smaller than 302's: 108..257 against 326..400.

THE DENOMINATOR DOES REPEAT, and it is measured rather than reasoned. Three
messages against thirty on ONE flow, driven end to end through
`analyze_request`, is one note either way and 109 bytes against 111 -- the
digits of the count and nothing else. Every note is pushed once per flow, once
per capture, or once per declaration the caller typed; none is pushed per
message.

THE ITEM'S TWO COORDINATES WERE BOTH STALE. `FieldNote` is at lib.rs:2522, not
2409. And "per flow" is true of FOUR of its seven variants: `CaptureNotReread`,
`PayloadRuleRefused` and `PayloadDeclarationUnbound` are capture-wide or
per-declaration, and `Disagreement` -- the one variant that does carry a
per-message list -- takes the same `--max-messages` bound as the rows, which
R311y681's test already holds. That is why the denominator claim is gated end
to end and not on a constructed value: where a note is PUSHED is the property
at risk, and a hand-built note cannot show it.

THE POPULATION IS HELD BY THE COMPILER, not by a list. The measurement matches
exhaustively over the variants, so an eighth kind makes five matches
non-exhaustive and the crate stops building. The failure this closes is
precisely a kind sitting unmeasured beside its measured siblings, so the guard
has to be the one thing that cannot be forgotten.

THE ITEM'S OWN "NOT MEASURED" LINE WAS THE WHOLE ITEM, AND THE ANSWER IS THREE
DIFFERENT ANSWERS.

Item 402 is the priority queue's head. It records that a sweep can read a
literal out of a COMMENT and count it as data, gives two instances, and then
ends on a line that is the actual deliverable: NOT MEASURED -- whether the
other sweeps of the same shape (`count_guard_lint.py`,
`analysis_surface_parity.py`, `dissect_name_census.py` itself) do it too.

Measured this round, by injecting a probe into the real files rather than by
reading the regexes:

  * `dissect_name_census.py` COUNTS a comment's literals, and is RIGHT to. A
    literal it claims must be DECLARED, so over-collecting cannot hide a name
    that reached the wire. Its failure message already says so at the point of
    failure: "a doc comment's and a test's included".
  * `count_guard_lint.py` COUNTS them and is WRONG to. A doc comment carrying
    `#[test] #[ignore]` on one line -- the shape a file uses to show the
    attribute it is about -- turned "1 #[ignore]d test" into 2 and made the
    lint accuse `run-ci.sh` of a stale guard. Both halves of that accusation
    were false.
  * `analysis_surface_parity.py` COUNTED them and was WRONG to, and that
    instance is MINE: R2130's claim resolver, written last round to close item
    242, searched whole files, so a reason could name something that exists
    nowhere but prose and still resolve. Measured with an invented token
    inserted as a comment: it resolved. Same seam, so it is repaid here rather
    than filed as a new number.

OVER-INCLUSION IS NOT UNIFORMLY SAFE, which is what item 402 already suspected
and what separates these three. Where a claimed name costs a declaration, too
many is safe. Where the sweep publishes a COUNT or resolves a CHECK, too many
is a wrong number and a check that passes on nothing -- and no floor catches
that direction, because too many clears every minimum.

MY FIRST PROBE WAS MORE LENIENT THAN THE LANE. Injecting `//! #[test]` alone
left `count_guard_lint` green, and the reason is that the guard on that file
reads the IGNORED bucket while a bare `#[test]` lands in the plain one. The
probe only bit once it carried `#[ignore]` too. Which bucket a guard reads is
part of choosing the probe.

ten resolve in stripped code and exactly one does not: `no callbacks run`, the

splits on the token's own shape -- a name with a space in it is a PHRASE and
answers to the documentation, a name without one is an IDENTIFIER and answers

would have been the same error in the other direction.

boundary is stated "in one comment and nowhere else"; the failure message states

nothing would notice it silently flipping. That is what the census's new
selftest holds.

THE ITEM'S PROPOSED FIX WOULD HAVE BEEN BORN GREEN, AND WOULD NOT HAVE CAUGHT
THE INSTANCE THE ITEM ITSELF RECORDS.

Item 405 is the priority queue's head. It records that
`dissect_name_census.py`'s exit 0 says one thing only -- the name was DECLARED
-- and that nothing measures whether the REASON declaring it is still true of
this tree. Its instance: the `priority` row sat asserting that a name there
"would be a table with no adjudicator behind it" while the same round put
`crate::qos::Priority::name` behind it. The gate said nothing about that
sentence; a human opened the table because six unrelated new names were
REJECTED, which is a discovery path by accident.

The item then offers a shape: if a reason cites a code symbol, check the symbol
still exists. That was PROBED before it was built, and it does not hold up:

  * Every in-tree symbol these reasons cite resolves today --
    `crate::qos::Priority::name`, `crate::qos::CongestionControl`,
    `Field::find`, `ext_name::ext_name`, `walk_wireexpr`. Red-first count: 0.
  * The two numeric claims the reasons make about in-tree types were measured
    too: `CongestionControl` has 2 variants and `Priority` has 8, exactly as
    written. Red-first count: 0 there as well.
  * Decisively, it does NOT catch the item's own instance. The stale `priority`
    sentence cited no symbol at all -- it asserted an ABSENCE.

So the built instrument is aimed at the population that is actually live, which
is the BACKTICK: the place where a reason stops arguing and NAMES something.
R2130 found the same seam one gate over, which makes this the second instrument
of that shape rather than the first.

INVARIANT 4: every backticked plain identifier in an `OWN_VOCABULARY` /
`AWAITING_WALKER` reason must resolve to a live name on this surface -- a
walker's, a codec's, or an `ext_name` row's -- or be declared in
`REASON_NON_NAMES` with what it is instead. Both staleness directions, on rule
3's own logic: a declared non-name that BECOMES a name fails, and one no reason
cites any more fails. The first of those is the `priority` shape.

TOKEN SHAPE IS THE DISCRIMINATOR, and demanding more would reject true prose.
A reason's backticks hold three kinds of thing and only one is adjudicable
here: names on this surface are, while upstream types and expressions
(`QoSType::is_express`, `ext.value as u8`) and file paths
(`network/request.rs`) belong to a checkout this repository deliberately
records no path for. Anything carrying `::`, an uppercase letter, whitespace, a
dot or a slash is left alone.

silently license a reason that argues about nothing. R2131 measured three
sweeps of this shape and got three different answers; this is the fourth, in

node can win -- which is also what makes it bindable twice HERE". Measured this
round, it is true only on a host whose resolver gives `localhost` ONE address.

assumption about it: one claimant per address the endpoint resolves to, plus
the one that must find nothing left. On a single-family host that is the two
nodes the fixture always had; on a dual-stack host it is three. The count is
derived, and `resolve_endpoint_addrs` refuses an empty resolution so the set
can never collapse to a single node whose collision nobody contests.

rejected for the reason this same file already states about bent fixtures: a
witness that has to manufacture the refusal is evidence about the manufacture.

THE ITEM SAID "WIRING, NOT DESIGN", AND BOTH HALVES OF THAT WERE WRONG. THE
CORRECTIONS ARE THE ROUND.

Open-debt item 223: `scouting/multicast/autoconnect` and its `_strategy` are
unhonoured, so "a wz that ANSWERED a Scout never dials the node that asked".
The item filed it as a wiring round on the strength of wz already having an
`AutoConnect` in `wz-routing-graph`. Read against the pinned checkout, neither
premise survives.

FIRST, the defect sentence. Upstream's `Runtime::responder`
(`zenoh/src/net/runtime/orchestrator.rs:1112`) answers a Scout with a Hello and
dials NOTHING. The dialling is `autoconnect_all` (:1090), a SEPARATE arm of the
same `tokio::select!` in `start_scout`, which SCOUTS with the policy's own
matcher as the Scout's `what` and dials whoever answers ITS scout. So the
trigger is not "I answered someone"; it is "someone answered ME, and my policy
admits their role and zid". Building what the item literally described would

the question an operator asks ("I moved the group on both boxes; do they still
find each other?") had no witness.

The item's SECOND half is what this round had to correct. It said a group-only
move fails to discriminate because Linux `IP_MULTICAST_ALL` "delivers to a
wildcard-bound socket BY PORT, and the joined group is irrelevant". Measured,
that is not the rule. `IP_MULTICAST_ALL` (ip(7), default 1) delivers the groups
joined GLOBALLY ON THE HOST. With nobody holding the other group there is
nothing to leak, and the datagram is refused at the host. Three arms, measured
here: no co-joiner -> not delivered; co-joiner present -> delivered; co-joiner
present with `IP_MULTICAST_ALL` cleared -> not delivered.

So the item's conclusion ("only moving the PORT discriminates") is TRUE, but
only in the arrangement it was measured in -- a same-host loopback pair, where
the node that moved IS the co-joiner that makes the leak possible. The cause is
the host membership, not the port. Written down the item's way, the new file
would have carried an explanation that predicts the wrong thing on two hosts.

THE THIRD FINDING IS THE ONE THAT DECIDED THE SHAPE OF THE REPAYMENT. Neither
zenoh nor zenoh-pico touches `IP_MULTICAST_ALL` (grep, both pinned checkouts),
and zenoh binds the wildcard exactly as wz does
(`io/zenoh-links/zenoh-link-udp/src/multicast.rs:308-312`). The leak is
therefore UPSTREAM-FAITHFUL BEHAVIOUR, not a wz defect, and clearing the option
would be a divergence dressed as a fix. There is nothing to repair in the
socket; what was missing was the lane. So this round ships no behaviour change
at all -- two new files, three wiring points, and no line of `lib.rs` altered.

port, ..)`: the other three are the `pub` fields of `McastSocketConfig`. A count

Round 2146.decision_summary:
CANCELLING AN ANNOUNCEMENT IS ALLOWED; THE MOMENT A SUCCESSOR REVISION
EXISTS, THE PROMISE BINDS.

Unregistered open-debt item 534 (R2121, the residue of 460) says
`DocumentShape::retiring` promises that a key leaves in the next revision
and that nobody measures whether it does. Measured this round: the
coordinates are exact. `doc_revision::audit` walks the revisions in
`windows(2)` and asks one question in one direction only -- when a key
LEAVES, did the row before it announce the departure. An announcement
that is never honoured is refused by nothing, so `retiring` could name a
key forever. A promise nobody measures is decoration, not a contract.

THE ITEM NAMED ITS OWN OPEN QUESTION AND THIS ROUND ANSWERS IT. Item 534
closes with "whether to permit cancellation is this item's real
question", because the obvious fix -- the successor MUST drop the key --
also forbids withdrawing an announcement. The answer is that
cancellation stays possible, and the reasoning is about who gets hurt:
KEEPING a key is the safe direction for a consumer. Someone who read the
announcement and prepared for the departure is not broken by its
absence, so a rule that drove every announcement to completion would
compel a removal nobody needed. What is refused is the third thing --
a successor that neither honours the promise nor withdraws it.

THE WAY OUT IS AN EDIT, NOT AN EXEMPTION. To cancel, the announcing
row's `retiring` is edited away in the SAME commit that adds the
successor revision. The promise and its withdrawal then land together,
which is a visible act; the failure this rule exists to catch is the
silent lapse, where a revision ships and the announcement simply stops
meaning anything. The refusal therefore NAMES BOTH EXITS -- drop the key
in the successor, or withdraw the announcement from the announcing row
in the commit that adds the successor. A message that named only the
first would push every reader toward the removal that item 534 itself
warned must not be compelled.

THE ITEM'S SECOND PRESCRIPTION IS DECLINED, ON THE RECORD. Item 534
offered two shapes: give an announcement an expiry (the next row must
drop it), or FAIL when an announcement has lived more than N revisions.
The first is what shipped. The second is not, because N is an arbitrary
threshold and an arbitrary threshold is a population of zero in
disguise -- it would pass for N-1 revisions of exactly the silence the
item objects to. An announcement in the NEWEST revision has no successor
yet and is legitimately in flight, and no rule over this table can force
the next revision to be written. That residue is named rather than
gated: the accounting test prints every in-flight announcement BY NAME
so it cannot go quiet.

THE CENSUS DENOMINATOR IS A FUNCTION OF WHAT THE FILE FILLS, AND THE SET
OF PLACES WHERE IT BENDS IS DERIVABLE RATHER THAN LISTABLE.

Unregistered open-debt items 215 and 217 (both R311y844) were paid in one
round because they are one seam, and that was MEASURED rather than
assumed. 215 says `connect/retry` is an opaque subtree, so honouring it
changes what the census denominator counts. 217 says the denominator is
the surface of an EMPTY config while an operator's real file is wider --
a fixture carrying `metadata: { name: … }` makes the ingest report
`metadata/name` where the canonical surface has `metadata`. Both are the
same sentence about the same set of keys.

THAT SET IS `DEEPENABLE_UPSTREAM_KEYS`, AND IT IS A DERIVATION, NOT A
CHOICE. The constant is DEFINED as the keys below which a real zenohd
accepts leaves this tree's census surface does not list, one zenohd run
per entry (R2078/R2079). So it is exactly the set of places a document
can add leaves the empty-file resolution does not show -- which is the
population both items are about. Measured this round: 17 members, 7
honoured and 10 not.

BOTH ITEMS' COORDINATES WERE STALE, AND THE STALENESS RAN OPPOSITE WAYS.
215 asks for a honoured-key matcher that handles subtrees; R311y849 had
already built one (`HONOURED_SUBTREE_LEAVES`, three fields under
`connect/retry`) and R2141 had already routed three more keys through
`MODE_DEPENDENT_CONFIG_KEYS`. So the fix 215 requested exists. What did
not exist was any instrument that looks: both rounds got it right BY
HAND, and a fourth key moved without its deeper leaves being claimed
would have shipped wz applying a block while reporting that block's own
fields as unhonoured. This round's output is therefore a RATCHET over a
population that is currently clean, and saying so is part of the claim
rather than a hedge appended to it.

217 IS THE OPPOSITE: WHAT IT CALLS A COST IS THE RIGHT CHOICE, AND WHAT
WAS MISSING IS ANYTHING THAT KEEPS IT. Taking the denominator from a
config that fills nothing is correct -- otherwise the census measures
the fixture. That reasoning lived only in `census_config`'s doc comment,
and prose is not a gate (the standing shape of item 530).

THE OBLIGATION HAS TWO SITES, WHICH IS THE LESSON R2143 PAID FOR. A
honoured key obliges two places and that round looked at one. Here the
denominator obliges (a) the surface constants and (b) the census fixture
that produces the surface. The constants are answered by a unit test in
`zenoh_config.rs`; the fixture is in ANOTHER CRATE behind `#[ignore]`,
so it is answered by a third site in `config_key_fixture_gate.py` --
the same static-read shape R2138 built for the same pair of files, for
the same reason: the leg that would otherwise notice needs a built
zenohd and runs only on hosted Layer Z.

SET ARITHMETIC IS NOT ENOUGH, SO THE SAME POPULATION IS ALSO DRIVEN.
Four constants can agree with each other while the reader does something
else, so a third test feeds every one of the 17 keys through
`from_json5` and asserts which partition the deeper leaf lands in. It
needs no per-key value knowledge, and that is deliberate: a table of
values would be a copy of the reader's own type expectations. The
mode-table probe names `router` while the document says `mode: "peer"`,
so the resolver answers "no instruction for this node" without ever
inspecting the value. That test earned its place immediately -- in the
red-first control it caught the mutation from a DIFFERENT direction than
the set test, naming a `WrongType` that showed the reader still read the
key as a mode table while the constant had stopped saying so.

The probe already separated a mode table from an opaque subtree and then threw
that apart away: `elif verdict in ("OPAQUE", "MODE_TABLE")` folded both into one

compared against nothing. `MODE_DEPENDENT_CONFIG_KEYS` decides two things —
whether `inside_a_mode_table` lifts every leaf under a key out of the ignored
report, and which claim mechanism R2147's partition rule demands — and a key
wrongly on it makes wz read an operator's typo as a row of a table it honours:
not applied, not reported, silent. This round cross-checks the two, in both
directions, against a running zenohd.

Two of the item's own claims were refuted by measuring rather than reading.

The item prescribed a symmetric both-directions comparison of the MODE_TABLE set
against the constant. Run that way it reds on `scouting/multicast/autoconnect_strategy`,
which belongs on the list: upstream declares it
`ModeDependentValue<TargetDependentValue<AutoConnectStrategy>>`, whose inner
`Dependent` arm accepts any object, so the probe's `{ zzz_not_a_mode: 1 }` parses
and the node starts. OPAQUE is therefore a fact about the PROBE's reach, not
about the key, and the two directions have to be asymmetric: a declared key is
refuted only by REFUSED, while OPAQUE is printed by name and folded into no pass.

The item also said both existing gates pass the wrong directions green. They do
not. Driven with the whole `zenoh_config::` module under three constant
mutations, each one reds a pre-existing test. What is new here is not a catch for
an ordinary slip but the QUESTION: every existing gate checks wz's constants
against wz's own reader, and `missing`/`stale` asks upstream only whether a key
takes a deeper shape AT ALL — precisely the question that conflates a mode table
with an opaque subtree. A wz that is wrong about upstream and self-consistent
passes all of them.

keys' behaviours. A group rationale is a claim about EVERY member, so one false
member is the whole group asking to be re-read.

Round 2151.decision_summary:
R2150 closed item 539 by making every CITED unhonoured key record why wz naming
it is not proof wz honours it. Its population is the keys wz's source NAMES —
nineteen of seventy-nine — and it reported the other sixty as outside what it
claimed. That gap is item 540, and the class it hides is the worse one: a key wz
grew a capability for under a spelling of its own leaves no citation, stays in
`UNHONOURED_BEYOND_WZ`, and an operator's file that states it looks like it works
and does nothing.

The obvious repair is a wider sweep. Three were built and measured, and all three
are FLOORS that miss DIFFERENT things.

  * Leaf identifiers — each key's own last segment, used only where it is unique
    across the 111-key surface: 30 of 72 candidates, dominated by homonyms
    (`data` alone hits 127 sites), and it misses `connect_certificate` outright
    because wz spells that `cert_chain_pem`.
  * Key segments against wz's module and crate names: a different 30, and it
    misses the entire TLS group, because `tls` is a segment twelve surface keys
    share and a shared segment cannot say which key a hit is about.
  * Upstream's own config type names: wz mirrors them when it implements
    (`AclConfig`, `DownsamplingRule`, `LowPassRule`) and not always
    (`PluginsConfig` → `PluginRegistry`, `TLSConf` → `tls_config`), so it caught
    one of this round's three findings.

Three measurements, three different holes, so the answer is not a better sweep.
It is to make the obligation PER ROW and cover the population by definition:
`UNHONOURED_BEYOND_GROUPS` accounts for every key in `UNHONOURED_BEYOND_WZ`, and
each group names the thing wz would need as an identifier that must NOT appear in
wz's code. The day wz grows that thing, the anchor appears and the group reds.

The first run moved eleven rows, 72/7 becoming 61/18, and not one of the three
was found by a sweep. `access_control/*` (5) sat under "a policy engine
(subjects, rules, permissions)" while `wz-access-control` IS one — `AclConfig`
carries `default_permission` and an ordered `Vec<AclRule>`, each rule a subject
selector, flow set, message set and permission. `enabled` moved with them because
wz's OFF state exists and is the default: a peer with no policy installed
enforces nothing, so the reader chooses not to install rather than building a
switch — which is what separates it from `scouting/gossip/enabled`, where the
switch would have to be built. `plugins` and `plugins_loading/enabled` (2) sat
under "a plugin host" while `PluginRegistry` loads, starts, stops and
admin-reports dynamic plugins; `plugins_loading/search_dirs` did NOT move, because
wz loads by explicit path and has no discovery. The four TLS keys sat among the
link knobs "wz does not expose" while `tls_config.rs` carries `ClientAuthPem` and
`ServerNameVerification`, and the C ABI already exposes both.

How the TLS group was actually found is worth more than the group: the leaf sweep
pointed at ONE key in that file, and reading the file produced its three
siblings. A hit is a reason to read the file, not a finding.

Two checks raise the cost — the anchor must also appear in the list's own doc,
beside the sentence a human reads, and the groups must account for every key —
and a determined author can still sub-group a failure away. That residue is
accepted, not closed.

Round 2152.decision_summary:
A residue sweep over this session's own two rounds, and one of the three things
it turned up was a false parity statement R2151 had just written.

R2151 moved `access_control/subjects` into `UNHONOURED_READER_GAP` and said it
"reaches only wz's zid axis". That was measured off `SubjectSelector` alone,
which is indeed `Any | Zid`. It is wrong about wz: R311y453 put two more subject
axes on `AclRule` beside it — `link_protocols` and `interfaces` — so wz reaches
THREE of upstream's five, and the two genuinely absent are `cert_common_names`
and `usernames`.

What makes this worth a round rather than a typo fix is where the right answer
already was. The `access-acl` catalog atom's reason has carried it since
R311y453, in those words, and the list R2151 was editing exists to answer
exactly the question the atom was already answering. A doc sentence about parity
that contradicts the atom grading the same capability is the open-debt-530 class
sitting in code written an hour earlier — and the frozen ledger is why the
correction arrives here as a new entry rather than as an edit to Round 2151.

The sweep's other two findings are registered rather than fixed, both probed
first.

Item 541: the two instruments 539 and 540 built can be walked past with both
halves green, and this round measured the exact path. `plugins` — a key this
session PROVED wz already acts on — went back into `UNHONOURED_BEYOND_WZ` in two
edits, python rc=0 and Rust 49/49. Re-kind its citation row from `wz-has-it` to
`not-this-key` keeping the SAME anchor, then give it a one-key group with an
invented anchor. The load-bearing observation is that `PluginRegistry` satisfies
both kinds: `wz-has-it` needs the anchor PRESENT to show wz has the thing, and
`not-this-key` needs it PRESENT to show the citation is about something else.
The gate never compares the two claims. Item 540's doc admitted this in prose;
what is new is that it is measured and the path is two lines long. Three
candidate repairs are recorded and none is probed — the cheapest of them would
red the tree as it stands today, because `PluginRegistry` is legitimately the
anchor for both `plugins` and `plugins_loading/search_dirs`.

Round 2153 carries a cost figure that was never measured, and correcting it
turned up a second error in the correction itself. The frozen ledger is why both

number is real. The after number was written into the entry, into CLAUDE.md and
into the register BEFORE any second timing run existed — reasoned from the leg's

The first honest measurement came back 92.3s, a delta of about 15s, and the
reason looked convincing: gate 3 builds `wz-runtime-tokio` at DEFAULT features
while gate 2h builds it with `zenoh-config-emit`, so one hook run alternates two

baseline. So the +15s was cargo building the second feature set ONCE, not a
per-push tax, and the standing cost is inside this tree's run-to-run spread. All

Two lessons, and the second is the one worth keeping. A number that reads as
measured must have been measured — that is the class this session spent three
rounds paying down in other people's prose, committed here by the round closing
an item about it. And a delta claimed from n=1 per condition is not a delta: the
first run after a build-shape change measures the build, and only the second
measures the steady state.

Item 541 recorded a measured escape and three candidate repairs, and said none of
the three had been probed. This round probed all three and rejected all three.

Banning an anchor from serving two kinds reds this tree TODAY: `PluginRegistry`
legitimately carries `plugins` and `plugins_loading/enabled` as `wz-has-it` and
`plugins_loading/search_dirs` as `not-this-key`, and all three are correct.

tree — which is worse than the item guessed from one sample. And "a one-key
group moved out of another group is red" needs history: a static reader of one
tree cannot see that anything moved.

So the repair is not a ban but an OBLIGATION, and its entire force is WHERE it
has to be discharged. A `not-this-key` row's mechanism must carry
`NOT-THIS-KEY: <key>` in a file that BOTH holds the anchor in code AND cites the
key — the one place a claim about a mechanism can be read against the mechanism.
Re-hiding `plugins` now requires writing "PluginRegistry is not what honours
`plugins`" into `plugin.rs`, next to the registry that loads, starts and stops
plugins. The gate cannot prove that false. A person opening the file cannot miss
that it is.

The boundary test is the whole fix, and that is measured rather than argued.
`plugin.rs` already carries `NOT-THIS-KEY: plugins_loading/search_dirs`, which
CONTAINS `NOT-THIS-KEY: plugins` as a substring. Replaying R2152's escape with
the disclaimer matched as a plain substring yields zero failures — it escapes
intact. Matched as a whole token it yields one. The same prefix pair that made
this tree a good place to build the check is the pair that would have defeated a

Round 2156.decision_summary:
R2157 closes unregistered open-debt item 543. The LEGS table in
`scripts/lib/nondefault-tests-gate.sh` held ONE leg, and nobody had
counted what the rest of the workspace leaves compiled-but-unrun.

THE POPULATION IS DERIVED, not guessed. Item 543 proposed the
derivation and this round ran it: per crate, the tests
`cargo test -- --list` reports at `--all-features` minus the ones it
reports at default features. MEASURED: 2519 tests across 11 crates
that only a feature build reaches, of which the table ran 84.

The central decision is that a leg NAMES its features and
`--all-features` is REFUSED BY NAME. An all-features leg would cover
the census population BY CONSTRUCTION, because the population is
DEFINED as what all-features lists; the remainder would be zero for
every tree forever and the check could never fire again. That is this
project's "a population of zero reports green" trap with the
population supplied by the check's own definition. A named list is a
PIN instead: tomorrow's feature enters the population and NOT the
leg, the remainder goes positive, and someone has to decide -- widen
the leg, or say in writing why not.

`wz-ap-demo` proves this is not theoretical. At `--all-features` it is
RED, and CORRECTLY so: its
`a_key_that_is_read_while_reaching_nothing_is_not_reported_as_applied`
is a ZERO-POPULATION guard over the keys a build drops, so turning
every feature on leaves it no subject. A crate-level all-features leg
could not have run that crate at all.

Each row carries a `hook`/`lane` SCOPE. Item 543's own criterion is
"safe AND QUICK to run on a developer's machine", and that is two
questions, not one. Twelve legs answered yes to both. The wide
`wz-runtime-tokio` leg is safe but not quick, so Layer C1bn runs it
through `--all-legs` while the hook defers it AND PRINTS that it did.
`--census` counts BOTH scopes, so the split changes WHERE a leg runs
and never whether the test is covered -- which is what keeps the
standing "pre-push is fast, not a mirror" policy honest instead of
quietly reversing it.

A fifth field is the HANDOFF. `wz-ap-demo`'s wide leg does not run the
zero-population guard, because the narrow leg runs it at the one
feature where it means something. The census VERIFIES that claim: a
handed-off test that no OTHER leg runs is refused. So the field can
only ever move a test between legs, never out of the gate.

The escape hatch of last resort is SKIPS -- a test NAME, never a count
and never a whole feature, each with what was measured about it. Three
rows, all in `wz-runtime-tokio`. Excluding the FEATURES those tests sit
behind would have excused hundreds of innocent tests instead of three.

Round 2159.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 229 recorded that `connect/{timeout_ms,exit_on_failure}` and the
`listen/*` twins were unhonoured, and its reading of why is correct and worth
keeping: a peer's upstream defaults are `-1` (never give up) and `false` (never
die of it), which is exactly what wz did, so the DEFAULT axis was already parity
and what remained unhonoured was every NON-default — "give up finitely, and
exit". The item then named the obstacle honestly: wz had no process-lifecycle
substrate to hang that on. That is not a reason to defer; it is the thing to
build, and this round built it.

`crate::startup_phase` is the substrate, and it is the home a sentence had
already promised. `retry_period`'s module doc says upstream's
`ConnectionRetryConf` has FOUR fields and wz's `RetryPolicy` takes three,
because `exit_on_failure` "is a process-lifecycle decision belonging to the host
that owns the retry loop, not to the schedule". There was no such host, so the
sentence named an address nothing lived at. `PhasePolicy` is that address, and
it carries `timeout_ms` with it because upstream reads the two together: the
budget decides whether there is a give-up MOMENT at all, and `exit_on_failure`
decides what happens at it. Either alone is unanswerable.

The keys are FIVE, not the item's four, and `listen/retry` is not a fifth thing
that came along. Upstream's `add_listener_retry(endpoint, retry_config)`
(`orchestrator.rs:534`) draws the bind phase's wait from the listen retry block,
so `listen/timeout_ms` honoured without it is a budget for a loop with no
schedule.

The item's four were also never in ONE state, and that is worth recording
because it is the shape a future item will have too. `connect/timeout_ms` was in
`UNHONOURED_READER_GAP` — R2150 had already found `StaticConnectRetry::timeout_ms`
implementing it — while the other three sat in `UNHONOURED_BEYOND_WZ` under the
`ListenConfig` group. What made them one ROUND is that they are one SEAM, not
one classification. That group is now gone entirely, which is the outcome R2151
built the group table for: the day wz grows the thing a group names, the group
reds rather than going quietly stale.

`PhaseBudget` is a private-field newtype over the `i64` upstream stores rather
than a three-variant enum, and that is the load-bearing piece of the design. The
readings are `< 0` (no bound), `== 0` (do not retry) and `> 0` (a budget), so a
`Bounded(0)` variant would be a fourth state meaning one of the other two
depending on who asked — the degenerate value `RetryPolicy` types its periods
`u64` to make unrepresentable. `from_ms` is the only way in and maps a zero onto
`NO_RETRY` by construction.

The two hosts are the MESH run-modes, and the narrowing is deliberate rather
than unfinished. `exit_on_failure: false` means "come up anyway", which is only
an instruction on a node that has somewhere else to be — upstream's own reason
for the asymmetric column. A one-shot `--connect` client has no listener to
survive a refused dial and a `--reconnect` client's supervisor governs re-dials
after an ESTABLISHED link is lost, not a startup phase; both already behave as
upstream's client column, so the expansion reports the keys withheld rather than
silently applying a flag that would change nothing.

The bind phase drives `drive_phase` directly. The dial phase cannot: `peer_loop`
owns the connect list, the re-dial schedule and the accept side in one loop
where upstream runs `connect_peers` as a step before its steady state. So the
budget is applied where upstream applies it — as a wall-clock around the phase —
and the phase's success is observed from the loop's own event stream. A give-up
rides a oneshot into the SAME graceful shutdown a signal takes, so teardown runs
and the summary prints; the error is returned after it.

The status is `3`, and the distinctness is the whole observable difference
between honouring `exit_on_failure` and merely dying. "The node stopped" is not
something a supervisor can act on: a fault exits `1` and an argv refusal exits
`2`, and before this round a listener that could not bind was indistinguishable
from either.

Round 2160.decision_summary:
R2159's work was right and its landing was not: the commit could not reach origin
because its own Layer C1bz rejected it, in BOTH directions at once. This round is
the landing, and the two failures are worth separating because only one of them
is the kind a round expects.

The upward arm is ordinary debt and the gate's prescription is unambiguous: a
count ABOVE budget is a link the push added, so fix the link and never the
budget. `wz-runtime-tokio` measured 526 against 523, and all three additions are
one mechanism — the trap this workspace has written down twice. `startup_phase.rs`
carries an inner `//!` module doc; `lib.rs` carries an outer `///` on
`pub mod startup_phase;`. Rustdoc MERGES the two and resolves the merged text's
relative links against the CRATE ROOT, where `PhaseArm` and `PhasePolicy` do not
live. The third is the same defect without the merge: `zenoh_config.rs` linked
`PhasePolicy::connect_default_for` with nothing of that name in scope, in a file
that already spells the sibling type `crate::startup_phase::PhaseBudget` in type
position. All three are now fully qualified, in the style that doc's own
`[`RetryPolicy`](crate::retry_period::RetryPolicy)` had already set, and the
count is 523 — the budget UNCHANGED, which is the outcome the rule asks for.

The downward arm is the one worth recording, because nothing in R2159's diff
looks like a doc change and the count still moved. `wz-ap-demo` measured 26
against 27, and the first hypothesis — that the round deleted a doc link — is
false and was refuted mechanically: the crate's intra-doc link multiset GREW from
207 to 218 occurrences with ZERO removals. So the finding that left was not a
link that stopped being written; it was a link that started RESOLVING.

Naming it took a measurement rather than a reading, and the measurement is the
method worth keeping: rebuild this crate's docs from the PARENT's sources against
the same dependency tree, and diff the two finding sets. That yields exactly one
line — `unresolved link to RetryPolicy::ZENOH_DEFAULT` — and the cause is then
visible. R2159 needed `RetryPolicy` as a VALUE in `runner.rs` and imported it at
module scope. Before that, `runner.rs` imported the name only inside its own

further down that file had never resolved — while the identical link in
`args.rs` always had, because `args.rs` carries the import at module scope.

The generalisation is the value: A `use` ADDED FOR THE COMPILER'S BENEFIT IS A
DOC-LINK EDIT. Intra-doc links resolve in the importing module's scope, so the
set of resolvable links is a function of the `use` block, and a round that
touches no doc comment at all can still move this count in either direction.
That is the same class this session paid for at R2137 with the count guard — a
ledgered number and the change that moved it going out of step — arriving through
an instrument nobody had pointed at imports. It is a genuine observation, but it
is NOT registered as new debt: the gate that would catch it already exists and
already caught it, in both directions, which is precisely why this round happened
at all. A class with a working instrument is not an open debt.

Open-debt item 199 was the one item in the register that had recorded its own
half-refutation: filed as "the remaining axes of item 60", it was re-measured
soon after filing and most of it was found already closed. So the first move
here was not repayment but RE-MEASUREMENT, and the question was not "what is
left of the axis" but "does 199 still own anything, or do item 220 and the
instruments this session built already own all three of its pieces?"

Measured, one piece at a time, the answer was: two of the three were already
somebody else's, and the third was 199's own -- and it had no instrument.

  (a) the zenoh crate's cargo CAPABILITY features. The item's number
      reproduced EXACTLY -- 19 capability features, 18 answered by a wz cargo
      feature, 1 not. What was missing was never the number: it was that
      nothing re-derived it. Every other instrument over wz's capability
      surface -- the A3 grade, `audit-catalog-status.sh`,
      `apfull_membership.py` -- starts from a WZ ATOM and asks what became of
      it, and starting from the wz side cannot see a capability wz has never
      heard of. Counting the instruments that run the other direction found
      exactly one, the config census; the two symbol censuses do run upstream-
      first but over C ABI symbols, which is a different surface from a cargo
      feature. So "18 of 19" was a number read by hand once, and while it stayed
      pinned at full marks the DENOMINATOR could move underneath it.

  (b) `zenoh/src/api/**` pub fn / pub type. The item's own verdict -- that this
      is NOT a replacement axis, because the shortfall is almost entirely
      zenoh's Rust usability layer (`*Builder`, `IntoHandler`, `DefaultHandler`)
      and wz never claimed source compatibility with that crate -- was re-checked
      and still holds. wz's drop-in claim is the two C ABIs and the wire, and
      both of those axes already have upstream-first instruments that run.

  (c) the CONFIG axis. Not 199's; several instruments hold it for breadth and
      item 220 holds it for depth.

So (a) is what this round pays, and it pays it the way this project pays a
"number nobody re-runs": with a census whose denominator is DERIVED from
upstream and which fails in BOTH directions.

The population is asked of cargo, not of the manifest, and that choice is

Round 2163.decision_summary:
Two hosted jobs were red on runs 33059064203 and 33059199683, for two
unrelated reasons, and this round pays both.

FIRST — `feature-gate NEG lanes` failed on a REAL test failure, and the
root cause is that a provisioning precondition lived inside one lane
while a second lane grew that ran the same tests without it.

`FixedSlotRing::register` pins the whole reassembly pool, and the kernel
charges those pages to RLIMIT_MEMLOCK. R311y593 established the
requirement (32 x 1 MiB) and put the raising, the probe and the
three-way verdict INSIDE Layer C1br. R2156 then widened
`nondefault-tests-gate.sh`'s `wz-runtime-tokio` leg to name
`runtime-tokio-uring` among its 80 features, so Layer C1bn began running
the same two registering tests with none of that provisioning.

The measurement is that both lanes ran in ONE job on ONE runner and
disagreed about the same two tests: C1br `pass (41s)`, C1bn
`1318 passed; 2 failed`, both `uring::tests::`, at
`RLIMIT_MEMLOCK soft=8388608 hard=8388608`. Every dev box in this tree
grants 3.9 GiB, so the asymmetry is structurally invisible locally --
the same shape as R2136's, and the reason the knowledge had to MOVE out
of the lane rather than be copied into the second caller.

A refuted premise is worth recording because it cost the first hour. The
first reading was that `register`'s body was wrong: it is generic over
`<SLOTS, CAP>` and reads `SLOT_COUNT` / `SLOT_SIZE` from module scope,
which looked like a signature promising more than the body delivers, and
looked like it would let a test size its pool to fit a small limit. It
is not a defect. `PooledStaging<SLOTS, CAP>` always wraps the ONE
SCE-generated `ReassemblyPoolAp`; its const params are the Router's
requested BOUNDS, checked as a subset in `ChainStaging::new`, not the
arena's dims. Measured: a `PooledStaging<4, 65536>` still yields
`free_count() == 32`. So `iov_len: SLOT_SIZE` describes the region that
really exists, the pool cannot be shrunk from a test, and the change was
reverted whole.

SECOND -- `validate + verify + test` failed on its own budget guard at
`1790s of 1800s (99%)` with every lane green. The guard's prescription
is to SPLIT a lane into its own job, never to raise `timeout-minutes`,
because the cost grows monotonically in atom count. Layer C1cn is the
largest single entry at 562s -- more than double the next -- and it is
also the newest and the fastest-growing: R2135 added it to the workflow
at all, and R2156 put a second half on it.

FIRST -- Layer Z issued a verdict about a subject it never reached.
`upstream_feature_census.py` returns 2 when it cannot READ its input
and 1 when it read it and the table disagrees. Layer Z branched on

feature table no longer matches what the pinned zenoh declares --
see the lines above for which feature and which direction". In the
hosted log the lines above are a HEALTHY census: 19 capability
features, 18 answered, the single UNANSWERED being
`tracing-instrument`, which is open-debt item 201 and expected. The
message sent a reader hunting for a feature and a direction among
lines that say nothing is wrong, about a comparison that never
happened. Not a wording bug. The KIND of verdict was wrong.

SECOND -- the arm never had its input on the lane it was put on.
R2162 placed `--upstream` on Layer Z reasoning "this is the layer
that already provisions a pinned zenoh". What the lane provisions is
the zenohd BINARY, restored from `actions/cache`. On a cache HIT the
build step is skipped by its own `if:`, so no source tree is ever
checked out and the anchor chain finds nothing. The hosted log
carries both halves: `Cache restored from key:
zenohd-1.5.0-ubuntu-22.04-167ace0a...` and, later, one path tried
and no source found.

This is R2163's shape one day later. There a precondition lived
inside one lane and a second consumer grew without it; here the
cache restores a build's OUTPUTS while a new consumer needs its
INPUT. Both are knowledge that has to MOVE to where the consumer is
rather than be assumed from the neighbourhood.

Of the three ways to give the arm its input, the choice is measured.

  (2) "move `--upstream` to a lane that has the source" is REFUTED,
      not preferred against. All three `build-zenohd.sh` invocations
      and the only `--layer Z` live in the ONE job `interop:`, and
      each build is gated `if: cache-hit != true`. No other job holds
      a zenoh source tree, so there is nowhere to move it to.

  (3) "declare the arm DEFERRED" restores exactly the blindness R2162
      built it to remove -- a capability upstream GREW is visible from
      no other instrument, because every other one starts at a wz
      atom. It is the only option that loses coverage.

  (1) is what this round does, in the form the cache makes cheap: the
      DERIVED answer travels instead of the tree. `build-zenohd.sh`
      installs `cargo metadata --no-deps` output as
      `zenoh-cargo-metadata.json` INSIDE `$INSTALL_DIR`, so it rides
      the cache that already restores the binary. Measured here: 196
      KB (200562 bytes) against a 29 MB source tree, beside an 88 MB
      cached directory.

The derived form is not a weaker input. Asking cargo rather than
parsing the manifest is R2162's own load-bearing choice -- cargo
reports 24 features where `[features]` declares 23, the extra being
the implicit feature for the optional dependency `zenoh-shm` -- and
storing cargo's answer preserves it exactly. Installing it beside the
binary also buys what R2109 bought for `DEFAULT_CONFIG.json5`: the
table is graded against the same upstream the interop runs against,
so the census and the reference oracle cannot disagree about WHICH
zenoh they mean.

table disagrees with upstream". Measured before the fix: exit 1 with
a traceback; after: exit 2 naming the file and the re-provision
command. A denominator that arrived damaged would have been reported
as a fact about zenoh, which is the exact sentence this round exists
to stop being said. It shares the seam, so it is paid in this round
rather than filed as a number.

in either cannot hide behind the other.

The chain also learned to say WHERE an answer came from. The three
sources have three different repairs, and an INPUT fault that omits
which one was read sends the reader to re-provision a file the run
never opened.

Peeling instead the next FOUR (C1j + C1z + C1bl + C1bi = 745s) lands it

was missing. MEASURED with the DEFAULT libclang and nothing else
changed: 101 without the flag, 0 with it.

THE REGISTER SAID EIGHT PCAP DOORS AND THERE ARE NINE. Re-measured off
the `Door` enum, which is the walk `wz_dissect_readable_surfaces`
reports: Summary, SummaryBounded, Census, CensusBounded, CensusWhere,

THE SHAPE, AND WHY IT IS NOT THE ONE THE ITEM PROPOSED FIRST. The item's
leading candidate was `wz_dissect_pcap_records(bytes, len, limits, out,
cap, *written)` -- a file in, an array of records out. That is the shape
this header already argues against, in its own words, about
`wz_dissect_pcap_summary`: "a capture holds an unbounded number of
messages and one string carrying all of them is a shape that works for a
test and fails for a session." An ARRAY of all of them is the same shape.
A caller whose buffer is too small would have to re-read the file to get
the rest, which is quadratic, or be given a cursor, which is state --
and state across calls is exactly what the live handle already is.

So the door hands back the HANDLE instead. Drained by
`wz_dissect_live_drain`, read by `wz_dissect_live_lost`, released by
`wz_dissect_live_close`: the short-count drain loop that already exists
IS the answer to the capacity question, and the consumer's code does not
fork on where the packets came from. The header had already described
this caller and had no door to name him --
`WZ_DISSECT_LIMITS_NONE` is documented as "a bounded replay you want
nothing discarded from", a sentence with no subject until now.

WHY IT IS A DOOR AND NOT ADVICE TO LOOP. The second candidate --
document the loop, let the consumer open the container and call
`wz_dissect_live_push` per packet -- fails on a fact this round measured
rather than assumed. `Dissection::from_pcapng_declaring_bounded` calls
`push_packet_on`, carrying the PER-INTERFACE link type, the interface
id, the Decryption Secrets Blocks, the Interface Statistics, and the
`finish()` that spends the gap patience a file's end makes final.
`LiveDissection::push` reaches `push_packet_at` only, so a push loop
must pick ONE link type for the whole file -- and `dumpcap -i any`
writes interfaces with different link layers. A frozen pcapng would then
read one way through the document doors and another way through the

changes_bullets: Commit 4ea64784 -- 2 files, +238/-13.
`crates/wz-capture/src/filter.rs`:
* `lex` no longer takes `source.as_bytes()`. It reads the character at
`i` (`source[i..].chars().next()`) and advances by `len_utf8()`, so
`i` is a char boundary at every iteration by construction and `at`
keeps counting BYTES;
* the word scan walks `source[i..].chars()` and accumulates
`len_utf8()`, so `j` lands on a boundary and `&source[i..j]` cannot
panic;
* the QUOTED scan is converted too, though it never panicked. It
