Round 2255.decision_summary:
ONE RED HID A WHOLE LANE, TWICE, AND NOTHING SAID SO. R2235 found three
peer-plane families that had not run since a pin, because Layer Z returns
at the first binary. R2246 found a scout regression hidden for rounds,
because Layer M died in its first cargo call and everything after it was
never attempted. Both survived several pushes. The general form is that a
compile error is a ceiling on what a lane REPORTED, not on what it
CONTAINS -- and the missing piece was never the stopping, it was the
count.

STOPPING IS USUALLY RIGHT, so this is REPORTING and not a gate. Measured
on `scripts/run-ci.sh`: 647 legs are guarded `|| return 1` and 22
accumulate into `rc=1`/`fail=1`, across 115 of its 176 functions, 669
legs in all. A later leg routinely leans on an earlier leg's output, so
rewriting those sites to accumulate would break the thing that makes them
correct. What was needed is for the lane to say what its red is covering.
The item's own figures were 641 and 8; the 8 became 22 when R2247 moved
Layer Q's thirteen declines onto `fail=1`, so the register's numbers were
re-derived rather than quoted.

ONE PLACE, NOT 669. `run_layer` is the single choke point every lane goes
through, so the report lives there and no leg was touched. The POPULATION
is derived from the lane's own body -- the non-comment guarded lines
between `name() {` and its closing brace -- and never written down. The
leg REACHED comes from a DEBUG trap under `set -T` that records the last
line executed inside that range, which is two integer comparisons per
command; this file runs `set -uo pipefail` with no errexit, so there is
nothing for the trap to interact with. Measured cost: Layer C0 was 68s
before and 62-64s after.

A COUNT THAT CANNOT BE ZERO FOR THE WRONG REASON, which is the item's
second condition and the place this kind of instrument usually rots.
Three states are said rather than collapsed into a number: a lane with no
guarded leg reports that there is no population for the failure to sit
in; a stop the trace could not place inside the lane -- a return from a
helper, or before the first leg -- reports that it is not known how many
were skipped, because "failed at the first leg" and "cannot tell" are
different facts; and a name that is not a function in this script says so.

planted after C0's second leg reports "reached 3 of 87 ... 84 did not

87 ... 0 did not run". The number follows the stop rather than being a
constant, and that is the whole claim.

supposed to refuse, so the default has to be the half that declines.

Round 2259.decision_summary:
open-debt item 593 named three planes upstream 1.10.0 added that wz builds
none of, and R2257 / R2258 took the two small ones. This round takes the
large one WHOLE: the LINK and TRANSPORT event surface, 92 symbols.

Taking it whole is the decision rather than a convenience. The families
look separable by name — link 31, closure 26, transport 25, declare 4,
info 3, undeclare 2, plus zc_internal_create_transport — and are not: a
z_link_event_t is reachable only through a z_owned_closure_link_event_t,
which is installed only by z_declare_link_events_listener, which is
undeclared only by z_undeclare_link_events_listener. Shipping any verb
alone leaves a header that promises a link which fails, which is the
defect item 593 names rather than a step toward fixing it.

Every value is READ off an established face; none is invented. The
walk that produces src/dst MOVED rather than being copied:
SessionLinkActions::admin_links was the adminspace's, behind
adminspace-core, and its "one entry per PHYSICAL link" rule is the fact
R311y472 measured wrong once. It is now link_endpoints_all, ungated, and
the adminspace renderer is a projection of it — one derivation, two
consumers. is_streamed and reliability are derived from the link
PROTOCOL, where the property lives (InterceptorLink::is_streamed /
is_reliable, new). The listener seam is face_up / face_down, through
SharedSession::watch_faces / unwatch_faces / fire_face_event, with the
sinks cloned OUT of the registry lock because a C listener may re-enter.

Two accessors report ABSENCE rather than a plausible number, which
upstream's own bool returns are what make expressible: z_link_priorities
(wz binds a band only under multilink + QoS and reads it back through no
public accessor) and z_link_group (a multicast join name; wz's C surface
is unicast). z_link_auth_identifier writes empty for a different reason —
wz's auth records no per-link identity string.

Three hosted verdicts were unread. Read: R2260 (33524058529) is
COMPLETED / SUCCESS — which is the hosted confirmation that R2260's three
repairs held — and R2261 / R2262 were still in_progress with 19 and 6
completed jobs, every one success. No red to repay, so the round took the
milestone's other branch: item 607.

607's prescription was "measure how far wz's SHM goes BEFORE anything
else — that premise sets the item's size", and following it is what made
this round. THE PREMISE WAS FALSE. The item says wz "does not build the
SHM provider / allocator plane". It does: `shm.rs` is ~1400 lines, it
exports 36 symbols, and its own module header already states the split —
the buffer allocator is implemented COMPLETELY and the transport
optimisation is not. The item read one census row (84 missing) as "the
plane is absent".

What the 84 actually are was then derived by grouping each symbol under
the TYPE it belongs to rather than by a guessed prefix — the correction
R2257 made for a different family, applied here: alloc_layout 12,
shm_provider variants 12, precomputed_layout 10, shm_client_storage 7,
shm_client_list 7, memory_layout 6, ptr_in_segment 6,
shared_shm_provider 6, chunk_alloc_result 5, shm_client 4,
posix_shm_provider 2, six strays.

And one of those groupings is a mirage: `z_owned_alloc_layout_t` is a
TYPEDEF of `z_owned_precomputed_layout_t`, so those two families are one
type under two names — 22 functions rather than two planes.

The round then built the piece that piece can be built alone:
`z_memory_layout_*`, a `(size, alignment)` pair with no provider, no
segment and no allocation.

THE PREDICATES, and they are two because the claims are two.

`TEST_ONLY_REACH` is crate-level. Its claim is "no workspace library
can name a path into this crate", and it is decided by walking consumer
edges UPWARD: a library consumer continues the walk, a package with no
lib target ENDS it, because nothing can depend on a `bin` so no path
runs through one. That transitive library set is pinned as a SET and
checked both ways. `publish = false` is the other half, and it is the
outside-the-workspace one: cargo refuses to publish a crate carrying an
unpublishable path dependency, so it closes the whole closure, not just
the crate.

but whose feature is. `wz-tls-record` is ordinary — `wz-analyze` takes
it as a normal dependency and `wz-replay` reaches it transitively — so
the crate-level predicate cannot hold it. What is test-only is
`fixtures`, and the check is that every workspace edge enabling it is a
dev edge AND that no feature definition anywhere enables it. That
second half is not hypothetical: `wz-session-lwip`'s
`buffer-pool-session-rx-slim` enables `wz-link-lwip`'s feature of the
same name, so an edges-only check would call this route unreachable.

`sn_res` codes TWO resolutions, and both come out named.

Open-debt item 576. The transport walker pushed `sn_res` as a bare byte, so a
reader was handed `10` and nothing else. Upstream packs two independent 2-bit
resolutions into it -- `Field { FrameSN = 0, RequestID = 2 }` read as
`(self.0 >> field) & 0b11`, with the vocabulary `Bits { U8, U16, U32, U64 }`
already spelled `"8bit" / "16bit" / "32bit" / "64bit"` beside it
(`zenoh-protocol`, `src/core/resolution.rs`).

DECIDED: `label` children, not `bits`, and not both. The complaint the item was
filed on is that the number is not readable, and `bits` children are `0..3`,
which repeats it. The codes are in BIJECTION with the words -- four codes, four
distinct strings -- so the human-readable form loses nothing, and the test
MEASURES that bijection rather than asserting it in prose. The raw `sn_res`
field is kept, and the children alias its span the way `whatami` aliases
`cbyte`'s.

DECIDED, second: ONE emitter for both call sites. INIT and JOIN carried the
same four lines, duplicated byte for byte, and item 576's sharpest point is
that fixing INIT alone leaves JOIN opaque and makes the reader's guarantee
asymmetric. `sn_res_and_batch` makes that asymmetry unrepresentable rather than
avoided once.

DECIDED, third, on the narrow reading the item insisted on: `sn_res` is itself
conditional on the S flag, so the requirement is NOT "the children always
appear" but "when `sn_res` appears, both children appear, whatever the byte
holds". Code `0b00` is `8bit`, a resolution a sender really picks, so emitting
only non-zero ones would confuse "the sender chose 8-bit" with "the field was
not carried" -- and the second is already said better, by an S-clear JOIN
having no `sn_res` field at all.

MEASURED, answering the consumer's §5.3 question with commands rather than
reasoning: `document.revision` does NOT move. The kind `label` is already in
`FIELD_VALUE_KIND_R3`, and dissect field NAMES are not a pinned vocabulary --

in `doc_revision.rs`. It arrives as a golden diff only.

Round 2271.decision_summary:
A zero-length batch is a batch of no messages, and reading it means doing
nothing.

Open-debt item 577. A genuine zenohd on its abandon path writes a zero-length
batch instead of the `0x3 Drop` marker (item 575's subject). wz met it as
`InboundParseError::Empty` and the link went `LinkLost(PeerClosed)`: one
harmless malformed batch from a peer ended the session.

The item forbade fixing before measuring all three implementations, and said
the verdict follows from whether they diverge. They do, and wz was the sole
outlier:

* zenoh (Rust, `zenoh-transport` 1.10.0): `read_messages` is
  `while !batch.is_empty()` (`unicast/universal/rx.rs`), `while reader.can_read()`
  on the lowlatency path, and `while !batch.is_empty()` again for multicast. An
  empty batch runs the body zero times and returns `Ok(())`. Link survives.
* zenoh-pico (`vendor/zenoh-pico`): the steady-state read task
  (`Z_WHATAMI_CLIENT`) calls `_z_unicast_client_read` then
  `_z_unicast_process_messages`, and the latter is
  `while (_z_zbuf_len(&zbuf) > 0)`. A zero length prefix returns TRUE with
  `to_read = 0`, the loop runs zero times, `_Z_RES_OK`. Session survives. (The
  `single_read = true` path does error on an empty decode, but that is not the
  default -- `zp_read_options_default` sets `single_read = false`.)
* wz: the empty payload went up to the parser and killed the link.

DECIDED: `poll_framed` skips a zero-length batch and reads the next frame,
which is the same sentence as their `while`. Nothing is lost by it: no
transport message is zero bytes long, so an empty payload can only mean "no
messages". Both prefix widths are covered, because upstream tolerates it on
both the universal and the lowlatency path.

NOT a busy loop: every pass through `Idle` reaches an awaited `src.read()`, so
an endless stream of empty batches costs one syscall each and stays
cancel-safe -- exactly what it costs the two implementations above.

FILED, not fixed, and it is why the control had to change: the intended control
was "malformed but NOT empty is still fatal", and that input could not be
built. `StreamEnvelope::decode` fails on exactly one condition, fewer than two
bytes remaining, and this call site always hands it `2 + payload_len` bytes
taken from those very two -- so the `Err(_) => Lost` arm has no path to being
true here. That is R2268's dead guard in another file, and whether the repair
is dropping the arm or not pre-sizing the buffer from an untrusted length is a
judgement of its own. Open-debt item 610.

Round 2278.decision_summary:
Which build of zenoh-c upstream PUBLISHES is a per-release fact, so it gets
one derived home and every sentence that states it is adjudicated against
that home. Open-debt item 612 reported the manifest's `[features]` comment
carrying a superseded attribution; the round measured the attribution rather
than repairing the copy, and the measurement went the other way.

Three readings, all taken this round and all agreeing: the installed
`zenoh_configure.h` at the default prefix declares both `Z_FEATURE_UNSTABLE_API`
and `Z_FEATURE_SHARED_MEMORY`; upstream's own `release.yml` builds the
standalone package with `-DZENOHC_BUILD_WITH_UNSTABLE_API=ON
-DZENOHC_BUILD_WITH_SHARED_MEMORY=ON`; and the published 1.5.0 archive,
fetched and unpacked, declares both as well. So the tree's older reading --
that the package is the no-unstable build -- was not stale, it was never true
at either pin. R311y540 read its arm off an install nobody had established
was the package, which is the third possibility item 612 itself raised.

The instrument is therefore a PREDICATE rather than a corrected copy: the
fact lives in one file, bound to the version pin so a bump cannot land
without re-deriving it, judged against upstream where upstream is present,
and used to adjudicate every prose sentence in the tree that states it.

Round 2281.decision_summary:
A second oracle is worth its build minutes only if it is a second ARM. Layer
C1ce existed to measure wz against the arm Layer C1cc does not have, and for its
whole life it measured C1cc's arm a second way.

Item 617's first condition is answered by running `zenoh-c-oracle-arm.sh` on
both prefixes: `~/.local` and `target/zenoh-c-shm` both read `unstable-shm`. But
a reading of two directories is one machine's state, and a clone with no oracle
installed would check nothing while "nothing installed" read as "no duplicate" —
which is exactly how this survived. So the arm is DERIVED FROM THE INSTALLERS,
which are in the tree on every clone: `install-zenoh-c.sh` unpacks upstream's
published archive, whose arm `zenoh_c_archive_arm` already owns as one derived
fact, and the wrappers name their arm as a literal argument to
`install-zenoh-c-arm.sh`. `scripts/lib/zenoh_c_oracle_arms.py` is that
derivation and the four refusals over it.

The subject of the duplicate rule is the PREFIX, not the lane. C1cc and C1cd
share `~/.local` deliberately — they differ in topology, not in arm — and a rule
over lanes would have called that a duplicate. Two separate INSTALLS of one arm
is the waste; two lanes reading one install is not.

The decision the item left open is to RE-AIM, not to delete. `wz-capi-c`'s own
default feature set models the `unstable` arm, and no real zenoh-c had ever been
compared against it; `nounstable` and `nounstable-shm` are neither published by
upstream nor modelled by wz. One of the four arms had a lane, one had a reason
to want one, and that is where C1ce now points. Deleting instead would also have
left the duplicate-detector with a population of one, where it could never fire
again.

The legs follow the HEADER they need, measured rather than argued: compiling all
29 upstream examples against each arm's header gives 0 failures on
`unstable-shm`, 5 on `unstable` (the SHM ones), and 7 on `nounstable`. The three
`*_shm` legs move to C1cc, whose oracle has shared memory; the two `z_advanced_*`
legs need only the unstable axis and stay.

Retiring `install-zenoh-c-shm.sh` is part of the same decision rather than
tidying after it: once nothing read `target/zenoh-c-shm`, hosted CI would have
kept spending minutes building an oracle no lane opens. The gate's fourth
refusal — an installer owning a fixed prefix no consumer names — is the mirror
of the duplicate rule and is what makes that impossible to leave behind.

Round 2286.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 616 asked a question rather than naming a repair: `wz-capi-c`'s
default feature set models the `unstable` build and upstream ships the
`unstable-shm` one, so should the default move? The answer is no, and the
reason is a property of cargo rather than anyone's preference.

Cargo features are ADDITIVE. The crate's two axis features are deviations, so
every one of the four builds has to be `default + <features>` -- and that holds
only while the default sits at the ORIGIN of both axes. With
`zenoh-c-shared-memory` in the default, the two builds without that axis become
reachable only through `--no-default-features`, which any dependent enabling
the default hands straight back. The library would then be the wrong SIZE in
exactly the configuration a consumer assembles by accident, and a size mismatch
is a corrupted caller frame, not a link error. So the default cannot move, and
that is derivable rather than argued: the reachable-arm count is a number this
gate computes.

The decision leaves a divergence, and a divergence nobody exercises is a
declaration. So it is PRICED. `zenoh_c_archive_arm.py` grew four arms, in the
file that already owns which build upstream ships:

  * every feature the crate declares is CLASSIFIED as an axis. No exemption
    list -- the lattice is SIZED from that table, so a feature it does not know
    makes the enumeration the wrong size, and that is a decision a round has to
    make rather than a row it can add.
  * all four arms are additively reachable from the default. This is the
    decision above, stated as a predicate.
  * while the default's build differs from upstream's, a named lane leg must
    RUN the feature set that reaches upstream's. C1cc's shared-memory leg is
    that payment, and deleting it now reds.
  * the selector that turns an installed header into a build must ADD every
    axis and must not reach for `--no-default-features`, which would mean the
    origin had moved.

Item 616's third completion condition was "do not close this by fixing a
manifest comment". The manifest does gain the decision, but as the DECLARATION
those four arms adjudicate: each one fires on the shipped bodies under
mutation, which is what separates a declaration from a comment.

One of the item's own premises did not survive re-measurement, and it is the
one that would have made moving the default expensive. It said the census
population (`--all-features` minus default) would shift. It would not:
`wz-capi-c` is absent from that census entirely, because `--all-features` is
not a superset for this crate -- it LOSES a test, which
`nondefault-tests-gate.sh` had already measured and written down. The
only-with-features difference is zero, so the default's position cannot move
it. The C1cc claim did survive, and the decision turns it around: the leg the
item feared losing is now the price the gate collects.

Open-debt item 610 CLOSED: the `StreamEnvelope::decode` failure arm in

SCOPE: the FRAMING layer's refusals in `crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/lib.rs`.
Whether a malformed batch loses the link is NOT in scope and did not change --
that judgement lives one layer up, in `parse_inbound` / `InboundParseError`.

WHERE THE MEASUREMENT CONTRADICTED THE ITEM, which is the expected outcome and
not an exception:

* The item recorded that `StreamEnvelope::decode` "fails on exactly ONE
  condition, `remaining() < 2`". Measured, it has FOUR failure exits (the
  length check, `peek_slice`'s `?`, the `_consumed > _frame_len` check, and
  `advance`'s `?`) -- and on a SHORT frame it takes none of them: it indexes
  `raw[2..2 + payload_len]` after checking only `remaining() >= 2`, so it
  PANICS. Probed directly: `catch_unwind` over a 2-byte buffer whose prefix
  declares 3 came back `Err`.
* That panic REFUTES the item's second repair option -- "change the framing so
  the arm becomes reachable, letting the codec adjudicate the length
  mismatch". A framing layer cannot hand this codec a partial buffer at all,
  so the option was never available.
* The item's CONCLUSION survived its wrong reason: the arm could not fire.
  Probed: for a completed frame, `env.payload` is BYTE-IDENTICAL to
  `&bytes[2..]`, because the length the codec re-reads is the length the loop
  just wrote and sized the buffer from.

zenoh answers a batch it cannot decode with `zerror!("{}: decoding error")`
and the `?` on it ends the rx task (`unicast/universal/rx.rs:265`). wz agrees,
one layer up. The empty-batch case (item 577) is the one where upstream
SURVIVES (`while !batch.is_empty()` runs the body zero times), and that
behaviour is unchanged. Two different upstream sentences, two different
answers, and this round did not swap them.

`z_internal_ptr_in_segment_check` / `_null`; `z_chunk_alloc_result_new_ok` /

THE REFACTOR. The provider handle was `Box<Arc<Segment>>` and is now

a range of a wz segment or a foreign descriptor plus the `PtrInSegment` that
keeps its segment context alive. `Drop` routes to the free list or to

where upstream passes `MaybeUninit` and `assume_init`s it — a callback that

for can never come — upstream's `BlockOn` deadlocks there;

Round 2289.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 607 (the `unstable-shm` SHM residue) — take the C-SUPPLIED
BACKEND plane whole: twenty symbols, 51 -> 31, and CLOSE that plane rather
than the item, which its own done-when asks to be paid plane by plane.

The item was re-measured before anything was written, per its own
prescription. `nm -D` against `~/.local/lib/libzenohc.so` (the published
1.10.0 archive, resolved as the `unstable-shm` arm by its own
`zenoh_configure.h`) reported missing=51, extra=0 — the committed BASELINES
number exactly, so the item's premise survived this round's re-measurement,
which is not what the last several found.

WHICH plane, and why this one. Grouping the 51 by the machinery each needs
gives four groups, and the keystone is a TYPE rather than a symbol:
`zc_threadsafe_context_t` / `zc_context_t`, which this crate did not declare
and which `z_ptr_in_segment_new`, `z_shm_client_new`, `z_shm_provider_new`
and every `_async` spelling all take by value. Declaring the two unblocks the
backend plane in one piece: the value types that cross the callback boundary
(`z_ptr_in_segment_*`, `z_chunk_alloc_result_*`), the constructors that
install a backend (`z_shm_provider_new` / `_threadsafe_new`), the call that
hands a backend-allocated chunk back as a buffer (`z_shm_provider_map`), and
upstream's two named spellings of the BUILT-IN backend
(`z_posix_shm_provider_new` / `_with_layout_new`).

Taken WHOLE for R2259's reason. `z_chunk_alloc_result_t` exists only to be
returned from `alloc_fn`; shipping it without `z_shm_provider_new` would leave
a header promising a link a program cannot use, which is the defect the item
names rather than a smaller version of it.

The four `_async` spellings are in this round on a different argument, and it
is about the other sixteen. `z_shm_provider_new` and
`z_shm_provider_threadsafe_new` differ ONLY in a thread-safety promise, and
upstream reads that promise in exactly one place: `alloc_async` returns
`Z_EINVAL` for the non-threadsafe arm. Shipping the constructors without the
async spellings would have stored a flag nothing reads — a dead arm, which is
the class R2288 paid for a round ago. So the round either builds both or
builds a distinction it cannot witness.

The design consequence accepted deliberately: the provider becomes polymorphic
(`enum Provider { Native, Foreign }`, and `ShmChunk` gains a `ChunkBacking`),
so a chunk is released to whichever backend issued it. That is a refactor of
the module's core rather than an addition beside it, and it is the extension
point the plane needs — the alternative, a second parallel provider type, is
the shortcut this tree's own rules refuse.

open-debt item 626 CLOSED: the hosted Layer C1 flake in wz-capi-pico's
matching re-entrancy test is a wz DEFECT, not a test artefact. A
declaration whose wire RETRACTION had already been sent was announced
again afterwards, so the peer re-inserted the remote subscriber it had
just been told to drop and its matching verdict was stuck `true` for the
rest of the link's life.

The item's own first-move candidate is REFUTED, and the refutation is the
finding. It read "does undeclare-then-close look like two face
transitions to the aggregate" — it does not. Instrumenting the C
aggregate showed ONE face (id 0) applying true, false, true and then a
single forget. Instrumenting `RemoteSubscriberRegistry` showed the
listener receiving DeclSubscriber(id=1), UndeclSubscriber(id=1),
DeclSubscriber(id=1) on frame SNs 225951277/278/279 — consecutive on one
reliable conduit, so `admit_rx_frame_sn` had already ruled out a
re-dispatch: the dialer sent the declaration twice.

ROOT CAUSE. `Subscriber::teardown` emits its wire `UndeclSubscriber`
BEFORE the local unregister (R311ou wrote it that way citing pico's
`_z_send_undeclare` then `_z_unregister_subscription`). On wz that gap is
not empty: the drive thread drains the staged interest-response chain
under the SAME observer mutex and resolves each staged reply against
`observer.subscribers`. A drain landing in the gap read a table still
holding the subscription and emitted the reply — after the retraction.
pico's ORDER is kept; what is removed is the window, by moving the emit
inside the acquisition that retires the entry.

POPULATION, derived from the DRAIN rather than from the handle that was
caught: `drain_declare_replies` resolves staged replies against exactly
two tables, `subscribers` and `local_tokens`, so exactly two handles can
retire something a staged reply still announces —
`Subscriber::teardown` and `LivelinessToken::teardown` — and both had the
same shape. Both fixed. The queryable handle has the shape but no staged
reply resolves against the queryable table, so it is outside the
population and is recorded as such rather than fixed on suspicion.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT defect surfaced on the way and is fixed too:
`sub_interest_reply`'s AGGREGATE arm resolved through the peer's
inbound-interest ROW, which an undeclare never touches, so it did not
keep the promise its own doc makes ("None when ... a subscription
dropped") and which the sibling CONCRETE arm keeps. Its remaining live
route is the DECLARE ROLLBACK, which nothing makes atomic: a failed wire
announce unregisters a subscription whose future-push reply is already
staged.

because the last four rounds each refuted theirs. Read as commands:
`Session::declare_subscriber` calls `register_subscriber_local` FIRST
(wz-runtime-tokio/src/session/mod.rs:3861), that call funnels through
`SubscriberRegistry::register_sink`, and its single table-insert path
runs `stage_future_subscriber_pushes` (wz-session-core/src/pubsub.rs:681)
against every standing inbound interest. Only THEN does
`announce_subscriber` run, and its `Err` arm rolls back with
`observer.subscribers.unregister(id)` — which touches `subscribers` and
nothing else, so the staged reply survives a subscription that was never
announced. The item's "this is the buildable side, not the dead-arm
side" call was right.

WHERE THE ROUND DIVERGED FROM THE ITEM'S PRESCRIPTION. The item scoped
the work to the AGGREGATE arm, because that is the arm R2290 added a
guard to. That is who noticed, not what the population is. Derived from
the structure instead: the rollback window's axis is the interest's
`aggregate` BIT, which is what `stage_future_subscriber_pushes` reads to
choose between `SubInterestReply::Aggregate` and `::Concrete` — and
those two are exactly the ANNOUNCING arms of that enum, `Final`
announcing nothing. A bool has two inhabitants and both are driven, from
the bit's own type rather than from a list, with the covered count
asserted so a loop that ran zero times cannot report green.

The LIVELINESS-TOKEN plane is OUTSIDE this population, and that is a
derivation rather than a decision not to look. R2290's population came
from `drain_declare_replies` reading two tables, `subscribers` and
`local_tokens`. But `pending_declares` — the token half's staging — is
written ONLY by `local_tokens.dispatch_iteration_event`, i.e. by an
INBOUND interest arriving (wz-session-core/src/observer.rs:531). No
declare stages into it, so a token declare has no reply to leave behind
and cannot have this window. Recorded as outside, not fixed on
suspicion, which is the shape R2290 used for the queryable handle.

TWO VEHICLE PROOFS, one per arm, because the arms cannot share one. The
aggregate arm's proof re-runs the SAME rejected declare with an
unrelated `home/temp` subscription alive across the window: the guard is
`any_subscription_matches` over the INTEREST's keyexpr, so that sibling
keeps the staged reply TRUE and it reaches the wire — which is the proof
that the rolled-back declare stages a reply at all. The concrete arm
cannot be mirrored that way: a `Concrete` reply resolves by SUBSCRIPTION
ID, so once the rollback has removed that id nothing can make it
resolve. What is shown instead is that the `else` half of the staging
branch fires at all, by declaring an ACCEPTED keyexpr under the same
standing interest and watching the future push leave on the next drive
iteration. Without it, a staging branch that silently staged nothing
would leave the concrete half of the guard test green for the wrong
reason.

open-debt item 627 CLOSED, with BOTH of its readings confirmed against

one `DeclSubscriber.id`, and an aggregate declaration had no retraction of

THE ITEM'S OWN HEAD SENTENCE WAS RIGHT, AND R2290'S REWRITE OF IT WAS ALSO
RIGHT. They are two halves of one defect and neither is safe alone.
Re-measured as commands: `aggregate_decl_id` occurs at exactly four sites
in this workspace (`pubsub.rs` definition, reuse, allocation, resolution)
and none of them retracts; the two id counters (`next_id`,
`next_sub_interest_decl_id`) both started at 1.

UPSTREAM SETTLED BOTH, and this is the round's central evidence rather
than an aside. zenoh 1.10.0 keeps ONE per-face id counter and draws the
simple resource's id AND the aggregated resource's id from it —
`face_hat_mut.next_id.fetch_add(1, ..)` appears twice, once per kind, in
`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/broker/interests.rs:118-130`. And its
aggregated resource carries `info: Option<SubscriberInfo>` where
`SubscriberInfo` is a UNIT struct, so `aggregate_many` yields `Some` iff
at least one simple resource is aggregated into it; `remove_simple_resource`
reports the AGGREGATE's own id when that flips to `None`
(`dispatcher/local_resources.rs:244-275`), and `maybe_unpropagate_subscriber`
turns each such report into `UndeclareSubscriber { id }`
(`hat/broker/pubsub.rs:115-143`). The transition, not the event, is the
trigger — and it is the aggregate's own id that goes out.

WHY THE TWO HALVES ARE ONE ROUND: the retraction is what makes the
collision harmful. Two declarations under id 1 were merely wrong while
nothing ever retracted an aggregate id (R2290 measured that the collision
had been MASKING the missing retraction, because one `UndeclSubscriber`
happened to take both). Emit a retraction into that same collision and an
`UndeclSubscriber(1)` becomes ambiguous on a peer that keys by id. Fixing
the retraction without the id space would have shipped a worse defect than
the one it closed.

WHAT THE ROUND DID NOT INHERIT FROM UPSTREAM: an `announced` flag. zenoh
needs none because its declare and its table insert are one transaction;
wz stages on the application thread and drains on the drive thread, so
"was this id ever put on the wire" is a fact that has to be recorded. It
is also exactly what keeps R2291's declare-rollback path silent — that
path unregisters a subscription whose reply was staged and then dropped,
and a purely structural "the last match went away" rule would retract an
id no peer was ever told.

THREE MEASUREMENTS THAT CHANGED THE DESIGN, all of them mutations that
FAILED to go red first:

1. Deleting the staging-time `any_subscription_matches` test left every
   wire assertion green. The drain-time re-check in

   claim now lives where it is observable — on the staged items — as
   `an_unrelated_unregister_stages_no_aggregate_retraction`, and the doc
   comments that had named the wrong mutation were corrected.
2. Deleting the DRAIN-time re-check ALSO left everything green, because
   the first control group put the sibling subscription in place BEFORE
   the drop, where the staging filter catches it. Two guards were hiding
   each other. The drain-time one exists for a window the staging one
   cannot see — a subscription declared BETWEEN the stage and the drain —
   and `a_subscription_declared_inside_the_retraction_window_keeps_the_
   aggregate` is the test that opens it. That is R2290's argument in
   reverse: what a RETRACTION says has to be true when it is SENT.
3. Layer C1c refused the first green tree: a `declare-subscriber`-without-
   `declare-undeclare` build died at `-D dead-code` on the `announced`
   field and `-D unused-mut` on a test counter. Same shape R2290's probe
   fixture died in one round earlier, and the fix is the same — gate on
   the UNION OF THE CONSUMERS, not on the feature that names the concept.

NOT EXEMPTED. "Every knob must be set by some test" reads like a ratchet and is

measurement; the response was to delete the rule and record why in the script,

Round 2293.decision_summary:
open-debt item 625 CLOSED: "a test whose ORACLE cannot construct the input its
branch needs measures nothing" now has an instrument, derived rather than
listed, plus the written statement of what the instrument cannot reach — which
the item itself calls half the work.

THE ITEM'S PREMISE HELD. Re-measured as commands: the instance is real
(`wz-capi-c/src/shm.rs`, the `under_deliver` harness flag and the
`alloc_calls == 1` assertion R2289 added are both still there), and nothing in
this tree measured the class.

WHAT THE GATE DERIVES, on both sides, over every tracked `.rs` file. A KNOB is
a `bool` field on a struct declared inside a `#[cfg(test)]` module which the
module's NON-test code branches on — that is, the test double itself switches
on it, which by construction makes it a switch on what inputs the oracle can
produce. A RECORD is a counter or log field on a struct in the same module:
what the double writes down about what it was asked. The rule is one sentence:
every `#[test]` that sets a knob must read at least one record in its own body.
A test that configures its double to misbehave and never asks whether the
double was called cannot tell "the code refused" from "the fixture refused",
which is exactly what R2289's survivor could not tell.

THE ROUND'S OWN READING WAS WRONG, AND THE MECHANICAL DERIVATION CAUGHT IT.
Before writing the gate this round read `a_blocking_request_waits_only_when_a_
release_can_come`, saw `always_fail = true` next to a discarded `_borrow`, and
recorded it as a second unwitnessed site. It is not: the test's CONTROL half,
forty lines further down, asserts `alloc_calls >= 2`. The gate — which reads
the whole `#[test]` body — got it right while the session's reading did not.
Of the three knobs a test configures, all three were already witnessed; the
discipline had held everywhere except the one place R2289 had already repaired.

THREE THINGS THE FIRST DRAFT GOT WRONG, each killed by a measurement:

1. A second rule required every knob to be SET by some test, on the argument
   that a knob nobody sets is an oracle branch nobody reaches. Run against the
   tree it reported five, and all five were FALSE POSITIVES: knobs given their
   interesting value through a STRUCT LITERAL rather than a field assignment.
   Widening the pattern to include literals does not rescue the rule, it
   destroys it — every field of every literal is then "set", including to the
   value that reaches nothing, and the rule can never fail. Which literal value
   is the interesting one needs the default, and the default is not derivable
   from the source shape. The rule is GONE rather than exempted.
2. The knob derivation counted `self.x = true` INSIDE the double as a read, so
   a bool the double RECORDS was classified as a knob. Fixed with a negative
   lookahead — and the first spelling of that lookahead, `\\b\\s*(?!=..)`, was
   silently useless because `\\s*` backtracks to zero and the lookahead then
   sees a space instead of the `=`. The `recorded-bool` selftest fixture is
   what found it.
3. The summary printed the KNOB count. Eight knobs, three of them configured by
   a test: a line reading "8 knob(s), each set and witnessed" invites the
   reader to take 8 as the number of judgements made. It now prints both, and
   a graded population of zero FAILS alongside a derived population of zero.

WHAT IT DOES NOT REACH, recorded in the script's own header rather than here
alone: it would NOT have caught R2289's survivor. That draft had no knob at all
— the harness simply refused and `under_deliver` did not yet exist — so there
was nothing to see. What the gate holds is the repair and every knob-configured
test written after it. The general form of item 625 is mutation testing over
the suite; this is not that, and the item puts that instrument on the same line
as open-debt item 374.

`z_shm_mut_try_from_immut` asks one question — "may this buffer be written
again?" — and wz already answers it in `z_shm_try_mut`, through the chunk's own

than being freed under a caller that still believes it owns one.

negotiates no SHM segment. wz's own `z_bytes_from_shm` COPIES the chunk's bytes

asserts through the segment's accounting rather than by claiming it.

oracle cannot construct the input, give it the ability to.

segments are process-local `Vec`s, so there is nothing for it to clean, no

carry_forward_bullets: THE RULE THIS ROUND HAD TO DERIVE: "derive the population, never hand-write it"
DOES NOT REACH THE BASELINE, and reading it as though it did would have built a
gate that cannot fail. A pin is a comparison between what was remembered and
what is now; if both sides are derived they agree by construction. That is
R2185's finding turned around — there a gate compared its own table against a
literal count and could never be wrong, here it would compare a derivation
against a derivation and could never disagree. So: POPULATION derived, BASELINE
declared, and the baseline placed THREE LINES from the revision it covers so the
two are edited together or the gate reds.
A THIRD ROUND MET THE SAME MUTATION TRAP. R2299 wrote a mutation the compiler
killed as dead code; R2300 did it again bypassing a function; R2301 did it a
third time with a `cfg` naming a feature that does not exist. The shape is
stable enough to state as a rule: A MUTATION MUST SURVIVE COMPILATION. Put it at
a LOOKUP or a VALUE, never at a definition the compiler can prove unused or a
name it can prove absent — otherwise the red is the compiler's and says nothing
about the witness.
THE MUTATION THAT MATTERED MOST WAS THE ONE THAT LEFT ANOTHER GATE GREEN.
Putting a door behind an off-by-default `cfg` reds the new pin and leaves
`capi_c_wz_door_header.py` passing, because that gate reads source and
declaration. Two gates over one surface are only worth their cost when a
mutation can tell them apart, and this is the measurement that showed it — the
artifact corner is not a duplicate of the source corner.
A GATE THAT READS AN ARTIFACT INHERITS WHERE THE ARTIFACT WAS BUILT. Every
mutation here needed a LOCAL rebuild, because `bx` relocates builds to the build
machine and the gate reads `crates/target/debug/libwz_capi_c.so` on this one. A
round that mutated, rebuilt remotely and re-ran the gate would have measured the
previous build and concluded the mutation was harmless.
WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY LEFT OUTSIDE, stated so a later round does not read it as
an oversight: this revision says nothing about the drop-in `z_*` / `zc_*`
surface. Upstream zenoh-c owns that contract and upstream's header declares it;
a number minted here would be a second and disagreeing opinion about somebody
else's ABI. The drop-in's own question — are the structs the size upstream's
are — is `wz_capi_c_layout`'s and is already answered.
NOTHING NEW FILED. The round's residue is the rule above, which belongs in the
lessons rather than in the register: it is not work owed, it is a way of writing
mutations that three rounds have now paid for separately.

Round 2301.decision_summary:
R2301 pays open-debt item 634, which R2300 CREATED rather than encountered:
shipping `wz_capi_c.h` made "which build of the library is this header for?" a
question a consumer can ask, and nothing could answer it. `wz_dissect.h` has
answered it since R311y748; the new header shipped with neither a revision nor a
gate.

THE DECISION THAT SHAPED THE ROUND is how to read the item's own instruction
that the population be derived and "never a hand-written list". Taken literally
it would also make the BASELINE derived — and a pin with a derived baseline
CANNOT FAIL, because the baseline follows the population wherever it goes. That
is R2185's finding in mirror image: there, a gate compared its own table against
a literal count and could never be wrong; here, a gate would compare a derived
set against a derived set and could never disagree.

So the two are separated explicitly:

  POPULATION (derived, three corners)  what symbols exist right now.
  BASELINE   (declared, one place)     what the current revision covers.

The baseline is written down, and it sits three lines from `EXPECTED_REVISION`.
That adjacency IS the enforcement: adding a door means editing both lines in one
commit, so the revision cannot be forgotten. `capi_abi_pin.py` records the same
reasoning for the record layout it pins — "two pins that move together are one
pin" — and this is a third pin placed for that reason rather than a copy of it.

THE REVISION IS TWO THINGS, and that pair is the item's real deliverable:
`WZ_CAPI_C_ABI_REVISION` (what a consumer COMPILED against) and
`wz_capi_c_abi_version()` (what it is RUNNING against). Comparing them is how a
consumer detects a library it was not compiled for — the one failure a header
cannot detect on its own, and precisely the gap item 634 named.

WHAT THE ROUND DECLINED: reusing the dissect revision, which the item forbids
and which would force a bump on every consumer of either library whenever either
moved. The MECHANISM is shared (this gate imports the header gate's derivation);
the NUMBERS are not.

ALSO DECLINED, and recorded rather than left implicit: minting a number for the
drop-in `z_*` / `zc_*` surface. That is upstream zenoh-c's contract, upstream's
header declares it, and a number here could only be a second and disagreeing
opinion about somebody else's ABI. `wz_capi_c_layout` already answers the other
question a drop-in raises — whether the structs are the size upstream's are.

changes_bullets: THE EMIT DOOR (`crates/wz-capi-c/src/config.rs`)
* `zc_config_to_string` renders `render_nested()`. A config that cannot BE a
document — `ConfigState` is a flat map and can hold `"mode"` and
`"mode/router"` at once, which upstream's tree cannot reach (it refuses the
second insert, `Z_EGENERIC`, measured) — is REFUSED with `Z_EGENERIC`, the
code upstream's own door returns when serialization fails, naming both keys.
* `render_all` is DELETED. It was the flat whole-document renderer and, once
upstream was measured, it answered a question no door of either implementation
asks. Two emitters for one document is a place for the two to disagree, and
they had. The test that pinned why the flat spelling loses path keys survives,
building its flat document from `ConfigState::render` — the surviving per-key
renderer — inside the test module where a control group belongs.
THE READ DOORS (same file)
* `install_parsed` parses a real JSON5 DOCUMENT (`wz_session_core::json5`) and
loads each leaf, instead of splitting the text on newlines and each line on
its first `:`. A non-object root is refused rather than installing an empty
config and reporting success.
* `zc_config_from_file` now calls it. It had its own copy of the line scanner;
`_from_file_substr` and `_from_env` reach it through that call, so all five
reader doors are one parser.
* Each leaf goes through `parse_json5_value`, the INSERT door's value parser, so
"a value this config can hold" is one rule and not two.
* A FLAT document still loads, deliberately: a top-level key containing `/`
yields the same leaf path as the nesting it spells. That is a superset over
upstream, which costs the drop-in claim nothing and keeps every config file
wz's own emitter wrote before this round readable.
THE VALUE MODEL (same file)
* `StoredValue.bracketed: bool` becomes `spelling: Spelling` — `Quoted`, `List`,
`Verbatim`. The renderer stopped GUESSING: it used to ask whether the stored
text "looked like" a bare literal and quote whatever did not, which is right
for a quoted scalar and wrong for every value the parser stores whole. `null`
re-rendered as the string `"null"`; an object as `"{\"enabled\":true}"`, which
is not json5 at all — both measured through the C ABI.
* `parse_json5_value` stores a non-string ARRAY verbatim, on R311y573's own
reasoning one delimiter over. Upstream's `zc_config_to_string` writes one
(`plugins_loading/search_dirs` mixes an object with strings) and it was the
ONLY leaf of 116 in a default document this parser refused.
* `braces_balance` becomes `delimiters_balance`, counting `[` and `]` on one
shared depth so `[{"a":1}` cannot pass as complete.
* `ConfigState::render` answers an INTERIOR path with the subtree beneath it,
re-nested and compact, as upstream's `get` does. Without it a key read out of
a nested document would be unreachable at its own path.
* `NestNode::write` takes a `Layout` (`Indented` for the document, `Compact` for
one value) — one writer, because the structure is what must be decided once.
THE READER (`crates/wz-session-core/src/json5.rs`)
* `Json5Value::to_json5_text` — the inverse of `parse`, compact, escaping through
the workspace's one JSON escaper.
* `Json5Value::leaf_entries` — the walk carrying its values. `leaf_paths` is now
expressed through it. A caller holding only paths must re-look-up with `get`,
which splits on `/`, so a flat key resolves to nothing; the first draft of the
C door did exactly that and refused a document it had just parsed.
* `wz-runtime-tokio` re-exports `json5`, on the `keyexpr_canon` precedent.
THE INSTRUMENT (`crates/wz-integration-tests/tests/zenoh_c_config_document_oracle.rs`,
new; run-ci Layer C1cc)
* ONE C probe, compiled once, linked against wz's cdylib and the real
`libzenohc.so`. Documents are written by each arm and read by BOTH, so the
four directions are a product rather than a list.
* Corpus: upstream's own `Z_CONFIG_*` defines out of `zenoh_constants.h` (12, ten
multi-segment). Witness values are DISCOVERED by asking the reference library
which rung of one generic ladder it accepts AND reads back differently from
that key's default; a key with no such rung FAILS rather than skipping.
* Expected values come from each library's own direct insert, so no
cross-implementation assumption about spelling is made.
* The reader-door population is derived from `zenoh_commons.h` and compared
against the set the probe reports driving. A config declaration this file
cannot classify is a failure.
TWO GATE HOLES THIS ROUND FELL INTO, CLOSED HERE
(`crates/wz-integration-tests/src/lib.rs`)
* `compile_zenoh_c_example` passes `-Werror=implicit-function-declaration`. The
probe called `strdup` (POSIX, hidden by `-std=c11`), the compiler implicitly
declared it returning `int`, the pointer was truncated and the wz arm
segfaulted — which read as a wz ABI defect. The helper discards every
diagnostic on a successful compile, so a warning there is invisible by

contract, and the two implementations could not read each other's.

`zc_config_to_string` is a drop-in door: a program calls it and hands the text
to `zenohd -c`, to a peer linked against the real zenoh-c, or back to its own
`zc_config_from_str`. wz emitted the FLAT key map its `ConfigState` stores
(`{"connect/endpoints": [...]}`) where upstream emits a NESTED document, and
nothing in this tree compared the two — measured before the change, `grep -rn
zc_config_to_string crates/` found no test and no lane touching it.

THE ITEM'S OWN CITATION WAS REFUTED, and that changed the verdict. It quoted
upstream's output as `{"mode":"client","connect":{"endpoints":[...]}}`; that is
the DOC EXAMPLE at `~/zenoh-c-ref/src/config.rs:259`. The real output, measured
by loading `~/.local/lib/libzenohc.so` 1.10.0 and calling the door, is zenoh's
whole `Config` serialized — 2,916 bytes across 116 leaf paths, most of them
`null`. So byte identity with upstream is not merely unmet, it is UNREACHABLE:
`ConfigState` holds only what a caller inserted and models no schema. The
contract the two sides CAN be held to, and the answer to the item's completion
condition (2), is MUTUAL READABILITY: each side's document is read by the other
with every value arriving intact.

The second measurement decided the item's completion condition (3), which asked
whether emitting nested breaks "put back what you took out". It does not, and
the reason is that upstream's own path keys are a QUERY OVER THE TREE rather
than a document spelling — upstream emits nested AND answers
`zc_config_get_from_str("connect/endpoints")` through the nesting. The pair that
actually round-trips is document-to-document; `zc_config_insert_json5` never
consumes a whole document and was never the other half.

The third measurement is why this did not close in one place. The item named ONE
door. Deriving the document doors from upstream's cbindgen header gave SIX, and
`zc_config_from_file` carried its own copy of the line scanner `zc_config_from_str`
used — two parsers that had already drifted. That file door is where a `zenohd -c`
configuration arrives, and every such document is nested, so fixing only the door
the item named would have closed the item and left the sharper half broken.

Upstream also REFUSES the flat spelling outright (`Z_EPARSE`, measured), so the
two document surfaces were mutually unreadable in both directions, not one.

Round 2305.decision_summary:
R2305 (open-debt item 642, CLOSED) — the config store is the document's LEAF
SET, so the two ways a caller can state the same config stop being two configs.

Upstream holds a TREE and its `/` keys are queries over it, so
`zc_config_insert_json5(cfg, "connect", "{\"endpoints\":[…]}")` and the same
value at `connect/endpoints` build one config, and
`zc_config_get_from_str("connect/endpoints")` answers either — measured on
`libzenohc.so` 1.10.0. wz's `ConfigState` kept whatever key it was HANDED, so
the object went in as one opaque entry at `connect` and nothing answered the
leaf beneath it.

THAT IS NOT A MISSING CONVENIENCE. `session.rs`'s open path reads
`cfg.first(CONNECT_KEY)`, which IS `connect/endpoints`, so a program upstream
configures correctly opened a wz session with no endpoints and connected
nowhere — with `Z_OK` at every door it called.

THE SECOND FACE, and it decided the shape of the fix. R2303 left this crate
with TWO json5 value readers: the document doors used
`wz_session_core::json5::parse`, while the insert door used a hand-rolled
half-parser. The hand-rolled one was LAXER, and the difference was not
academic — measured at the real schema key `timestamping`, where key validity
is not the variable:

    value                 upstream insert   wz insert   wz to_string   wz re-read
    {"enabled": true}           0               0            0             0
    {enabled: true}             0               0            0             0
    {enabled: bare}          -128               0            0            -2

`{enabled: bare}` is not json5 — an identifier is a key spelling, never a value.
Upstream refuses it AT THE DOOR; wz accepted it, emitted it into a document, and
then refused its own output. That is item 636's failure shape still alive
through a different door.

So the two halves are one fix: hold the document as its leaf set, and hold the
values in the reader's own type. There is then no second representation for the
doors to disagree about and no second grammar for them to disagree about.

WHAT THIS COST, and it is the point rather than a side effect: 155 lines of
`parse_json5_value`, `render_stored`, `bracket`, `delimiters_balance` and
`unquote`, plus the `StoredValue` / `Spelling` pair they existed to fill, are
DELETED. Every one of them existed only because the store held text rather than
values.

R2306 (open-debt item 156, CLOSED) — `_anyke` had three readers, only two were
ever compared, and the third was WRONG.

The item recorded the duplication: `wz-capi-pico`'s `reply_keyexpr_is_covered`
was folded onto the workspace SSOT at R311y833 and `wz-capi-c`'s twin was left
standing, and `parameters_has_anyke` was a THIRD parser beside session-core's
and pico's. Re-measuring it — which is what the round discipline asks for
before taking an item — found the duplication was not the whole of it.

THE THIRD PARSER SPLIT THE SELECTOR PARAMETER LIST ON `&`. zenoh's separator is
`;` (`commons/zenoh-protocol/src/core/parameters.rs` @
`LIST_SEPARATOR: char = ';'`, read at the pinned checkout), and
`Parameters::reply_key_expr_any` is `contains_key("_anyke")` over that split
(`zenoh/src/api/selector.rs` @ `fn reply_key_expr_any`). So the flag was found
ONLY when `_anyke` was the entire parameter string. `_max=5;_anyke` read as
absent.

The consequence is not cosmetic. `parameters_has_anyke` feeds the reply-coverage
gate on BOTH sides of the C ABI — the responder's `QueryMarshal` and the receive
path in `crate::get` — and `_anyke` is the querier's explicit opt-out of that
gate. A querier that asked for any-key replies alongside any other selector
parameter had those replies DROPPED, silently. wz's own GETs emit exactly that
shape: `wz-runtime-tokio`'s history selector builds
`_max=2;_time=[now(-30s)..];_anyke`.

WHY NOTHING SAW IT, and this is the part worth keeping: the crate's own test
asserted `a=1&_anyke&b=2`. It was written from the code beside it rather than
from zenoh, so the parser and its test agreed with each other and with nothing
else. Two readers were compared; the third had only itself.

THE TWO SURVIVING READERS ARE DELIBERATELY DIFFERENT, and collapsing them would
be the mirror of this defect. zenoh splits on `;` and takes everything before
the first `=` as the key, so `_anyke=true` CARRIES the flag; pico's byte scan
requires `_anyke` to end the list or precede `;`, so `_anyke=true` does NOT.
`wz-capi-c` mirrors zenoh-c, whose queries are zenoh's `Query`; `wz-capi-pico`
mirrors pico. Each ABI follows its own reference, which is why the answer is
"exactly these two" rather than "exactly one".

R2308 (open-debt item 641, CLOSED) — a deferral now has an END, and the

THE MISMATCH, named: DEPTH IS STATIC and rule (14)'s reason is DYNAMIC. A
chain's depth never falls, because `@from:` is written once and stays; an
item past `reaim_cap` is past it forever. But the thing the cap defends
against is a round chasing its own residue while older debt sinks, and that
danger expires on its own once other rounds have run on other chains. The
hold therefore needs a clock, and the unit of that clock is rounds.

WHERE THIS DIVERGED FROM THE ITEM'S OWN PRESCRIPTION, twice.

(1) The item proposed "let the census SAY so when DEFERRED has been
non-empty for N rounds". Saying is not a procedure: it leaves the judgement
with a person, which is exactly the defect being paid. So this round went
further — the census DERIVES the expiry, prints a RELEASED line ABOVE the
critical line, and puts the lifted item at the FRONT of the take order.
Rule (14)'s "first candidate" is now the line a round actually reads.

(2) A hold's start date is NOT the parent's round. `@from: n` means "the
round paying n created this", but that round may have filed the residue
without managing to close n — which leaves the parent open and undated
forever. The walk therefore climbs to the nearest ancestor that is CLOSED
and carries a round stamp. The control group for this is the sharpest one
in the round: stopping the walk at the parent turns 13 of the 33 selftest
arms red, because the fixture's item 19 sits between 20 and its dated
ancestor precisely to be an open, undated parent.

deliberate anchor, because item 639's own title listed the axis names and a
whole-header scan read it as claiming both rankings at once. And giving an

only thing stopping a round from raising the frontier to dodge the whole

CLOSED ONES INCLUDED -- and the lineage of a closed item is history nobody

LINEAGE still refused, RANKING now welcome.

  * A ranking cannot be used to dodge anything. Ranking an item makes the
    unranked count SMALLER, which is the direction rule (12) already wants,

frontier, a whole-header scan outside inline code would call ZERO of them

Open-debt item 645 — hosted Layer Ewirez was red: the Z64 extension-body
witness panicked in 0.17s with "the stock querier got no reply", at
`crates/wz-integration-tests/tests/zenoh_ext_body_foreign_witness.rs:429`,
on run 33737007770 (`e90cf264`, a commit that changed one ledger JSON).

THE CONDITION, FOUND RATHER THAN GUESSED. The item forbade closing this as
"intermittent", and it is not. Both foreign example families print their
readiness line BEFORE the call that declares: upstream
`~/zenoh-ref/examples/examples/z_queryable.rs:28` prints "Declaring
Queryable on" and calls `declare_queryable` on line 30, and zenoh-pico's
`vendor/zenoh-pico/examples/unix/c11/z_queryable.c:107`, `z_sub.c:71` and
`z_querier.c:72` print theirs above the matching `z_declare_*`. That line
therefore proves the declarer's SESSION is open and NOTHING about the
router having registered anything. A querier that dials the router
separately can arrive first; the router finalizes the query against an
empty route at once, the one-shot prints no reply and EXITS, and the test
reads a lost race as a routing failure. The hosted capture is exactly that
shape: z_get printed "Sending Query" and nothing else, while z_queryable
had printed only its intent line.

WHY IT NEVER REPRODUCES LOCALLY, MEASURED. On this host the window closes
before the querier's process spawn finishes: 15 rounds of a probe that
waits for the marker and then queries were answered on attempt 1, 40 of 40
attempts; the test passed 10/10 plain, 10/10 under `taskset -c 0`, and 6/6
under six spinners pinned to the same core. So `taskset` — the memory's
standing suggestion for this class — is NOT the condition here, and load is
not either. The condition is an ORDERING, and it was reproduced by
constructing it rather than by hoping for it.

WHY NOT A SLEEP. The window is a scheduling quantity, not a duration. A
sleep long enough for the bad case is dead time in every good one and still
guesses. The fix polls the condition.

THE POPULATION, DERIVED. The pairing that creates the window is a foreign
DECLARER plus a foreign QUERIER in one test, read out of the
`*_binary("...")` resolver call sites: 9 tracked files. Nine spawn sites in
four of them believed a single attempt. The tree already held the right
prescription, written once and inline, at `wz_to_zenohd_router.rs`'s pico
z_get leg ("a query fires once — so retry the whole one-shot until a reply
lands"); it had never been lifted.

WHERE THIS PARTED FROM THE ITEM'S PRESCRIPTION. The item said the fix must
be a gate that polls for readiness. It is, but a bare attempt count would
have been an escape hatch: some legs MUST ask once — a deny leg, where an
absent reply is the finding, and a leg that counts exactly how many queries
its queryable saw. So the single-attempt form carries its reason in the
TYPE (`QueryAttempts::Once { because }`) and the compiler requires it,
rather than a comment nobody checks.

* ext_qos on the API plane — already paid, by R311y801, and paid EXACTLY:

THE DEFECT. `LinkstateForwarder::propagate_current_interest` is wz's
counterpart of those hats, and it chose between the two API-plane builders by
mode: `build_interest_liveliness_subscriber` for CurrentFuture,
`build_interest_liveliness_get` for Current. The first arm was therefore right
BY ACCIDENT — it inherited a stamp that R311y801 applied for the api plane —
and the second went out bare, where every upstream hat writes the ext. One
builder cannot be right for both planes, because the planes disagree.

THE FIX IS A THIRD BUILDER, not a stamp at the call site. `build_interest_
propagated` names the plane it serves and stamps unconditionally, so the
CurrentFuture arm's correctness becomes a decision instead of an inheritance,
and the api-plane builders keep the DEFAULT that mirrors upstream. Applying the
stamp one layer lower — in the shared `build_liveliness_token_interest` — would
have been the cheap edit and is exactly wrong: it makes wz uniform where
upstream is not. That direction is a control group below, not an argument.

WHY NOTHING COULD SEE IT. Three independent reasons, each of which alone would
have been enough. The builders live in `wz-session-core` and the propagation in
`wz-runtime-tokio`, so pre-push gate 3 (changed-crate tests) never puts them in
one run. The propagation is behind the NON-DEFAULT `routing-interest-pending-gc`
feature, so the default build does not compile it. And the seam's own witness,
`a_brokered_interest_reaches_the_upstream_and_withholds_the_clients_final`,
COUNTS FRAMES — `frame_count == 1` is true of a copy carrying anything at all.

`QOS_DECLARE` is the byte applied and it is upstream's INTEREST value:
`QoSType::INTEREST` and `QoSType::DECLARE` are both `Priority::Control` with
`CongestionControl::Block`, since `DEFAULT_INTEREST` and `DEFAULT_DECLARE` are
the same variant. The names differ upstream, the byte does not, and wz holds
one constant for the byte.

Round 2317.decision_summary:
R2317 closes unregistered open-debt item 647 ("a root-less upstream citation is
invisible to the anchor gate, and 49 of the hidden ones are wrong at the pin").
Every number the item wrote re-measured EXACTLY -- which is unusual here -- and
the round still diverged from its prescription in four places, three of them
found by measurement rather than by reading.

THE DEFECT, in the item's own terms. `upstream_citation_anchor_gate.py` anchors
its path pattern at a repository root (`io|commons|zenoh|plugins`), and it has
to: without that anchor it matches from the MIDDLE of a longer path and reports
fragments that never existed, which cost 34 false findings of a measured 334
when the gate was first written. The price of the anchor is that a citation
written WITHOUT its root is not ANCHORED, not LINE, and not BARE. It is
INVISIBLE: counted in no budget, never reaching the resolution arm, and
therefore unable to go red however far upstream moves away from it. Measured:
172 such occurrences over 49 files, while the gate printed "407 upstream
citation(s) across 1166 tracked file(s)" as though that were the population.

WHERE THE ROUND DIVERGED FROM THE ITEM, four places.

(1) "49 wrong" WAS A FLOOR. The item checked whether the file exists and
    stopped there -- it did not apply the past-EOF check the gate ALREADY had.
    Re-measured: 49 root-less citations name a file that is gone at the pin AND
    46 more name a line past the end of a file that still exists (1.5.0 line
    numbers on files that have since shrunk: `hat/router/queries.rs:1426` where
    the pin holds 559 lines, `hat/router/mod.rs:812` of 642,
    `hat/client/token.rs:276` of 253). Ninety-five, not forty-nine.

    The round pays the 49 and RATCHETS the 46, and the split is a judgement
    worth stating rather than a convenience: a path that is gone leaves no
    reading of the sentence true, while a stale line number on a live file is
    the ordinary rot the LINE form was always going to suffer -- which is why
    the ROOTED population has a budget rather than an amnesty. The root-less
    population arrives with a backlog because nothing had ever graded it, so it
    gets the same instrument: `ROOTLESS_STALE_LINE_BUDGET = 46`, checked in BOTH
    directions, so the backlog can only shrink and a NEW stale line reds. Filed
    as item 650, because it is a different defect with a different repair
    (re-point a path vs. drop a line number and choose a needle).

(2) THE POPULATION WAS ONE SEGMENT OF FIFTY. The item scoped its claim to
    `hat/`, and that scope was honest about itself. But deriving the class
    structurally -- the directory COMPONENTS of the root-anchored citations this
    tree already writes, minus this tree's own directory names, minus the known
    roots -- proposes 50 candidate segments, and 38 of them carry 736 root-less
    occurrences beyond `hat`: `net` 134, `dispatcher` 80, `unicast` 77, `api`
    57, `zenoh-protocol` 43, `zenoh-codec` 40. So the residue is now a NUMBER
    the gate prints every run and a ratchet that can only shrink
    (`ROOTLESS_UNDECLARED_BUDGET = 736`), not a sentence in a register. Filed as
    items 649 and 652.

    The derivation is PIN-FREE on purpose, so the completeness arm runs in the
    FORM arm too -- the one every hosted C0 job runs. A residue graded only
    where a checkout exists is a residue graded almost nowhere. The looser rule
    was tried first and is wrong: keeping only "not a directory of this tree"
    yields 80 segments and 203 tokens matching no upstream file, and almost all
    of that is not upstream at all (SCE's `sce-build/...`, this repo's own gate
    fixtures `alpha/...` and `beta/...`, `OUT_DIR/...`). The component rule
    admits none of them.

(3) ADDING `hat` TO `_PATH` -- the item's first suggestion for condition (1) --
    IS THE WRONG DIRECTION, and the item's reassurance about it answered a
    different risk. It was right that the lookbehind keeps a root-anchored
    citation from being counted twice. What it missed is RESOLUTION: a root-less
    path is not a path relative to the checkout root, so `<ref>/hat/...` does
    not exist and the resolution arm would report all 172 as "gone at the pin",
    including the 123 that name a live file perfectly well. Hence a SEPARATE
    axis whose location is derived from the pin (`rootless_locations()`, a glob
    that requires the directory to be UNIQUE and answers None -- a hard FAIL --
    when it is not).

(4) THE ITEM'S TARGET MAPPING WAS REFUTED. It guessed "p2p_peer -> client-ish,
    linkstate_peer -> mesh peer, since that was 1.5.0's split". Measured at the
    pin: 1.10.0 unified BOTH peer hats into ONE `hat/peer`, which selects
    between them with a `Gossip`/`Network` enum, and gossip left the hat layer
    entirely for `net/protocol/gossip.rs`. `TreesComputationWorker` went to the
    ROUTER hat. The vanished-symbol list is longer than the item's two:
    `schedule_compute_trees`, `egress_filter`, `local_peer_qabl_info`,
    `declare_token_interest`, `insert_target_for_qabls`,
    `send_sourced_subscription_to_net_children` and `propagate_locators` are all
    gone as names, so a repair had to re-read what each sentence CLAIMS, not
    substitute a path. The item said as much for two of them and was right to.

A CLASS THE ITEM DID NOT SEE, and the reason the next round is ordered.
Some citations name a path BECAUSE IT IS GONE -- "1.10.0 folded the old
`lowlatency/tx.rs` into the transport", "1.10.0 replaced the flat
`zenoh-transport/src/shm.rs` with `common/shm/`", "there is no
`multicast/close.rs` with special logic". Those sentences are TRUE, and
repairing them into a resolving anchor would make them FALSE -- the repair
runs backwards. The gate has no declared form for "this path must NOT exist at
the pin", so declaring the segments those sentences live under would red true
prose and leave "raise the budget" as the only exit, which is exactly the move
item 647 forbade. Filed as item 651 and marked CRITICAL: it BLOCKS 649, and at
least 17 of 649's 22 wrong-today citations are this class. R2317 sidestepped one
instance in `declare_ext_qos.rs` by naming the hats instead of the paths, and
records that as an evasion rather than a repair -- that measurement was taken
against `49c8a53`, which is no longer the pin, so a path there could never
resolve and should not be written as one.

THE CONTROL GROUP FOUND ONE OF MY OWN GUARDS DEAD. Six new guards, mutated one
at a time. Five red as written. The sixth -- the row asserting that adding
`hat` to a pattern must not double-count the `hat/...` INSIDE a root-anchored
citation -- stayed GREEN with the lookbehind deleted, because its fixture used
the ANCHORED form and `scan` MASKS anchored spans before the root-less passes
run. The inner segment was invisible either way. Re-cast on the LINE and BARE
forms, which are not masked when those passes see them, it reds. This is the
gate's own doctrine turned on its author: a guard whose fixture cannot reach the
branch has not tested it.

ALSO REMOVED, deliberately: a first draft carried a "every DECLARED segment must
also be DERIVED" check. It is the wrong direction and it is gone. The derivation
exists to PROPOSE segments nobody declared; a declared segment need not have a
root-anchored citation, since citations written WITHOUT a root are the whole
point of the axis. What validates a declaration is the PIN, via
`rootless_locations`, not this tree's prose.

Round 2322.decision_summary:
Item 649's closing condition could not reach zero and R2322 replaced it.
The diagnosis in the item was right and both of its prescriptions were
refuted by measurement.

The old rule: a segment could enter `ROOTLESS_SEGMENTS` only if the pin
carried it as a UNIQUE directory, because `rootless_locations()` resolved
the SEGMENT to one place and every citation under it inherited that
answer. Seven residue segments are not unique at the pin (`net` 2, `api`
3, `transport` 2, `core` 3, `common` 5, `shm` 3, `client` 2), so 271 of
731 occurrences -- 37% -- were permanently undeclarable and the item's
own closing condition could never be applied to them.

The item proposed two repairs and this round measured both before
choosing. (1) A declared segment -> location TABLE: refuted, because
`api` alone resolves into TWO pin directories, so one declared location
must be wrong for one of its citations; a table would also be a second
copy of upstream's layout, which `rootless_locations` says it will not
keep. (2) A LONGER PREFIX as the declaration unit: refuted, because 149
of the 271 name a file sitting DIRECTLY under the ambiguous segment, so
there is no longer prefix to lengthen to; it covers `net` and nothing
else.

What was actually wrong was WHERE uniqueness was demanded. A segment
makes no claim; a CITATION does. So the location is now derived per
citation across every directory the pin gives the segment, and exactly
one of them must hold the file. The refusal did not weaken -- it moved
onto the claim. Measured over the whole 731: 658 resolve under exactly
one, 56 exist under two and are refused per occurrence with "write it
with its root", 17 exist under none and are the ordinary gone finding.
Every occurrence therefore has a route out of the residue -- declare it,
root it, or mark it `@ REMOVED` -- which is a condition that reaches zero.

The item also recorded that a declaring round must choose between moving
its citations to anchor form and declaring a new baseline, and that the
gate "cannot draw the distinction mechanically". It can. A declaration
CONSERVES the sum of the three root-less numbers (one leaves the residue
and arrives in a bucket) while a newly written citation raises it, so
`ROOTLESS_TOTAL_BUDGET` tells them apart whatever the individual budgets
were set to. A declaring round now moves three numbers and leaves the
fourth alone, and that is the proof rather than a sentence in a commit.

questions, and move its resolution from FILES to FIXTURES.

still exactly 110 across that movement, which is the shape of a per-file budget

Both halves the item named are real, and they are NOT the same size:

The file resolution also made the gate's STATED contract false. "A new spawning
fixture with no freshness check RAISES the number -> red" cannot hold when the
number counts files: a fixture landing in a file the corpus already holds moves
nothing, and 110 of 131 files were uncovered, so that is where a new fixture

bidirectionally, and the route classes are DERIVED from structure rather than

status". The route is read with the freshness call's own argument masked, so
whether a fixture CHECKS cannot change which class it is IN.

What the file resolution had right is kept as printed context rather than as the
gate: one edit in a shared helper covers a file's fixtures (R311y840), so the
FILE count predicts edit cost while the FIXTURE count states exposure.

Round 2326.decision_summary:
Unregistered open-debt item 10 said no mechanism measures a FOREIGN ORACLE's
staleness -- `zenohd_binary` / `zenoh_pico_cli_binary` pick the file up if it
exists -- and prescribed comparing against the vendored submodule's HEAD.
Re-measuring first, per the standing rule that an old item's reasons go stale,
found the item HALF PAID and half UNDERSTATED, and both halves changed what
this round built.

PAID, so this round does not rebuild it. R2240 already closed the zenohd
family with `scripts/lib/oracle_pin_gate.py`: it derives its population from
`build-zenohd.sh`'s own `INSTALL_DIR=` assignments and reads each binary's
`--version`. That is a STRONGER axis than the item prescribed -- the binary's
own answer rather than a claim about it -- and it was written after the SHM
oracle was found the expensive way, a lane GREEN against v1.5.0 for months
after the pin moved to 1.10.0.

UNDERSTATED, which is where the work was. The item named two resolvers; the
resolver layer resolves SEVEN `target/…` oracle roots. The two it did not name
are `target/mbedtls`, whose headers EVERY pico drop-in compile needs, and
`target/zenoh-pico-build`, whose CMake-generated `config.h` is what the pico
ABI layout probe measures against. Naming a resolver is "who noticed", never
the population.

The decision this round had to make is WHY the pico oracles could not simply
join the zenohd mechanism, and the answer is measured rather than argued:
`strings target/zenoh-pico-cli/z_put` finds no version, `readelf -d` reports
libzenohpico.so's soname as the unversioned `libzenohpico.so`, and the
submodule they came from is at `1.9.0-10-g3b3ab65c` -- a state no release
number names at all. An oracle that CANNOT ANSWER has to be GIVEN a record.
So the item's own prescription is honoured for these roots (the comparison
target is the submodule's state) by a provenance STAMP, while the roots that
can answer keep the stronger reading they already had. One class, two
mechanisms, because the oracles differ in what they are able to say.

carry_forward_bullets: Open-debt item 10 stays CLOSED; this entry corrects HOW, not WHETHER.
THE LESSON, and it is about the shape of the verification rather than the
code: Round 2326 verified the LIBRARY and not the PROVISIONER. Every control
group invoked `vendored_oracle_stamp_root` by hand, which is the function the

unmatchable. A control group over one's own new function is the most permissive
possible control group; the discriminator has to reach the PRODUCTION CALLER,
which here meant running the real script.
That is a sharper instance of a rule already in this workspace: the control
group belongs on the door the product actually opens. Round 2326 read that
rule as "the surface the gate reads" and satisfied it for the GATE, while the
STAMP's production caller went unexercised. Two mechanisms shipped in one
round, and only one of them got a real caller.
THE SECOND LESSON: this round's own library documented "the record must not
change the thing it records" and the round still walked into it, because the
warning was written about the STAMP's LOCATION (do not put it inside the
digested tree) and the hazard was in the TOKEN's TIMING (do not take it while
a transient modification is in effect). A hazard note phrased about one axis
does not cover its sibling axis, and the phrasing is now widened in that file.

provisioner that PATCHES its source, the oracle's source state is
`checkout AS COMMITTED + recipe`, not the checkout at any moment. The recipe
half is not defensive padding -- without it, editing a patch changes the
binaries under an unchanged token, which is exactly the class item 10 names.
Any future provisioner that transforms its checkout inherits this: use
`vendored_oracle_recipe_token`, not `vendored_oracle_git_token`.
`build-sce.sh` patches nothing and correctly keeps the plain form.

provisioner's stamp matches what a consumer recomputes" has no instrument.

builds the oracle, then runs consumers with `WZ_PICO_REQUIRE=1`);
`install-mbedtls.sh`'s stamp has no such witness at all. Before filing this as
a debt item, derive its population -- how many provisioner/consumer token
pairs exist -- rather than filing the one instance that hurt, which is the

changes_bullets: `scripts/lib/vendored-oracle.sh` — two functions added.
`vendored_oracle_recipe_digest <file>...` is `git hash-object` over the files'
bytes concatenated in the order given, so the Rust side reproduces it by
reading the same files in the same order; git stays the only dependency.
`vendored_oracle_recipe_token <checkout> <file>...` is
`<checkout token>-<recipe digest>`. Both carry the measurement that forced

leftover patch and the patches this script applies begin on the next line, so

The stamp is still WRITTEN only after the install succeeds; computing early
and writing late is the whole shape: the token describes the source state, the
write attests that the build worked.

Round 2326b.decision_summary:
A CORRECTION to Round 2326, filed as its own entry because the frozen ledger
is not rewritten. Round 2326's verification section is accurate about what it
ran and INCOMPLETE about what it had not: every gate and every control group
passed, and then the FIRST RUN OF THE REAL PROVISIONER left a correct, freshly
built oracle reading STALE.

The defect was in this round's own mechanism, and the reason is worth the
entry. `scripts/build-zenoh-pico-cli.sh` PATCHES four vendored examples in
place (`z_put.c`, `z_sub_attachment.c`, `z_queryable.c`, `z_get.c`), builds,
and reverts them in a single `EXIT` trap. Round 2326 took the provenance token
beside the STAMP WRITE, which sits after the install and therefore INSIDE the
window where those patches exist. So the token folded them into its dirty
digest, the trap then reverted them, and the recomputed token no longer
matched: `…-a65f49a9…` stamped against `…-e69de29b…` wanted, permanently.

That is the "the record changes the thing it records" trap this round's own
library documents for `target/` — met in a variant it did not anticipate, with
a deliberate transient modification in place of a build artefact. The library
had the warning and the round still walked into it, which is the part worth
carrying: the warning was written about the STAMP's location and the hazard
was in the TOKEN's timing.

The repair is not to move the write later. Writing after the trap would stamp
on any exit including a failed build, which is the exact lie the "AFTER
success" rule exists to prevent. The repair is to say what the source state of
such an oracle actually IS: the checkout AS COMMITTED, plus the RECIPE that
transforms it. The patches are not submodule state -- they are derived from the
script's own text, deterministically, on every run.

Folding the recipe in also closes a hole the naive reading would have left,
and this is the half that makes it a correctness fix rather than a timing one:
with only the checkout in the token, EDITING a patch would change what the
binaries embody while the token stayed put -- a stale oracle passing, which is
the very class open-debt item 10 is about. Round 2326 would have shipped a
mechanism blind to the one edit most likely to invalidate these binaries.
