2326 had only ever invoked the stamp library directly, so it had verified the
library and not the provisioner. The real run printed
`pin = 3b3ab65c…-a65f49a9…`, and the verdict against the recomputed token came

against the recomputed token. `--test pico_abi_option_layout -- --ignored`
gives `running 1 test` … `1 passed` with NO warning and NO refusal printed,
which is the cross-language check: had the Rust token differed from the
shell's by a byte, it would have said STALE and named both.
REPAIR CONFIRMED, backwards -- the recipe half is what a control group has to
bite on, since the timing half is only provable by the forward run above.
Inserting ONE comment line into `build-zenoh-pico-cli.sh` reds the lane, and

UNCHANGED. So the two halves are independently readable and the recipe half is
what moved; a token carrying only the checkout would not have moved at all.
Reverted, and the baseline returned (`1 passed`).

Round 2327.decision_summary:
Unregistered open-debt item 11: several `_runci_guarded_test` calls run the
SAME cargo-test filter under DIFFERENT feature unions, and no lint requires
their asserted counts to be consistent with each other. Re-measuring the item
first, per the standing rule that an old item's reasons go stale, changed both
the population and the mechanism.

THE PREMISES, re-measured. The item's two named groups are BOTH still live and
one of its numbers had rotted: `--lib multicast_glue` still has FOUR sites
(C1q 23/27/29 + C1AX 26, exactly as claimed), while `routing_forward` still
has two but asserts 61/62, not the 29/30 the item recorded. The item also
understated the population by a factor of six: the structure holds THIRTY-SIX
groups with two or more sites, the largest with nine. Two named groups is who
noticed, not the population.

THE PRESCRIPTION IS REFUTED, and that is this round's substance. The item asked
for a lint requiring a group's members to move BY THE SAME DELTA, hedging that
"both cases were +4, so same-delta is the first thing to try -- but two points
are not a design". The hedge was right and the rule cannot exist: a test added
to the module is either unconditional, in which case every site moves, or
`cfg`-gated on a feature, in which case ONLY the sites carrying that feature
move -- legitimately, which is the entire reason these groups hold different
numbers. A same-delta rule reds the ordinary case, so it would have to be
suppressed there, and a rule suppressed on the ordinary case is not a gate.
"Did they all move" fails identically.

WHAT IS DERIVABLE is the FEATURE LATTICE, and it is strictly better than what
was asked for: it needs no base revision, no build, and no diff. Enabling a
feature can only compile tests IN, never out, so within a group a strict
feature SUPERSET must not assert a LOWER count than a subset (47 comparable
pairs), and two calls selecting identical cases must agree (3 pairs).

That it catches the history is checked against the real numbers rather than
asserted. `C1q` base is `{transport-multicast}` at 23; `C1AX` is
`{transport-multicast, routing-namespace}` at 26, a strict superset, so the
invariant requires 23 <= 26. Before R311y772 the pair was 19 and 22; that
round raised the subset to 23 and left the superset at 22, and 23 > 22 is
exactly a violation. The check the item could not formulate is the one its own
history demands.

WHY THIS IS NOT `count_guard_lint.py` AGAIN, measured rather than assumed.
That lint checks a guard's number against the tests the SOURCE defines, and
its own summary states its limit: of 305 guards, 111 are statically checked
and 194 are OUT OF SCOPE, almost all because `#[cfg]` makes the set
feature-dependent -- the hook comment beside it calls that list "honest and
also the hole". The lattice reaches the hole precisely because it derives no
count at all; it relates the hand-written numbers to each other, and
feature-dependence is what makes them relatable. Of the 47 pairs here, 45 have
BOTH sites in that out-of-scope set, and 53 of the 56 constrained sites are.
Near-disjoint by construction, and neither instrument subsumes the other.

carry_forward_bullets: THE LESSON, and it is the same one two rounds running, which is why it is worth
stating as a rule rather than an anecdote: A CONTROL GROUP OVER CODE THE ROUND
JUST WROTE IS THE MOST PERMISSIVE CONTROL GROUP THERE IS.
R2326 verified the stamp LIBRARY with six control groups and never ran the
provisioner; the provisioner had a `trap` that made the scheme unmatchable, and
hosted charged three jobs. R2327b then wrote a check for exactly that class --
and its FIRST version compared the stamp against the variable that wrote it, so
its own control group returned green. Two rounds, two instruments, one failure
shape: the thing being checked and the thing doing the checking shared a source.
The structural fix is the transferable part. Do not pass a VALUE to a verifier
when the caller computed that value; pass the RECOMPUTATION and let the
verifier run it. `want` and `have` must have independent provenance, or the
comparison is a tautology wearing a diff.
THE SECOND LESSON: a hosted red can cost three jobs and buy NOTHING. This one
reported a defect whose fix was already committed and pushed, because the run
was queued against the pre-fix commit. That is not an argument against
push-and-continue -- the fix landed faster than the run finished, which is the
policy working -- but it IS the argument for a local instrument: the value of a
signal is what it tells you that you did not already know, and this told
nothing while charging full price.
RESIDUE, stated: the shell verifies the shell. The Rust consumer must produce a
byte-identical token, and nothing DIFFS the two implementations -- they are held
together by both being run on a real tree and agreeing, which is evidence and
not a gate. Building that gate would mean a third reader of the token format,
which is the open-debt item 47 shape this mechanism has twice declined; if it
is ever wanted, the honest form is one implementation invoked from both
languages, not a comparison of two.
changes_bullets: `scripts/lib/vendored-oracle.sh` — two functions.
`vendored_oracle_assert_fresh <root> <label> <recompute-cmd> [args...]` reads
the stamp on disk and compares it against a token the CALLER'S COMMAND
produces. An unestablishable token is not a failure (the provisioner already
left the root unstamped for that case); a STALE or UNSTAMPED verdict is, and
the message names the likely cause by construction -- a token taken while a
transient source edit was in effect, which is R2326's defect stated as a
diagnosis rather than left to memory.
`vendored_oracle_release_token <installer> <var> <prefix>` re-reads an
installer's `VAR="${VAR:-…}"` default out of the file, which is byte-for-byte
the route the Rust consumer's `mbedtls_pinned_token` takes. It exists so the
mbedtls assert has an independent `want` too.
`scripts/build-zenoh-pico-cli.sh` — after stamping, calls
`restore_pico_example_patches` EXPLICITLY and then asserts both roots. The
explicit restore is load-bearing rather than belt-and-braces: the example
patches are still applied at that point (the `EXIT` trap has not fired), so
recomputing there would see the dirty tree and mis-match a token correctly
taken from the committed shape. The call is idempotent by design -- it is the
same function the top of the script runs for the same reason -- and the trap
stays as the failure-path net.
`scripts/install-mbedtls.sh` — asserts on BOTH paths, the fresh install and
the idempotent early exit, since the latter is the only one that ever visits an
already-correct prefix.

`target` component, run both ways: at HEAD it yields rc=2 and the hosted

ancestor named `target` is somebody else's decision; `CRATES` is

THE POPULATION WAS DERIVED, not guessed. Every `InterceptorContext`
implementation in the tree -- two production, one mock -- and both production
ones read the SAME `peer_zid_routing(&face.actions)`. So "which governed faces
can be subject-less" reduces to "when does that one function answer `None`",
which is a question with an answer rather than a survey.

FIVE STEPS, EACH MEASURED IN THE TREE:

  1. the InitSyn's zid is stored VERBATIM -- `*slot = Some(body.zid.as_slice()
     .to_vec())` -- with no session-layer validation;
  2. `Zid::try_from` REJECTS an empty / all-zero / oversized slice, so
     `peer_zid_routing` answers `None` for such a peer;
  3. `register` inserts the face UNCONDITIONALLY, with `link: None`; and a
     Client-tier face has no graph link in any case, so for a client the zid is
     used for nothing except this enforcer's subject;
  4. a governed Request reaches that face through a client-tier fan-out whose
     builder is `|id, _zid|` and discards the zid -- `fan_out_tier` does not
     skip a zid-less face, it delegates to each builder, and four builders take
     `_zid`;
  5. `intercept` admits on the missing subject, before `policy.decision` is
     called -- so wz's own `link_protocols` / `interfaces` axes are unreachable
     for that face too.

THE DOC THAT LOOKS LIKE A DEFENCE IS ABOUT SOMETHING ELSE. `peer_zid_routing`
says a face whose zid is absent or rejected "is held WITHOUT a routing identity
(it routes nothing)". True -- of the GRAPH: no link is added, no flood fires.
A client face never had a link, so that sentence constrains nothing on the plane
this enforcer governs. Reading it as coverage is the mistake this round nearly
made and the reason step 3 is written out.

AND THE JUSTIFICATION POINTS AT A BRANCH UPSTREAM CANNOT REACH. The comment on

Upstream derives its subject from the transport it governs, and every governed
multicast face there is a per-peer face -- both anchored in the atom now. So
upstream has no unattributable governed transport, and "we do what zenoh does"
describes a case zenoh never takes.

verification_bullets: THE DERIVATION, in the order it was taken, each step a command against the tree
rather than a reading of the residual:

production and one mock, and both production ones are one line:
`peer_zid_routing(&self.face.actions)`. That is what collapses the question

* `peer_zid_routing` = `actions.peer_zid().and_then(|b| Zid::try_from(b).ok())`,
and `Zid::try_from` rejects empty / all-zero / oversized. So None means

between the wire and that slot.

builder and let it decide. FOUR builders take `_zid` and discard it; the
client-tier query fan-out is one of them, and Request is a governed kind.
* `intercept` admits before `policy.decision`, so `link_subject()` is never
consulted for such a face.

open-debt item 655 is CLOSED by repairing the ENFORCER's early exit, not by

The defect: `AclInterceptor::intercept` answered an unresolvable subject
ITSELF -- `let Some(subject) = ctx.subject() else { return true; }` -- so a
peer that presented an all-zero zid at INIT was exempt from every ACL rule,
a wildcard `SubjectSelector::Any` deny included. The zid is stored verbatim
from the peer's own INIT body and nothing on the way to the slot validates
it, so the exemption was a state the PEER could choose. That is what made it
a security defect rather than a corner case.

The repair: `AclPolicy::decision` now takes `Option<&Zid>`, and the absent
subject takes the SAME four decision steps as any other request rather than
a fifth of its own. `SubjectSelector::Any` does not READ the subject, so it
matches an absent one; `SubjectSelector::Zid` NAMES a peer, and an absent
identity is not that peer. Fed through the deny-first / default / allow-narrow
order, that pair is fail-closed in BOTH directions: a wildcard deny reaches
the unattributable face, and a zid-targeted allow does not rescue it from a
default-deny policy.

WHERE THIS DIVERGED FROM THE PRESCRIPTION, stated rather than hidden. The
entry offered three repairs: (1) reject a malformed zid at the session layer,
(2) DENY rather than admit an unattributable message, (3) stop a zid-less
face receiving anything. This is a refinement of (2), and deliberately not
(2) as written: a blanket deny would make a face that has merely NOT FINISHED
ITS HANDSHAKE undeliverable under any policy, which is a different and worse
fix. Routing the absent subject through the rule set instead means an
unattributable request that matches no rule lands on the configured default.

PARITY, measured against the pin by direct read rather than from memory.
Upstream cannot reach this branch at all: its zid is validated at CODEC
DECODE (`commons/zenoh-codec/src/core/zenohid.rs` @
`ZenohIdProto::try_from(&id[..size])`, which goes through `uhlc::ID`'s
`NonZeroU128` and returns `Err` for an all-zero slice), so a transport with
no valid identity never opens. Where upstream comes CLOSEST -- an `authn_ids`
that matches no subject entry -- it leaves the verdict at the configured
default rather than admitting
(`zenoh/src/net/routing/interceptor/access_control.rs` @
`let mut decision = policy_enforcer.default_permission`). So this is not a
divergence from upstream: it is what upstream would do if it could reach the
branch.

THE ROUND DID NOT CLOSE ITS ATOM, and that is the finding rather than a
shortfall. `liveliness-history` stays PARTIAL; the axis stays at 83.

The prompt's own rule anticipates this: "고른 atom 이 닫을 수 없는 것으로
드러나면 그것을 기록하고 다른 atom 으로 옮겨라." This entry is that record.

## Why it cannot close under either condition

The atom has exactly ONE clause left, and it reads: "only REMOTE tokens are
replayed -- locally held tokens are replayed by neither upstream either, so
replaying them here would be divergence, not a fix."

Condition (2) is DISPROOF BY MEASUREMENT. It fails because the measurement
CONFIRMS the clause rather than refuting it. Measured three-sided at the pin,
by direct read:
  * zenoh replays `state.remote_tokens` only (`zenoh/src/api/session.rs`
    @ `let known_tokens = if history {`);
  * zenoh-pico iterates `zn->_remote_tokens` only and carries its own
    `add support for local tokens` todo above that iterator;
  * wz iterates `peer_token_table` only.
All three agree. wz is at parity, and "fixing" this would be divergence.

Condition (1) is CODE PLUS A TEST THAT REDS WHEN REVERTED. It fails for a
sharper reason, and the round PROVED the failure rather than assuming it: the
exclusion is STRUCTURAL. `LivelinessSubscriberRegistry` holds no local tokens
and cannot reach them, so there is nothing to implement and nothing a
mutation inside the replay can break.

## The probe that settled it, and why its weakness is the result

A control mutation was written to make the replay emit an extra local-looking
token. It reds the CONTROL test and NOT the guard -- because
`replay_known_tokens` returns early on an empty `peer_token_table`, which is
exactly the state the guard sets up. So the guard cannot be broken from inside
the replay at all.

That is a REGRESSION FENCE, not a mutation-provable guard, and the test's own
doc now says so in those words. It would red against a FUTURE wiring of the
two registries -- which is worth having, since they sit side by side on one
struct -- but it is not evidence that anything but the type system defends the
exclusion today, and it must not be cited as such.

## What this leaves for the owner

An atom whose last clause is a TRUE parity statement fits neither closing
condition as written. Moving the tag on the strength of that sentence is
exactly the trap named when the unit changed, so this round did not move it.
Whether "the clause is true and describes parity" should itself be a third
closing condition is an OWNER decision, not one to take by retagging.

Both halves are now code. `bind_unixsock` performs upstream's `new_listener` order step for step (`io/zenoh-links/zenoh-link-unixsock_stream/src/unicast.rs` @ `let lock_file_path = format!("{path}.lock")`): open `{path}.lock` O_CREAT at mode 0600, take an exclusive NON-BLOCKING flock (`io/zenoh-links/zenoh-link-unixsock_stream/src/unicast.rs` @ `FlockArg::LockExclusiveNonblock`), and only then unlink the socket file and bind. It returns a new owning `UnixsockListener`, and `BoundListener::Unixsock` carries THAT instead of a bare `UnixListener` — so the production `bind_locator` seam is arbitrated, not only the primitive the e2e harness calls. `UnixsockListener::close` is the `del_listener` counterpart (`io/zenoh-links/zenoh-link-unixsock_stream/src/unicast.rs` @ `async fn del_listener`), and `Drop` runs the same teardown, which is STRONGER than upstream's registry-only lifecycle: an early return or a panic no longer leaks a socket file.

THE DISCOVERY: FOLLOWING UPSTREAM EXACTLY WOULD HAVE SHIPPED A RACE. Upstream's `del_listener` also unlinks `{path}.lock` (`io/zenoh-links/zenoh-link-unixsock_stream/src/unicast.rs` @ `let tmp = remove_file(lock_file_path)`). `flock` binds to an open file DESCRIPTION, not to a path, so that unlink reopens the very window the lock exists to close — a process that opened the lock file before the unlink keeps locking the now-unlinked inode, while the next arrival's `O_CREAT` makes a DIFFERENT inode at the same path and locks that one. Two holders, one path, and the second is free to unlink a live socket. wz therefore RETAINS the lock file, and the divergence is measured rather than argued: `zenohs_lock_file_unlink_reopens_the_stale_window` drives BOTH orders through ONE helper and reports 2 holders under upstream's and 1 under wz's. Retaining is invisible to upstream, which opens its lock file `O_CREAT`.

WHAT THE CLAUSE SAID, AND WHAT WAS BUILT. wz rebuilt the whole Digest from the stored set on every publication cycle (`build_digest` over `latest` chained with the wildcard registries), so a replica's digest cost grew with its store on a fixed `interval_ms` timer, where zenoh has kept an incrementally-updated log since it had a digest at all (`plugins/zenoh-plugin-storage-manager/src/replication/log.rs` @ `pub struct LogLatest`, read off by `plugins/zenoh-plugin-storage-manager/src/replication/log.rs` @ `fn digest_from`). `ReplicationLog` is now that structure: `(interval, sub-interval)` buckets whose fingerprints are XOR-maintained by the write that changes them, rolled up into eras only at digest time. The publication cycle no longer walks the store.

THE PROPERTY THE SWAP TRADES AWAY, AND WHAT REPLACES IT. A recompute cannot be stale — it reads the authoritative state every time. A maintained structure can be, and the way it goes stale is that a write path is added and does not tell it. Two things answer that. `replication_digest` debug-asserts maintained == recomputed on EVERY call, so every test in this tree that writes and then takes a digest is a witness; and `scripts/lib/replication_log_funnel_gate.py` derives the digest's source fields from `replication_event_stream` (the storage's own definition of what the digest is a function of), takes the population to be every `&mut self` method naming one, and requires each to name the log. Measured: 3 sources, 3 write paths. `build_digest` survives as the second derivation rather than as dead code — two derivations that must agree are worth more than one that cannot be wrong.

THE DERIVATION FOUND A WRITE PATH THE CLAUSE DID NOT NAME. The obvious reading of "maintain the digest" is "hook the two `latest.insert` sites". The digest has THREE sources, not one — R2351 made the wildcard registries replication events — and the third mutator is the GARBAGE COLLECTOR, the only path in this storage that removes an event outright rather than replacing one. Nothing drove it with a digest in play before this round. A sweep that dropped registrations without telling the log would leave the replica advertising a fingerprint for wildcard updates it no longer holds: a divergence manufactured by the collector, which no peer could ever resolve.

WHERE THIS DIVERGED FROM ITS OWN PRESCRIPTION. The module's first justification for carrying an event COUNT beside each fingerprint was that a cancelled bucket would otherwise vanish from the hot map. A control probe REFUTED it — pruning on a zero fingerprint produces the identical digest at that instant, because `build_digest` filters a zero fingerprint out anyway, and the probe came back green. The count is load-bearing for a different reason, one transition later: two events with the same fingerprint (a wildcard put and a wildcard delete on one keyexpr at one timestamp) cancel to zero while both are present, and a bucket dropped there has nothing to XOR out when one of them is re-issued, so the survivor's fingerprint leaves the digest permanently. The doc now says that, and `a_cancelled_bucket_must_still_give_its_events_back` is the case that reds the probe. The first-written justification was wrong and is recorded as wrong rather than quietly replaced.

claim in them independently, and repair four defects found while doing so.

THE SUBSTANCE. zenoh sets TCP_NODELAY inside each link family's SHARED
dial+accept constructor, so every TCP-backed zenoh link runs with Nagle off in
both directions. wz applied the same tuning at each CALLER of its shared connect
primitive, and two of the four callers never took the step: `dial_ws` and
`dial_tls` both dialled with Nagle ON, while the accept half was uniform because
tcp/ws/tls all accept through `accept_tcp_on`. The divergence was therefore
DIAL-ONLY and scheme-specific. The tuning moves INTO
`iface_bind::connect_tcp_bound`, so every TCP-backed wz dial is tuned by
construction; `dial_tcp_host`'s unbound arm, the last dial-side `TcpStream`
producer outside that primitive, now walks the same resolved list through it.

Separately, `accept_bound_on` took a `&TcpListener` and was the last seam in the
tree that forced a listen endpoint down to tcp: the same `ws/...` string worked
on `--router` and on the one-shot `--listen` and failed at BIND on
`--storage-host`. It now borrows a `BoundListener` and runs the same two steps
its two siblings do, so `BoundListener::into_tcp` -- whose own doc had asked to
be retired once `accept_loop` was generalized -- is DELETED rather than left
unused.

WHERE THIS DIVERGED FROM WHAT WAS HANDED OVER. Four repairs, each measured:

1. THE NEW GATE'S ESCAPE HATCH WAS WIDER THAN ITS OWN SENTENCE. The opt-out
   marker was matched against `f["raw"]` -- the WHOLE FILE -- while the constant
   beside it called it an "in-body opt-out". One marker anywhere would have
   exempted every producer in that file. The gate's own selftest ENCODED the
   leak (it expected two exemptions where one item was marked). Scoped to the
   item's own comment block plus body.

2. THE ROUND'S OWN UPSTREAM CITATIONS WERE GRADED BY NOTHING. They were written
   in the crates.io REGISTRY layout (`zenoh-link-ws-<version>/src/..`), which
   matches none of the pin's declared top-level roots, so they landed in NO
   bucket -- not anchored, not line, not bare, not even a root-less candidate.
   This is the identical shape the citation gate's own comment records for
   `zenoh-ext/..`: twenty-four citations, all correct, graded by nothing. Eight
   were converted to the anchored repo form.

3. A LINE WRAP SILENTLY DEMOTED FIVE OF THOSE TO `bare`. The anchor tolerates a
   comment leader between the path and the `@`, but not between the `@` and the
   needle. Breaking after the `@` cost the anchored form, and `BARE_BUDGET` sits
   exactly on 60, so it would have red the gate.

4. THE REWRITTEN `accept_bound_on` DOC ADDED A BROKEN DOC LINK. It carried three
   `[`accept_bound`]` links -- public doc to a private item -- where the old doc
   had two, putting the crate one over its C1bz budget. The links are repaired
   to code spans, which is what this tree prescribes for an item that cannot be
   linked; the budget then FOLLOWS the links down.

The judgement running through all four: a gate is only worth what its most
permissive path allows, and a citation is only worth something if something
grades it.

THE FINDING THAT SHAPED THE ROUND, and it made the work SMALLER rather than
larger: the oracle already exists. `upstream_citation_anchor_gate` is already
version-anchored and needle-based, already carries the owner's 2026-09-01
decision that upstream claims take no line numbers, already has the `@ REMOVED`
marker for a path cited BECAUSE it is gone, and already refuses to resolve
against a checkout that does not declare the pinned version. Nothing in that
list needed building. What was missing was a POPULATION.

That gate skips three prefixes, one of them the store, for a reason written
beside the constant: the LEDGER quotes citations verbatim, so scanning it would
grade frozen history. That reason is correct and it covers `changelog_entries`.
It does NOT cover `inventory_entries[*].reason` -- the live impl-axis verdicts,
prose that is REWRITTEN on every re-grade. The store itself proves the
distinction: one reason carries `CORRECTION (R311y440): ... no longer exists;
the method is at ...`, which is an edit to a verdict, not a record of one.

So the round did NOT widen `SKIP_PREFIXES`, which would have swept the frozen
ledger in and started demanding repairs to entries that must not change. It
reaches the reasons through the inventory mapping, so the ledger stays out BY
CONSTRUCTION rather than by a promise.

WHERE THIS DIVERGED FROM THE PRESCRIPTION. The brief said to build an oracle and
warned that a result of 0 would mean it had read nothing. The opposite risk is
the one that materialised: a naive oracle produces a LARGE and confident number
that is almost entirely false. Every aggregate rot count this round produced
dissolved on individual inspection, four separate times and for four different
reasons -- claims resolved against a version they never declared (87% of the
population declares 1.5.0 while the tree pins 1.10.0); a capability that MOVED
rather than died; a citation that names a path deliberately, to say it is gone;
and a regex sweeping ordinary prose. The hard part of this instrument is not
detection, it is not crying wolf, so its verdicts are five-way -- judged, moved,
deliberately-dead, unjudgeable-here, rotten -- and only the last is a defect.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE HERE. The ten unresolved claims are not repaired
in this commit. Three are ordinary citation defects with their repairs already
derived and their needles verified at the pin; each is a surgical edit to a long
reason blob through `set-inventory-status --reason`, which replaces the whole
prose, so each belongs in its own commit with its own before/after. The other
SEVEN are not citation defects at all -- they are STALE GRADINGS across five
atoms, and repairing them means re-grading those atoms against the pin. The
budgets are therefore seeded at what the command PRINTED, which is the shape
this tree already uses for inherited debt and the reason the instrument lands
green instead of landing red and being disabled.

was silently untrue.

subscription record has no history bit to gate on and cannot behave this
way. Where the two references disagree, the side that keeps
`history = false` truthful is the one worth being.

Round 2361.decision_summary:
THIS ROUND SET OUT TO CLOSE `transport-link-serial` AND DID NOT. It says so
plainly, and it also paid a red the PREVIOUS round pushed.

The intent was a closure: the atom's "STILL PARTIAL" sentence names three
clauses, and two of them were expected to fall to measurement. They did.

  1. THE `SerialTarget::Pins` CLAUSE IS REFUTED, AND IT DESCRIBED PARITY.
     It debits wz for refusing a GPIO pin-pair target on the host tty
     backend. zenoh has no pins concept at all -- not one occurrence of
     pin, gpio or uart in its serial link. zenoh-pico HAS one, and its
     POSIX backend implements it as a pure refusal that discards all four
     arguments and returns invalid. wz does the same thing and slightly
     better, with a typed Unsupported carrying a reason. Refusing is
     correct on BOTH references; this was never a gap.

  2. THE FOREIGN-WITNESS CLAUSE IS STALE. It says the witness composes its
     acceptor by hand instead of through the seam. It goes through
     `accept_endpoint`, and the test's own comment records the move. The
     clause was written in the round that fixed it and never updated --
     a correction landing in one copy and not the other.

  3. THE MESH CLAUSE IS REAL, and it is why the atom stays PARTIAL.

WHAT MADE 3 BIGGER THAN IT LOOKS, and the reason this round scoped instead
of building. Two claims sit inside it and only one is a gap.
ONE-PEER-AT-A-TIME IS PARITY: upstream serialises too, spinning on a shared
flag until the previous link drops before re-opening, and wz's own doc is
right to say so. REFUSING THE LISTEN OUTRIGHT IS NOT: a zenoh router can
listen on serial and serve successive peers, while wz's mesh caller
fail-fasts at bind and a second accept parks. Conflating the two is how
this clause could be "closed" by argument, so they are now written apart.

The seam names the missing piece in its own words -- it carries no
link-liveness feedback -- which is exactly upstream's flag. Building that
is a feature, not a clause: a guard whose lifetime is the link's, reaching
through the accept enum into the wiring function and the read driver, plus
a single-face arm in the mesh loop, plus a witness that a second peer is
served after the first drops. Scoping it took reading the seam; the design
is recorded on the atom so the next round starts from a design rather than
a sentence. Starting it here would have left a half-built feature in the
tree, which is worse than a round that reports what it found.

Close the PARTIAL atom `ext-pubsub-serde-codec` by DERIVING its remaining
surface from upstream instead of reading it off the atom's own residual
prose -- and close every clause the derivation and the prose between them
name, so the tag moves because the work landed rather than the other way
round.

The pick was made after the census: the PRIORITY queue was empty and the
analyzer plane was empty, so the round took a PARTIAL atom, and it took
this one because its residual list is unusually CONCRETE -- six named
type families, a wire divergence, and two trait hooks -- which makes it a
place where "close the atom" and "close a list" can be told apart.

The first thing re-measured was the grading target. The reason grades
against zenoh-ext 1.5.0 and this tree pins 1.10.0, so every clause was a
claim about a zenoh wz no longer targets. Both checkouts are on this
machine, which was confirmed rather than inherited, and the round re-read
the pinned serialization module.

That re-reading changed one clause outright. The reason said wz's `VarInt`
reuses the protocol VLE SSOT, that the two encodings agree below 2^63, and
that the divergence point is "physically unreachable" because a Rust
collection length is bounded by isize::MAX. The first two halves are true.
The third is false, and it is false for a reason the clause states two
sentences earlier without noticing: `VarInt` is PUBLIC `Serialize` surface.
An application can serialize `VarInt(usize::MAX)` without a collection
anywhere in sight, and wz emitted nine bytes where upstream's leb128 emits
ten. The deeper error is the framing: zenoh has TWO varints -- the protocol
ZInt and the serialization-format LEB128 -- and "one varint SSOT, zero
drift" was two formats sharing one encoder. The module now carries its own
LEB128, module-private, so the protocol SSOT keeps its own subject.

The instrument is the round's real argument. A format re-implementation
owes a POPULATION, and `cargo test` structurally cannot fail on an absent
impl: an unwritten `Serialize for X` is a compile error only at a call site
nobody wrote. So the round built a gate that DERIVES both populations by
parsing the two serialization modules with ONE parser and compares eight
axes, refusing an empty population on each. The alias table is the only
hand-written part and an alias is not a skip: it names the wz counterpart
and the gate then requires that counterpart to exist.

What the derivation returned was AGREEMENT, and that is recorded as the
result rather than dressed up as a discovery. All 23 findings it makes
against the pre-round module correspond to clauses the prose already named.
What changed is that the list is now standing rather than one-shot, that an
upstream addition reds it, and that it was finally checked by something
other than the person who wrote it. The gate is not a superset of the
reason either: it grades the type SURFACE and is blind to an ENCODING, so
the `VarInt` clause stays the tests' job and the reason says so.

Close the PARTIAL atom `transport-link-unixpipe` by BUILDING the one live residual it had -- zenoh's `file_mask` locator config key -- and derive the population that residual belonged to, so the class cannot recur on the next link.

The atom was picked from open-debt item 15's track (census: PRIORITY queue empty, analyzer plane empty, CRITICAL head = item 15). THE DECISION ABOUT THE DEFAULT, which is where faithfulness and copying part. Honouring the key does not mean adopting upstream's 0o777 default: a FIFO pair in a shared directory IS the link, so that default lets any local account write frames into another user's session. wz keeps 0o600 and now makes the permissive mode REACHABLE, which is the half that was missing. The divergence is declared in the constant's own doc rather than left to be rediscovered, and the accepted SET of values is upstream's exactly -- a plain decimal `u32`, upstream's own spelling.

THE SECOND DECISION: the residual's POPULATION is not "this key". It is "every locator config key an upstream link crate declares", which upstream itself writes down in `pub mod config` blocks and which nothing in this tree had ever derived. Deriving it is what turns a fix into a gate, and the derivation immediately found a gap nobody had looked for.

Round 2364.decision_summary:
Close the PARTIAL atom `runtime-coop` by making the MCU session RIDE the
cooperative executor, which was its sole residual clause.

The residual named the obstruction as `Runtime::spawn`'s `F: Send` bound.
That framing invites relaxing the bound, and relaxing it is the wrong
repair: `Runtime: Send + Sync` is load-bearing because the AP profile
genuinely moves spawned tasks between worker threads, and the MCU bundle's
`Rc` is equally load-bearing because `alloc::sync::Arc` requires
`target_has_atomic = "ptr"` and ARMv6-M does not have it -- so making the
bundle `Send` would wall the MCU session off the very targets the `Rc`
exists to reach. Both ends are right and simply do not meet. The decision
is therefore to put a `!Send` pool BESIDE the contract rather than to
weaken the contract: `CoopLocalSet` + `spawn_local`, the shape tokio
reached for the identical problem. The `Runtime` trait is untouched.

Second decision: extract the per-iteration sequence (`SessionPump::step`)
so ONE sequence serves both drivers. Two loops over one sequence would be
two things to keep in step, which is the duplication this crate's own
module doc refuses between the AP and MCU profiles.

Third decision: the executor pass belongs to the DRIVER, not to the step.
The synchronous `run_session` still takes it because nothing else drives
that runtime; `session_task` must not, because a task that pumps the pool
currently polling it rebuilds the exact inversion this round removes.

R2366 gave every production task a subsystem to run on, and the last
step of that round -- the push -- never landed: pre-push gate 2h found

wz-capi-pico. This round is that red, paid off as its own round. It
does NOT close a PARTIAL atom, and says so rather than reaching for a
cheaper unit: the tree could not publish anything until this was fixed,
which is the priority order this workspace already declares.

The regression is R2366's, and it is a product defect rather than a
test artifact. `WriterHandle::spawn` used to spawn onto the AMBIENT
runtime, so a writer task died with its owner's runtime whatever else
was true. That gave every wz link a floor under its writer's lifetime
that nobody had to think about, and `WriterHandle`'s drop leaned on it:
dropping the handle DETACHED the writer and fell back to sender
liveness. R2366 moved the writer onto the process-wide `WzRuntime::Tx`
subsystem -- correct for the partition, and what zenoh does at the same
seam -- and removed that floor without noticing. A detached writer then
outlives its owner's runtime, an outstanding sender clone pins it for
the life of the PROCESS, and it keeps holding the link's write half. So
the socket never closes, the peer never sees the FIN, and the far side
goes on crediting a vanished peer with a matching subscriber. The
aggregate never flips again either, so a genuine later match is
suppressed as "no change".

DIVERGED FROM THE OBVIOUS PRESCRIPTION. The one-line revert to the
ambient runtime is what the control probe found, and taking it would
have undone R2366's partition to fix R2366's leak -- treating the
subsystem as the defect when the defect is the lifetime contract that
came with it. Upstream settles which: zenoh ALSO puts its tx task on a
process-wide transmit runtime, and terminates it EXPLICITLY through a
cancellation token at link close rather than by letting a runtime fall.
A shared TX pool and an implicit close signal do not go together in
either implementation. So the seam moves, not the subsystem: dropping
the handle now SEALS the queue -- finish what is buffered, then exit --
which is the RAII form of the `drain` this type already had.

The tree had ALREADY decided this question once. The multicast pumps
treat a closed stop-channel as an RAII shutdown, in as many words, and
for the same reason. `writer_queue` was the single seam that had
answered it the other way, and the disagreement only became a defect
when the ambient floor went away.

Round 2373.decision_summary:
R2373 took the PRIORITY claim (open-debt item 661) and ACCEPTED it:
`wz_dissect_live_follow` feeds a GROWING capture container into a live handle
that already exists. ABI 14 -> 15. The consumer asked for an explicit answer
either way and said it reads silence as "not yet answered", so this entry is
the answer.

The claim was re-measured before it was taken and it held: `wz_dissect_live_*`
is six doors (open, push, drain, lost, message_bytes, close), the only
container-to-handle door is `wz_dissect_pcap_replay` and it CREATES a handle,
and the Rust `LiveDissection` has the same three byte inlets the report named.
Nothing about this item had gone stale.

WHERE THIS DIVERGED FROM THE PRESCRIPTION. The item and the consumer report
specified the door's SHAPE and left its construction open, and the direct route
is a second parser that walks a growing prefix. That would put the second
reader this item exists to prevent INSIDE the library rather than outside it.
So the block walk itself moved into a resumable cursor and both whole-file
readers became callers of it: `pcapng::parse` and `pcap::parse` now run the same
`PcapngCursor` / `PcapCursor` a follower runs, with `Halt::Complete` and
`Halt::Partial` carrying the one distinction that separates a damaged capture
from an unfinished one. `LiveDissection::from_capture` likewise CALLS `follow`,
so "the frozen door and the growing door read the same bytes the same way"
stopped being a claim in a comment and became one function calling another --
and a replayed handle can now be followed as the writer appends, which neither
the item nor the report asked for and which falls out of the construction.

WHAT THE UNIFICATION FOUND. `PcapngFile::ts_millis` resolved a packet's ticks
against the interface list the FILE ENDED with, and a Section Header Block
clears that list. On a multi-section capture every earlier packet went through a
later section's `if_tsresol` -- microseconds read as milliseconds, wrong by a
thousand. It was not found by reading that function. A follower has no
"afterwards" and so had to be handed the answer where the block is read; once
one door resolved early the two disagreed, and the disagreement is what named
the older one as wrong. `Packet::ts_millis` is now the stored value and both
doors read it.

THE CONTROL PROBE CAUGHT THIS ROUND'S OWN GATE. Reverting the fix to the naive
"re-parse the prefix each window" left the every-cut sweep GREEN, because the
fixture's messages were TCP and a re-read hands the reassembler the same bytes
at the same sequence numbers, which it absorbs as a retransmission. A
stream-only fixture cannot tell the door from a re-reader. One datagram in the
fixture -- no sequence space, so a packet handed over twice is a message twice
-- and the sweep reds. The natural choice (build a straddle out of TCP, since
TCP is what straddles) was the most permissive one available.

WHAT WAS BUILT FOR THE OTHER CLAUSE. It read: "the PER-GET resolve has no witness
HERE: nothing on this host's wire mutates its permissions". That is exactly right,
and the missing piece was a CAPABILITY rather than a test. Upstream's config is a
json5 document whose admin PUT routes any pointer into the live `Config`, so an
upstream node can be told over the wire to change `adminspace/permissions/read`; wz's
typed intents had no such key, which made wz NARROWER than upstream on a key upstream
carries. `AdminConfigWrite::AdminReadPermit` adds it, and Layer E6i now drives GRANT

froze the permit into a value captured beside `get_cfg` -- precisely the defect the

than a weakness of the assertions: `get_cfg` is created inside the ACCEPT LOOP, and a
stock pico `z_get` is a one-shot process, so every GET arrives on its own connection.
A per-connection resolve and a per-GET resolve are indistinguishable to any client
this tree can drive. So what the new witness establishes is PER-CONNECTION liveness,
which is strictly more than the structural-parity argument the clause rested on and
strictly less than the clause.

The gap is not academic: this host multi-accepts and serves many GETs on one client
session, so a per-connection resolve is the frozen permit again with its scope
reduced from a process to a session. The instrument that would settle it -- a client
issuing two GETs on ONE session with a permit change between them -- does not exist
here: zenoh-pico's `z_get` takes no repeat flag and the demo's client mode emits one
Query. Registered as open-debt item 665 rather than answered with the word

R2375 took the PARTIAL atom `transport-multicast` and DID NOT CLOSE IT. It closed
the one residual clause the TREE still named, re-derived three clauses the atom's
own reason still asserts and found them stale, and struck a CI comment that had
been corroborating one of them. The atom stays PARTIAL, and the reason it stays is
recorded below rather than left for the next round to rediscover.

WHERE THE ROUND WAS AIMED, AND WHY THAT WAS NOT WHERE THE WORK WAS. The carry said
this atom's only named residual had already been refuted twice -- true, and both
refutations are in the reason: R311y772 BUILT the graceful multicast stop the
module header had deferred, and R311y789 re-established by direct read that the
"no graceful multicast.stop" clause described code that no longer exists. A third
clause, R311y772's own "WHAT REMAINS: NO PRODUCTION CALLER DRIVES IT", was closed
by R2333 and never written back into the reason. So the atom's text names nothing
live. Reading the CODE instead of the atom found one clause that IS live, and it
was in the AP module header rather than the store: "The MCU loop
(`wz_session_lwip::multicast_drive::run_multicast_session`) has no stop signal at
all yet, so it has no departure point to announce from -- that half is still open."

WHAT WAS BUILT. That half. `run_multicast_session_with_shutdown` takes a
`FnMut() -> bool` polled once per iteration; the first `true` multicasts the
departing Close (`encode_multicast_close` -- the SAME datagram the AP loop has
sent since R311y782), pumps lwIP so the datagram actually leaves, then drives
§3.1 Running -> Stopped, which clears the peer table. Until this round an MCU
member went silent on departure and every group peer held its entry until the
lease expired; now both profiles announce, and a peer frees the departing member
at once.

A PREDICATE, NOT A CHANNEL, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN DECISION. The AP twin's signal
is a `tokio::sync::watch::Receiver`, which has no `no_std` analogue and nothing to
await on in a busy-poll loop. A predicate composes with whatever the deploy has --
an ISR-set `AtomicBool`, an application `Cell`, a countdown. The surface stays two
names over ONE body (`run_multicast_session` is this one with a predicate that
never fires), which is the same call the AP loop made when its own shutdown door
landed; a second copy of a busy-poll loop drifts at the first arm anyone touches.

WHERE IT DIVERGES FROM THE PRESCRIPTION. The obvious shape -- arm the predicate on
the e2e's existing drive -- is wrong, and measurably so: that e2e reads
`active_peers` off the dispatcher AFTER the loop, and a stop folded into that
drive clears the peer table before `peer_admitted` can witness it. So the shipped
caller departs in a SECOND phase, and every round-trip signal keeps meaning what
it meant. The unit witness is two-phase for the same reason the AP one is.

WHAT IT IS PROVEN BY. Three unit tests over a real lwIP loopback group, each with
its control probe run and read: dropping `dispatcher.stop()` reds the FSM/peer
assertions and nothing else; dropping the Close send reds exactly the two wire
assertions; moving the stop poll below the `max_iters` check reds exactly the
precedence test and no other. A fourth probe (`|| false` at the shipped caller)
reds the e2e's `departed` assertion. And Layer Q.6 boots the departure ON-TARGET
on mps2-an385 / an386 / an500 -- the MCU profile takes its last §3.1 transition on
the CPU it ships on, not only on a host.

WHY THE ATOM STAYS PARTIAL. Its module header still carries "Not yet here:
`MulticastOutcome::LinkLost` -- the MCU poll loop has no link-loss event". That is
a residual of this atom by the cfg-site rule (the module is `transport-multicast`
gated), so COMPLETE would be a claim the tree contradicts one screen above the
code this round wrote. `audit-catalog-status.sh` reads the same before and after,
which is the honest number.

functional multi-node proof is "OPT-IN Layer M (WZ_RUN_LAYER_M=1, ci.yml:457-460
deliberately not wired)". R311y421 wired Layer M onto the hosted `interop` job
with `WZ_M_REQUIRE=1`, which makes every SKIP path in it fatal; Layer A4's own
EXECUTION lines now list `M` for both the pico and zenohd adjudicator families.
The companion clause -- the pico multicast interop being `--skip`'d out of the

present tense, "NOT wired here, deliberately: Layer M (multicast)" -- in the very

METHOD NOTES worth carrying:

A clause list is not a mechanism list. Three of this atom's four residuals were ONE pico function, and that was invisible from the clause text -- it took reading `_z_open` and both of its arming sites. Prefer reading the upstream FUNCTION a clause cites over enumerating the clauses.

pico's failover is scout-branch-ONLY. A round that "adds multi-locator failover" to a configured client would be building a shape upstream does not have, which is the R2332 trap. The asymmetry is the specification.

An accumulator with no reset is a reconnect hazard: `ScoutingActions::scouted_hellos` grows, so any per-attempt re-use of one binding silently answers the new window with the old window's peer. Check for a reset before reusing any discovery state across a reconnect.
A test whose acceptor half only completes on success HANGS on regression instead of failing. Bound it. The first control probe here hung, held the build host, and had to be killed.
A cfg-gated enum variant is a dead-code error waiting for the build that omits its only constructor. Passing the operation (a closure) instead of naming it (an enum arm) avoided it and is more open.

Round 2376.decision_summary:
Close the PARTIAL atom `session-reconnect` by retaining the reopen PLAN instead of a resolved address, and by letting a lost multicast group face re-join.

PICK, DERIVED NOT CHOSEN: `debt_plane_census.py` reported PRIORITY queue EMPTY (rc=0), which REFUTES this run's brief -- it opened by naming a standing PRIORITY claim as the first round's subject. With the queue empty the census names the next take itself: CRITICAL item 15, the PARTIAL atom track. Inside that track the atom was derived by residual-clause count over every inventory entry whose reason starts PARTIAL, then read before picking.

THE FINDING THAT SHAPED THE WORK: the atom's four residual clauses are not four things. Reading pico rather than the clause list shows `_z_client_reopen_task_fn` re-enters `_z_open`, and that ONE function is where three of them live -- its no-locator branch scouts again and loops the answering Hello's locators, and its multicast twin `_zp_multicast_failed_result` arms the SAME task. So "no re-scout" and "no multi-locator failover" are one mechanism, and pico's failover exists ONLY on the scout branch (the config branch opens locators[0] and returns its error). wz's gap was structural: the supervisor retained the ADDRESS the plan had resolved to, where pico retains the PLAN.

The fourth clause is refuted rather than built, and by measurement: the backoff knobs exist and the flat default is deliberate pico parity. Its sibling `router-connect-reconcile` had already closed the identical clause at R311y789 while this copy never followed -- the debt-47 shape, recorded as refuted rather than quietly dropped.

DESIGN. `ReconnectTargets` is injected rather than an enum: the scouting arm needs `scouting-active` and a bound socket, so a cfg-gated variant would put the supervisor's own shape behind a feature flag. Failover deliberately does NOT go through `open_session_static` -- the atom's own entanglement note warns that it has no production caller, and building there would have repeated the R311y503 shape. It goes through `--scout --reconnect`, which already shipped and already re-dialed one discovered address forever.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT CLAIMED: the re-joined group face replays nothing, because that loop has no declaration cache -- the per-peer declaration plane is `router-multicast-faces`' deferred I3 milestone, not this atom's residual.

Also pays R2374's unpaid A4 red (the foreign-adjudicator pin), which was attribution-complete but unfixed, so this round does not push onto a known red.

`declare-keyexpr` CLOSED -- PARTIAL 62 -> 61, COMPLETE 79 -> 80. Both surviving clauses closed, and they closed as ONE seam because on this one message the mapping bit does not exist.

THE PICK WAS THE MILESTONE'S, AND THE MEASUREMENT MOVED IT. The clause said "build_declare_kexpr hardcodes the declared wireexpr scope to 0, so wz can only declare literal-rooted mappings and has no _nonlocal sibling". Read as an instruction that would have meant BUILDING AN EMITTER. The R2384 dead-code test says otherwise on both halves, and what was actually missing turned out to be somewhere else entirely -- inbound, in a place the clause did not name.

(1) THE `_nonlocal` HALF IS REFUTED BY THE WIRE, not by taste. D_KEXPR's header has no M bit: its flag module declares N at 1<<5 and Z at 1<<7 and comments 1<<6 as reserved, and the WireExpr codec DROPS `mapping` on write and reads it back as the default. So "upstream's field is a full WireExpr with scope and mapping" is true of the STRUCT and false of the WIRE -- a `_nonlocal` DeclKexpr builder would emit BYTE-IDENTICAL bytes. `declare_build.rs` had argued this from the pico side since R121i-d; the protocol settles it structurally.

(2) THE OUTBOUND SCOPE HALF IS REFUTED BY PRODUCER COUNT. Neither upstream ever writes a non-zero scope on a DeclareKeyExpr. zenoh has exactly two producers: the api-level prefix declarer writes `scope: 0` literally, and the routing one builds its WireExpr through `impl From<String>`, which pins `scope: 0`; the namespace interceptor rewrites only the SUFFIX. pico has two, and both leave the id null. wz emitting scope 0 is byte-identical to both, and a scoped EMITTER would have put wz ALONE on the wire -- the fourth round running where the useful output was stopping a wrong build.

(3) AND THEN THE FINDING, which no clause named: BOTH DECODERS RESOLVE A NON-ZERO SCOPE, IN OPPOSITE SPACES. zenoh leaves the decoded mapping at `Mapping::DEFAULT`, which IS `Receiver`, so `register_expr` reads the RECEIVER's `local_mappings` -- ids WE declared. pico decodes the same field with `remote_mapping` true and stamps the peer token, so it reads `peer->_remote_resources` -- the SENDER's. The two upstreams DISAGREE with each other, and the wire has no bit to settle it. wz's generated decoder pins the `WireexprLocal` arm because there is no bit 6 to derive it from, which is pico's answer -- so a zenoh-shaped scope resolved to NOTHING here.

(4) BUILT, and this is where the mapping-bit clause closes too. `resolve_declared_keyexpr` consults BOTH spaces for this one message and answers only where they cannot disagree. R311y771's retraction of the mapping-bit clause for the two sibling atoms -- "the two arms ARE the bit by construction" -- does NOT transfer here, which is the R2377 lesson arriving a second time: on D_KEXPR the arm is a decoder constant and there is no bit for it to be.

`domain_census.py` had two arms. Both iterate the BUNDLES and derive each

13 / routing 9 / transport 5) and was structurally blind to 40 across EIGHT
namespaces. The tally printed "3 carried / 0 new" over a population that
excluded 40 atoms by construction.

That is "a population drawn from the checker's own definition can never
fail" -- the same shape as the `--census` leg that may not be

OR-contributor. It had reached this file too, and 72 rounds ran past it.

Round 2388.decision_summary:
A ROUTER NOW TELLS A FACE THAT HAS JUST COME UP WHAT IT ALREADY KNEW.
`RouterForwarder::register` replays its subscribers, queryables and tokens to
the new face, unsolicited. Open-debt item 671 is closed for the router
forwarder; the peer forwarder is scoped OUT with a measured reason.

THE DEFECT, and how it hid. Every proactive push in `router_forward.rs` is
triggered by LEARNING: an inbound declaration arrives on one face and is
forwarded to the others (`push_future_subscription` and its two siblings).
Reading every caller of those three shows the same shape and no exception --
there was no face-up trigger anywhere. So a peer that connected AFTER a
declaration was learned only ever heard about it by ASKING.

AND THE PEER THAT MATTERS DOES NOT ASK. zenoh-pico's `_z_add_interest`
(`vendor/zenoh-pico/src/net/primitives.c`) writes on the wire only when the
session is a client, has a router peer, or is multicast; in PEER mode over
unicast against a non-router it registers the interest LOCALLY and satisfies
it from `_z_interest_replay_declare`, which sits OUTSIDE that condition and
reads declarations the remote PUSHED. pico can afford that because pico
pushes -- `_z_interest_push_declarations_to_peer` runs on accept. Against a
wz router that never pushed, such a peer's publisher write filter never
learns a matching subscriber exists and suppresses its Puts silently, which
is the failure `response_sink.rs` already calls "SILENT in exactly one
direction".

BOTH UPSTREAMS DO THIS AND NEITHER THE SAME WAY, measured at the pin. pico
pushes to every accepted peer. zenoh repropagates on a new transport face
(`new_transport_unicast_face` -> `repropagate_subscribers` / `_queryables` /
`_tokens`), emits `interest_id: None`, and gates it on the face being
north-bound.

THREE PRESCRIPTIONS WERE WRITTEN AND TWO WERE REFUTED BEFORE ANY CODE. (1)
"implement pico's accept-time push" -- refuted: the unstamped emitters already
exist here. (2) "call those emitters at face-up" -- refuted: they select
targets from the FUTURE-interest store, so a peer that stored no interest
receives nothing. (3) "synthesise an interest for the new face, as zenoh does
with INITIAL_INTEREST_ID" -- refuted by wz's own invariant: the future stores
admit a CLIENT face only and refuse a match-all target on purpose ("match-all
(target None) is not stored (current-dump parity)"). Each refutation came
from reading the mechanism rather than from running into it.

WHAT SURVIVED is the shape this file already had for the same problem.
`re_advertise_self_cross_tier` exists "so a late-joining child converges on
self's full cross-tier bubble"; the new function is that, with the trigger and
the destination changed from a new tree child to a new FACE. It reuses the
three derived accessors unchanged, and the queryable arm carries the MERGED
`derived_cross_tier_qabl_info` so a late face is told what a late tree child
is told rather than a default a later merge would contradict.

SCOPED OUT, WITH THE MEASUREMENT: `LinkstateForwarder` does not get this.
Its known-set accessor (`subscriptions`) is gated on
`adminspace-introspection-handlers` rather than general, it keeps interest
tables rather than the derived cross-tier sets, and it has no token pusher at
all -- so the port is a different derivation, not a copy. Saying which
forwarder was done is part of the claim.

answer is unanimous by default rather than chosen between references.

THE DECISION THIS ROUND MADE IS THAT THAT WAS NOT A CLOSURE, BECAUSE THE PATH COULD NOT RUN. Read end to end before claiming the residual, the shipped code was inert in three independent ways, and the three compose into one lesson: a feature whose only production caller is a demo is a feature no unit test can reach, so its correctness rests entirely on a lane, and there was no lane.

(1) The demo built its STRIP PREFIX out of the SUBSCRIPTION PATTERN — `format!("{write_key}/")` where `admin_config_write_key` already ends `/**`. `parse_admin_config_write` does `keyexpr.strip_prefix(write_prefix)`, which then never matches, so every PUT decoded `NotAWrite` — an outcome whose handler arm is correctly SILENT. The two sibling hosts spelled the same prefix by hand from `admin_config_key` and got it right; the third built it from the pattern and got it wrong. Nothing in the types relates the two shapes, and the round's own unit tests could not catch it because they pass the prefix as a `const` literal: the demo was the only caller that had to DERIVE it.

(2) The router-hat's admin permissions were built `{ read: !no_admin_read, ..Default::default() }`, and that `Default` is `write: false` (zenoh's `PermissionsConf`). `--config-write-permit` is parsed for `--peer` and `--storage-host` and reached no router-hat field, so the gate was shut and no flag could open it. Because the permit is checked BEFORE the prefix strip, this defect masked the first one.

(3) `derived_cross_tier_subs_into` documents itself as the SET form of `self_advertises_sub_into` — "a K is in this set IFF that predicate holds, same sources". The round added the host-sub contributor to the PREDICATE and not to the SET. The register-time flood therefore reached members already in the mesh, and the tick re-advertise that serves LATE joiners silently omitted host subscriptions, so a publisher behind a child that connected after registration had no route and dropped its Put. The `register_local_subscriber` doc comment asserted both halves were covered and named the wrong derive.

The re-measurement refuted it. wz mirrored the `messages` selector as a three-variant DownsamplingMessage {Push, Query, Reply} and carried a doc comment justifying the coarseness as upstream's own -- "zenoh dispatches at the NETWORK-BODY level, one kind per body ... the asymmetry is upstream's, and porting each faithfully reproduces it". So wz could not express "rate-limit the deletes and leave the puts alone", which the pin can, and the COMPLETE grade was recording a divergence as a port.

The round therefore BUILDS rather than re-tags, which is the difference between paying item 675 and forging it: the missing kind ships, the atom's declaration moves to the pin, and the ratchet's budget follows the measurement down by one.

THE MECHANISM, in three steps that are each individually reasonable. A control probe damages the code. `git add` is run so the remote builder can see it -- the builder sends tracked files, so probing and staging are habitually paired -- and the DAMAGE is captured in the index. The working tree is then repaired by hand, and a lane is run and passes, because the working tree is correct at that moment. Later, `git stash push --keep-index` resets the working tree BACK to the index, silently undoing the repair; the commit carries the probe's value.

leaf EXCEPT `__path__`". So the most-literal matching row wins, the
document says so, and the gate enforces both that the rule picks a row
and that no two rows tie. Merging the pair into one row was the
alternative and it loses the encoding axis, which is one of the three
questions asked.
`RecordingReply` now keeps the encoding it used to discard, which is
what makes the encoding column checkable at all.
Round 2413.decision_summary:
Item 676 (owner-designated PRIORITY head, filed 2026-09-07 from a
consumer report) asked that the adminspace surface describe itself:
which keys this build answers, what encoding each carries, and whether
a `null` means "none" or "this build does not say".

MEASURED FIRST, live, before any design — the item's own instruction,
because the reporting consumer stated it had never received a live
adminspace reply and that its encoding claims came from reading this
tree's tests rather than from bytes. A wildcard GET against a real
session, twice:

  adminspace-core only            -> 2 keys: root, config
  + metrics/introspection/plugins -> 3 keys: root, config, metrics

Both replies carried explicit encodings (root and config
application/json, metrics text/plain), and the two builds differed in
one further place the item had identified as its core: the root
document's `plugins` field is `null` in the first and `{}` in the
second. So the bytes ALREADY discriminated "this build does not report
plugins" from "this node has no plugins" — and nothing declared that,
nothing gated it, and a consumer could only learn it by reading this
repository. That is the finding the item was reaching for, and it
sharpened the claim rather than refuting it: the ambiguity was real,
and one third of it was already answered by accident.

DECISION — a new leg `@/<zid>/<whatami>/wz/surface`, answered by the
same answerer, carrying the three axes as one document.

Why a separate key and not the root document: `AdminLocalData::to_json`
is pinned byte-exact against the upstream `local_data` emitter, and the
reporting consumer had recorded that its own first candidate for the
census question — adding a key to an existing envelope — collided with
exactly this class of contract. Reading that contract confirmed it
would collide here too.

Why in-band and not a library door: the precedent the consumer named
(`wz_dissect_readable_surfaces`) is a statement about the LOCAL library,
and the build being described here is the REMOTE node's. A local door
would describe the wrong build. The census precedent's own argument
(open-debt item 554) transfers and strengthens: the answer must travel
with the document, and a wildcard GET delivers both in one query from
one node at one instant.

Why under `adminspace-core` rather than its own feature: a build that
has an adminspace but cannot say what is in it returns the consumer to
guessing, which is the defect. Self-description is part of what having
an adminspace means here.

BEYOND-ZENOH, and declared as such rather than as parity: the pin
registers no handler of this kind, so the `wz/` chunk keeps the name
out of a namespace upstream may later occupy. R2412's lesson — an
extension written up as parity is one a later reader cannot catch —
applied deliberately.

`the_manifest_describes_exactly_the_legs_this_build_answers` RUNS

THE ORDERING RULE THIS ROUND HAD TO FIND BEFORE WRITING THE CODE, and
the reason the terminator is not where the obvious edit would have put
it. OpenMetrics ends at `# EOF`, and this node appends its
transport-stats block AFTER the build-info block -- so copying
upstream's literal with its terminator into `metrics_text` would have
buried the counters behind the end of the document and produced an

appends last. Upstream never has content after EOF either: its

terminator at the end, which is what establishes it as terminal rather

into a wire format is not fidelity. Everything before it is the pin's,
byte for byte.

mentions -- because counting mentions punishes exactly the rounds that
pay the debt, since an honest re-measure must NAME the old version to
say what it refuted.

declaration to the pin in the same motion moves two axes at once.

encodings -- the surface document it built has an encoding column, and
filling that column honestly required reading what the pin actually
replies. The divergence fell out of that reading and was filed as item

rather than chosen from a list.

WHAT THE RE-MEASURE FOUND: five axes had drifted, four of them in bytes
a foreign consumer reads. Encoding (the pin's named constant
`application/openmetrics-text; version=1.0.0; charset=utf-8`, predefined
id 15 plus the remainder as schema, where wz replied text/plain, id 4);
TYPE (`info`, where wz declared `gauge`); sample name (`zenoh_build_info`,
where wz emitted `zenoh_build` -- an OpenMetrics info family named
`zenoh_build` emits its sample with the `_info` suffix, which is why the
two names differ by design); labels (`local_id` and `local_whatami`
beside `version`, where wz carried `version` alone); and the `# EOF`
terminator, which wz emitted not at all.

The encoding is the axis that matters most to the consumer that
prompted this: told `text/plain` by wz and `application/openmetrics-text`
by a real zenoh node, it had no way to reconcile the two. Id 15 is
agreed independently by zenoh's table, by zenoh-pico's, and by this
crate's own -- so this was an unused capability, not a missing one.

rather than for the field:

is that test, by name
The rest of the suite is indifferent to the wiring; only this test
speaks for it.

would prove nothing": the fixture session has no peer, so `sessions[]`

That leg is SCOPED in its own comment, deliberately: a pico client

Round 2417.decision_summary:
Take the PRIORITY head (item 675, the grading-pin ratchet) and pay it by
re-declaring ONE atom at the 1.10.0 pin -- but pick the atom by the property
the item warns about rather than by cost: `transport-multicast`, whose closing
sentence claimed an EXEMPTION from the whole exercise ("the parity target is
pico rather than zenoh -- this reason declares no zenoh 1.5.0 and so owes no
pin re-measurement").

Measure that exemption before trusting it. It is FALSE: upstream ships a
2153-line multicast transport whose subjects are exactly that atom's -- a JOIN
beacon on a `join_interval` timer, lease-driven peer expiry, a Close on
teardown, and a per-peer receive record. An atom is not exempt from one
reference because a second reference is closer to it, and an exemption is a
grading claim no instrument in this tree could object to, which is item 675's
whole argument arriving as a clause instead of as a version string.

The re-measurement is expected to produce PRODUCT, not a tag move. It did: two
sentences in the shipped code were false at the pin -- "a multicast Join
advertises no `0x7` ext and there is no per-peer Init exchange to take a
`min()` over", and, of upstream, that its marker gate reads "the manager config
rather than a per-peer negotiation". Both references carry the Patch extension
ON THE JOIN by name, and both hold the negotiated `min()` as a field of the
per-peer record. So wz's multicast RX was discarding a chain-boundary signal
that a stock zenohd or pico peer already sends unconditionally.

Build the four seams that were missing under those sentences (announce, chain
the MORE bit, decode by WALKING the chain, negotiate + arm per peer), prove them
with a discriminator that holds everything equal but the announced level, and
run every control probe rather than asserting the reverts would red.

Keep the atom COMPLETE only if the residual list is genuinely empty for the axes
it owns; file what the re-measurement opens as its own register item rather than
double-counting one gap across two atoms.

changes_bullets: PRODUCT -- wz now enforces the M (mandatory) bit on establishment extensions, which it had never done anywhere:

`crates/wz-session-core/src/ext_chain.rs` gains `reject_unknown_mandatory_ext`, which refuses a decoded chain carrying an extension the caller's known-set does not list when its M bit is SET, and accepts it when M is clear. That is upstream's rule exactly: its unknown-extension reader logs and continues for M clear and returns `DidntRead` for M set. The bit's whole purpose is that the SENDER declares whether a receiver may proceed without understanding the extension, and until this round wz proceeded either way.

It is a SEPARATE pass rather than part of `decode_ext_chain` because that decoder is carrier-blind by design: the establishment, zenoh-body and scouting chains reuse the same numeric ids for different extensions, so "is this id known" is answerable only by a caller that knows its carrier. Folding a table into the decoder would hard-code one carrier or burden every caller, and only establishment has a rule to enforce today.

`crates/wz-session-core/src/parse_error.rs` gains `UnknownMandatoryExt { ext_id }`, which names what it refused. It is distinct from `Codec` for the reason `ReservedEncoding` is: nothing is truncated or malformed -- the bytes parse and the sender has said they may not be ignored.

`crates/wz-session-core/src/inbound.rs` calls it from the `T_MID_INIT` arm, which is the single site BOTH InitSyn and InitAck reach, so the rule cannot hold for one role and lapse for the other. Upstream likewise enforces it in the codec, beneath either FSM.

`crates/wz-session-core/src/ext_header.rs` gains `REGION_NAME = 0x08` and `ESTABLISHMENT_EXT_IDS`, the recognised set DERIVED from the id table rather than retyped, so an id added to the table cannot be forgotten by the rule and start refusing an extension wz itself speaks. Recognised is deliberately WIDER than implemented: RegionName is listed precisely because wz implements nothing for it, since the question the rule turns on is whether wz KNOWS what an id means -- which is also what upstream's codec does, having a real handler so the id never reaches its unknown path.

THE SHAPE OF THAT COUPLING, measured rather than quoted:

So whether a captured sample could be REPUBLISHED turned on whether its reader had opinions about payload encodings, and a replay tool had to hand over a decoder mapping it would never read purely as a side channel.

AND REFUSAL WAS THE ORDINARY CASE, not the exception. This tree's own doc calls a capture begun AFTER the declarations "the ordinary shape of a capture taken on a running system", and in such a capture every keyexpr is named by id alone. The claim therefore does not remove the refusal path; it reduces refusal from the ordinary case to the genuinely unresolvable one.

It was four lines inside `plan()`, and that is exactly as far as it could travel: a caller holding capture times but no `Samples` -- every C consumer, which cannot build a `Samples` at all -- had to write it again.

THE WALK IS TWO COUPLED DECISIONS, not one expression, and the second is the one a second implementation gets wrong: a gap is the SATURATING difference of two capture times (a clock stepping backwards yields zero, not a wrapped enormity), and a sample with NO capture time DOES NOT RESET THE ANCHOR -- the last resolvable reading sticks, so the pair either side of a hole measures across it.

`plan()` is now one of `Pacing`'s callers rather than its only site. Feeding only the TAKEN samples into the walk is what keeps R311y703's rule true: `excluded` never reaches it, so a selector that drops the message between two kept ones still widens the interval as it should.
PRODUCT (new) -- `crates/wz-capi-replay/`: the C ABI. Five symbols, and each is a shape this tree already uses rather than a new invention.

`wz_replay_plan_delays` -- the schedule as scalars, the capture times in (`WZ_REPLAY_NO_TIMESTAMP` per entry), one `wz_replay_emission` per emission out, plus the total. A caller-owned, caller-sized buffer, exactly as `wz_dissect_live_drain` hands records, so the no-callback clause holds word for word.

`wz_replay_mutate` -- the mutation half, sized first and read second. The length comes from RUNNING the mutation, including on the sizing call: a formula predicting it would be a second opinion about `Mutation::apply`, which is the class of defect this whole crate closes.
`wz_replay_schedule_check` -- the cheap door, for validating a control surface as an operator types into it rather than when they press play.

`wz_replay_emission_layout` -- the record layout as the ARTIFACT reports it, on `wz_dissect_record_layout`'s stated reason: a layout pinned by a Rust test AND a C block is pinned twice by the same commit, so both move together and the tree agrees with itself while the ABI number stands still.
`wz_replay_abi_version` -- the number a consumer refuses a library by.

THE VOCABULARY IS MIRRORED IN TWO DIRECTIONS. Rust -> ABI is held by the COMPILER: every enum is mapped by an exhaustive `match`, so a variant added upstream stops the crate building. ABI -> HEADER is held by nothing a compiler can see, and that is what the gate below is for.

REFUSALS THAT ARE THEIR OWN CODES, not a generic one: an unnamed `timing` word and an unnamed `mutation` kind are REFUSED rather than defaulted, on the rule the command line already applies to `--timing` and `--side`. A caller who asked for a pace this build cannot give and silently got the declared gaps would believe they were replaying the capture's own timing.

`WZ_REPLAY_ERR_PLAN_TOO_LONG` STILL WRITES THE DELAYS AND THE TOTAL. That is `Plan::within`'s own stated rule rather than leniency -- the refusal is asked of the finished plan precisely so an operator who hits it can SEE what was too long, and a door answering with an error and an empty buffer leaves them a number and no listing.

Round 2441.decision_summary:
Open-debt item 693, PRIORITY head and named by the owner: `wz-replay`'s PLAN half had no C door. A consumer that links the C ABI could not call it, so it implemented the pacing judgement a SECOND time and filed a report saying so. This round opens the door: a new crate `wz-capi-replay`, five symbols, a header, and two gates.

NOT A DEFECT REPORT, and the consuming crate said so first and at length: the crate is careful, its module doc taught them the rule they would most likely have got wrong, and a CLI is a reasonable place to put it. What was reported is REACH -- that everything good about it was unreachable from where they stand.

THE CLAIM RE-MEASURED RATHER THAN QUOTED, with their own three commands:
- `grep -rn "wz-replay" crates/*/Cargo.toml` -> its own manifest and nothing else.
- `grep -rln "wz_replay" crates/ --include=*.rs` -> `crates/wz-replay/src/main.rs` alone.
- No `wz-capi-*` crate exported any of it. It is a `[[bin]]` with a library beside it that nothing links.
All three stand. So does the shape their claim rests on: `live = ["dep:wz", "dep:tokio", "dep:log"]` and exactly one `#[cfg(feature = "live")]` in `lib.rs`, so the plan half genuinely builds without the session runtime and is the natural shape for an ABI.

WHY THE ANSWER IS ONE DOOR AND NOT TWO. The report offered to split pacing from mutation and expected to file the identical report for the mutation half next. Splitting was not available: `plan(samples, schedule, MUTATION, selection)` takes the mutation as an argument, so a pacing-only ABI would have to hard-code `Mutation::None` and then change its own signature next round -- an ABI break by construction rather than by growth. Both halves ship.

WHERE THE DOOR LIVES, and the tree decided this rather than the consumer. `wz-capi-replay` is its own crate, not a door in `wz-capi-dissect`, on that crate's own manifest argument one layer up: a surface answerable to a different authority "would mean a consumer could no longer tell which half of the library it was linking against". Two mechanical consequences, either sufficient alone -- `wz_dissect_abi_version` is "the number a consumer refuses a library by", and folding a second vocabulary into it moves that number for every consumer who reads captures and will never replay one; and `wz_dissect.h` opens by calling its memory rule "the whole contract", which R2102 spent a paragraph revising for ONE exception, so a second door with its own allocation story turns that contract into a list of exceptions.

THE COST OF THAT PLACEMENT, stated rather than left to be found: a consumer wanting both halves now links two artifacts. Accepted, because the plan half shares no call, no handle and no allocation with the read half -- it takes scalars a caller already holds and answers in scalars -- so the two libraries are independent in fact and not only in name.

THE MEMORY RULE IS STRONGER THAN ITS SIBLING'S, deliberately: NOTHING crosses this boundary allocated. No strings, no handles, no callbacks; there is no free function because there is nothing to give back. That was available here and was not available in `wz-capi-dissect`, where a dissection must be kept alive between packets and a field tree has no fixed size. A promise that can be kept absolutely is worth more than one carrying an exception.

The enum set comes from parsing wz-replay's plan half; the plan half itself comes from `lib.rs` plus every `pub mod` without `#[cfg(feature = "live")]`; the constant sets come from the two files. CONTROL PROBE 4 -- the `#[cfg(feature = "live")]` removed from `pub mod live;`. FAILED, demanding a door for `LiveError`. So the live exclusion is DERIVED FROM THE CFG and load-bearing, not an accident of the filename -- and `live.rs` really does carry a `pub enum` today, so the exclusion is exercised by the tree as it stands rather than only by a probe.
